exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Teen Age Riot' — the opening track was originally named after Dinosaur Jr.'s J Mascis, a fantasy about an alternative rock revolution. Then 'The Sprawl' — inspired by William Gibson's cyberpunk novels. Thurston Moore and Lee Ranaldo's guitars are tuned to at least four different tunings across the album.

tracks.title: Trilogy" * a) "The Wonder" * b) "Hyperstation" * z) "Eliminator Jr.

synopsis: Daydream Nation (1988) is the double album where Sonic Youth turned noise into one of the most beautiful sounds in rock. The band had spent years developing their signature approach, retuning their guitars in dozens of unusual ways and playing with screwdrivers, drumsticks and other objects jammed between the strings, and on this record they finally made all that experimentation cohere into songs. 'Teen Age Riot' opens the album with one of the great opening tracks of the era, a song that seemed to promise a new kind of rock music led by the young, while 'Silver Rocket', 'The Sprawl' and the closing 'Trilogy' show the band at their most ambitious, moving between delicate melodies and torrents of feedback. Kim Gordon and Thurston Moore shared vocals, with Gordon's cool, deadpan delivery a perfect counterpoint to the noise around it. The album was a critical triumph that made Sonic Youth the most important underground band in America, and it is now heard as the bridge between the 1980s underground and the alternative rock explosion of the 1990s.

name: Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness
teaser: Smashing Pumpkins 1995 — a 28-song double album spanning 121 minutes, recorded over a year in Chicago. Billy Corgan wrote nearly 50 songs for the project. The album debuted at #1 and sold 10 million copies. The recording process was so intense that drummer Jimmy Chamberlin entered rehab shortly after completion.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to '1979' — the drum machine loop was a mistake; Corgan programmed it wrong and liked the off-kilter result. Then 'Tonight, Tonight' — the orchestra was the Chicago Symphony, recorded in an old church. Corgan demanded 35 string players; the producer thought he was insane until he heard the playback.

tracks.title: Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness
Fuck You (An Ode to No One)
We Only Come Out at Night

synopsis: Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness (1995) is The Smashing Pumpkins' sprawling double album, a 28-song, two-hour monument to ambition that became one of the best-selling records of the decade. Billy Corgan wrote nearly fifty songs for the project and recorded them over a year in Chicago, pulling together every sound the band had explored: the heavy metal crunch of 'Bullet with Butterfly Wings', the dreamy pop of '1979', the gothic strings of 'Tonight, Tonight', the industrial rage of 'Zero', the gentle balladry of 'Thirty-Three'. The album was conceived as a journey through a single day and night, and its mood shifts constantly, from triumph to despair and back again. It went straight to number one and sold over ten million copies, making the band one of the biggest in the world at the height of the alternative era. Its scale and confidence have never quite been matched since, and it stands as the grandest statement of the 1990s alternative boom.

name: Ten
teaser: Pearl Jam 1991 — recorded in 3 weeks at London Bridge Studio in Seattle for $25,000 while the band was still called Mookie Blaylock (a basketball player who later sued). The album went 13x platinum but the band famously refused to make music videos for it, pulling back from the spotlight even as they were propelled into it.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Alive' — Eddie Vedder wrote the lyrics imagining a son discovering his father is actually his stepfather. The guitar solo by Mike McCready was played in one take; he thought it was just a warm-up. Then 'Jeremy' — based on a real suicide by a 15-year-old in front of his classmates in Richardson, Texas.

synopsis: Ten (1991) is Pearl Jam's debut album, recorded in three weeks in Seattle for a tiny budget while the band was still called Mookie Blaylock, after a basketball player. The album was released in the same year as Nirvana's Nevermind, and together the two records defined the sound of grunge for the world, but Pearl Jam's approach was different: Ten was built on big, anthemic choruses, Eddie Vedder's powerful, emotive baritone and the guitar interplay of Stone Gossard and Mike McCready, who owed as much to classic rock guitar heroes as to punk. 'Alive', 'Even Flow' and 'Jeremy', the latter a song about a school shooting that became an MTV staple, made the band stars, and the album sold over ten million copies in the US alone. The record took a while to catch on, but once it did, Pearl Jam became one of the biggest bands on earth, and Ten remains the definitive statement of the Seattle sound, combining the anger of grunge with a classic rock grandeur.

name: Superunknown
teaser: Soundgarden 1994 — the grunge band that could actually play anything. Chris Cornell's four-octave range and Kim Thayil's odd-time-signature riffs met on songs in 5/4, 7/4, and 9/8 without sounding prog. The album's cover art is a distorted photo of the band in a field of fire, representing their emotional state at the time.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Black Hole Sun' — Cornell wrote it in 15 minutes, thinking it was too poppy for the band. The surreal, melting-face music video defined 90s MTV. Then 'Spoonman' — the title refers to a real Seattle street performer, Artis the Spoonman, who plays spoons on the track. The song is in 7/4.

tracks.title: The Day I Tried to Live

synopsis: Superunknown (1994) is the album where Soundgarden, the most technically gifted band of the grunge era, reached the peak of their powers and made a record too big for any single genre. Chris Cornell's four-octave voice could move from a whisper to a scream in a phrase, and Kim Thayil's guitar playing, with its odd tunings and willingness to go anywhere, made the band capable of anything from crushing metal to eerie psychedelia. The album's biggest hits, 'Black Hole Sun' with its surreal, dreamlike melody, and 'Spoonman', built on a riff inspired by a street performer, made the band global stars, but the deeper tracks show their range: the crushing 'My Wave', the paranoid 'The Day I Tried to Live', the monumental 'Fell on Black Days' and the eerie '4th of July'. The record went to number one and sold millions, and it proved that the grunge movement contained musicians of genuine, lasting craft, not just attitude. It remains Soundgarden's masterpiece and one of the essential albums of the 1990s.

name: Dirt
teaser: Alice in Chains 1992 — the darkest grunge album, a raw chronicle of Layne Staley's heroin addiction. The band was using heavily during recording. Staley's vocal harmonies with Jerry Cantrell created a sound that was simultaneously beautiful and terrifying, like a choir singing from the bottom of a well.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Down in a Hole' — Cantrell wrote the lyrics about his own failing relationship, but Staley sang them as if about his addiction. Then 'Would?' — the bassline by Mike Starr is one note for nearly the entire song, creating a trance-like foundation. The track was a tribute to Andrew Wood of Mother Love Bone, who died of a heroin overdose.

synopsis: Dirt (1992) is the darkest record to come out of the Seattle grunge scene, an unflinching chronicle of addiction written by a band living through it. Layne Staley's lyrics detail the grip of heroin with a candor that is still hard to listen to: the opening 'Them Bones' is about the fragility of life, 'Junkhead' describes the addict's code with terrifying clarity, and 'Down in a Hole' and 'Angry Chair' are dispatches from inside the disease. The music, built on Jerry Cantrell's sludgy, blues-metal riffs and the band's eerie twin vocals, matches the lyrics' darkness, but the album also contains their biggest hit, 'Would?', written about the death of their friend Andrew Wood, and 'Rooster', a powerful song about Cantrell's father's experience in Vietnam. Recorded over several months with producer Dave Jerden, the album went multi-platinum and made Alice in Chains stars, but the cost was real: Staley's addiction would ultimately claim his life. It is a masterpiece that is painful to hear, and that is exactly the point.

name: Purple
teaser: Stone Temple Pilots 1994 — the album that proved they weren't grunge imitators. Recorded in a mansion in Atlanta, the band fought constantly. Scott Weiland wrote the lyrics while struggling with heroin. Despite the chaos, the album debuted at #1 and produced three top-10 singles.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Interstate Love Song' — the opening riff came to Dean DeLeo in a dream during a thunderstorm. Then 'Big Empty' — written in a single afternoon when the band needed one more track. Weiland's vocal floats over a sparse arrangement that builds into a wall of guitars, perfectly capturing the push-pull of addiction.

synopsis: Purple (1994) is the album where Stone Temple Pilots proved they were far more than grunge imitators, a charge that had dogged them since their debut. Recorded in a mansion in Atlanta while the band fought constantly and experimented freely, the album showed a group finding their own voice, blending the heavy rock of the Seattle scene with glam, psychedelia and classic rock songcraft. 'Interstate Love Song' became one of the biggest rock hits of the decade, a deceptively easygoing track built on a descending riff and Scott Weiland's smooth, seductive vocals, while 'Vasoline' and 'Big Empty' added darker textures, and 'Still Remains' and 'Silvergun Superman' showed the band's growing range. The record was a huge commercial success, going six times platinum, and it silenced most of the critics who had dismissed them a year earlier. It stands as the moment Stone Temple Pilots stepped out of grunge's shadow and became one of the most successful rock bands of the 1990s in their own right.

name: Loveless
teaser: My Bloody Valentine 1991 — recorded over 2 years across 19 studios, nearly bankrupting Creation Records. Kevin Shields used the tremolo arm of his guitar on every chord, creating a sound that literally bends pitch. The album cost £250,000 and the label's founder said it 'nearly destroyed us', but it became the definitive shoegaze record.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Only Shallow' — the opening guitar sounds like a jet engine taking off. Then 'When You Sleep' — Shields recorded the guitars at a low volume so the microphones would pick up room sound, creating the sensation of distance. The vocals were deliberately buried in the mix so you'd strain to hear them, like listening through a wall.

synopsis: Loveless (1991) is the album that took shoegaze to its logical conclusion, a record of such dense, swirling beauty that it nearly bankrupted its record label. Kevin Shields spent over two years and hundreds of thousands of pounds recording it across nineteen studios, obsessively searching for the perfect guitar sound, which he finally achieved by pressing the tremolo arm down and retuning the guitar so that chords blurred into an impossible, shimmering wash. The vocals, shared by Shields and Bilinda Butcher, were buried so deep in the mix that they became another instrument, and the songs, from the towering 'Only Shallow' to the dreamy 'When You Sleep' and the glacial 'Sometimes', feel less like pop songs than like memories of pop songs heard underwater. Creation Records nearly went bankrupt funding the sessions, and the toll on the band was such that they would not release another album for twenty-two years. Loveless is now regarded as one of the greatest albums of the 1990s, the record that made guitar noise sound like pure emotion.

name: Souvlaki
teaser: Slowdive 1993 — recorded during a period when the British music press had turned viciously against shoegaze. Rachel Goswell and Neil Halstead had just broken up emotionally while still being bandmates. Brian Eno contributed keyboards to two tracks after randomly meeting them in the studio hallway.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Alison' — Halstead wrote it about a friend who'd died, but the lyric is ambiguous enough to be a love song. Then 'When the Sun Hits' — the song is structured like a wave: quiet verse, massive wall of guitar for the chorus, retreat, repeat. Eno's contribution on 'Sing' is a single sustained note held for three minutes.

synopsis: Souvlaki (1993) is the album where Slowdive perfected the dreamy, melancholic sound that would come to define shoegaze for a generation of listeners who discovered it decades later. The British music press had turned viciously against the genre by 1993, and the band recorded the album under constant critical attack, which may be why it has such a hushed, inward quality. Rachel Goswell and Neil Halstead's voices blend into a single hazy instrument, floating over guitars that shimmer and sigh rather than attack, and the songs, from the gorgeous opener 'Alison' to the drifting 'Machine Gun' and the elegiac 'Dagger', are built on atmosphere rather than hooks. The band even worked with Brian Eno, who contributed to the title track, though the sessions produced little usable material. Souvlaki sold poorly on release and the band broke up a few years later, but the album was rediscovered by a new generation and is now considered one of the essential shoegaze records, the sound of sadness made beautiful.

name: Nowhere
teaser: Ride 1990 — the album that defined the heavier side of shoegaze before the term existed. Produced by Marc Waterman, who insisted on recording the drums in a stairwell to get the right amount of natural reverb. The guitar interplay between Andy Bell and Mark Gardener became the blueprint for what a two-guitar band could do without a lead guitarist.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Vapour Trail' — the string arrangement at the end is not strings at all but layered and pitch-shifted guitar feedback. Then 'Dreams Burn Down' — the song builds over four minutes from a whisper to a hurricane, with the drums seemingly trying to escape the song. The album's closing 8-minute title track is a single chord cycle that never resolves.

synopsis: Nowhere (1990) is the album that defined the heavier, more propulsive side of shoegaze before the term even existed. Ride were four friends from Oxford who made music of stunning confidence for such a young band, and their debut full-length, produced by Marc Waterman, who insisted on recording them in a huge hall to capture their live sound, is a wall of interlocking, feedback-laced guitars topped by the harmonized vocals of Mark Gardener and Andy Bell. 'Seagull' opens the record with ten minutes of soaring, repetitive beauty, while 'Vapour Trail', the closing track, became the band's signature song, a perfect distillation of the genre's euphoric melancholy. The album went to number one on the UK indie chart and made Ride the leaders of the shoegaze movement, beloved for their epic live shows and their refusal to compromise. It remains a landmark of British guitar music, the record that showed how loud, beautiful and strangely spiritual three chords and a lot of reverb could be.

name: Heaven or Las Vegas
teaser: Cocteau Twins 1990 — Elizabeth Fraser's voice as a musical instrument, singing in a self-invented language of sounds rather than words. The album was recorded during a period of severe drug addiction and the birth of Fraser's first child. The title came from a neon sign Fraser saw while driving through Nevada.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Cherry-coloured Funk' — try to make out the lyrics. You can't, and that's the point; Fraser's voice was an additional instrument, not a vehicle for meaning. Then the title track — the most straightforward song they ever recorded, with Robin Guthrie's shimmering guitar and Simon Raymonde's melodic bass finally letting Fraser's voice float above rather than within.

synopsis: Heaven or Las Vegas (1990) is the Cocteau Twins' most accessible and beloved album, the record where their dreamlike music finally found a warm, human center. Elizabeth Fraser's voice, which the band had always used as an instrument singing in a private language of sounds rather than words, was pushed higher in the mix than ever before, and the result is extraordinary: her singing on songs like 'Cherry-Coloured Funk' and 'Heaven or Las Vegas' is one of the most expressive and otherworldly sounds in all of pop music. Guitarist Robin Guthrie's shimmering, heavily effected playing and bassist Simon Raymonde's melodic bass lines create a lush, weightless backdrop, and the album's production, by the band themselves with Raymonde, gave the music a clarity their earlier records had lacked. The album was their biggest commercial success and is now regarded as their masterpiece, the moment a band who had spent years making beautiful noise finally made beautiful songs you could almost sing along to.

name: Definitely Maybe
teaser: Oasis 1994 — the fastest-selling debut in British history at the time. Recorded in 19 days at Monnow Valley in Wales, then completely re-recorded at Sawmills in Cornwall. Noel Gallagher wrote every song; Liam Gallagher sang them with a sneer you could hear through walls. The album captured a specific British moment: late Thatcher hangover, early Cool Britannia optimism.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Live Forever' — Noel wrote it in response to Nirvana's 'I Hate Myself and Want to Die', deliberately creating an anthem of defiance. Then 'Slide Away' — Liam's vocal take was his first and only; he went outside for a cigarette and never came back to re-record it. The album sounds like someone kicking open every door in the house.

synopsis: Definitely Maybe (1994) is the album that launched Britpop, the fastest-selling debut in British history at the time, and the sound of a band who believed they were the greatest in the world. Oasis were five working-class lads from Manchester led by the brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher, with Noel writing the songs and Liam snarling them out with a rock star arrogance that Britain had not seen in years. The album was recorded in nineteen days in Wales, then completely re-recorded when the band were unhappy with the sound, and the finished record is a glorious wall of swaggering guitars, built on the band's love of the Beatles, T. Rex and the Sex Pistols. 'Live Forever', 'Supersonic', 'Cigarettes & Alcohol' and 'Rock 'n' Roll Star' became instant anthems, songs full of ambition and hope delivered with total conviction. The album went straight to number one and made Oasis the biggest band in Britain, setting the stage for the rivalry with Blur that would define the rest of the decade.

name: Parklife
teaser: Blur 1994 — the Britpop album that made Damon Albarn the voice of suburban British youth irony. Recorded in a small studio on Borough High Street in London. Phil Daniels (the actor from Quadrophenia) narrated the title track as a cockney geezer. The album is a love letter to a very specific, very mundane version of England.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Girls & Boys' — the disco beat was Graham Coxon's idea, played on a drum machine. The lyrics about package holidays and casual sex were Albarn observing British tourists in Magaluf. Then 'This Is a Low' — the lyrics are weather shipping forecast regions: 'Biscay, Trafalgar, Dogger, Rockall.' Albarn turned the BBC shipping forecast into poetry.

synopsis: Parklife (1994) is the album that made Blur the kings of Britpop, a wry, witty celebration of everyday British life that turned suburban detail into pop art. Damon Albarn had spent the band's early years singing about the angst of London life, but on Parklife he embraced a new persona, writing songs about the mundane rituals and small pleasures of ordinary people: dog racing, going to the park, staying home on a Friday night. The album mixes punk-funk grooves, music hall singalongs and wistful ballads, with Graham Coxon's guitar work and Albarn's theatrical vocals backed by spoken-word interludes. 'Girls & Boys' became their biggest hit, a danceable satire of holiday romance, while the title track, sung by actor Phil Daniels, and 'End of a Century' and 'This Is a Low' showed the band's range. The record went to number one, beat Oasis's debut in the chart battle of 1994 and made Blur the defining band of the era, the sound of British pop at its most clever and affectionate.

name: Different Class
teaser: Pulp 1995 — Jarvis Cocker's magnum opus about class, sex, and the absurdity of British life. Cocker was 32 when the album came out, having been in Pulp since he was 15. The album cover was shot at a wedding reception; the band photoshopped themselves into the guests.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Common People' — Cocker wrote it based on a real Greek art student who told him she wanted to 'live like common people.' The song builds from a single keyboard note to a full-band crescendo over 6 minutes. Then 'Disco 2000' — based on Cocker's childhood crush Deborah, who he found on Facebook 25 years later.

synopsis: Different Class (1995) is Jarvis Cocker's masterpiece, the album where the awkward outsider finally got his revenge and became the voice of British pop. Cocker had been making music for nearly two decades as a cult figure, and Different Class made him a star at the age of 32, with songs that turned his experience of class, desire and social embarrassment into universal pop. 'Common People', the album's centerpiece, tells the story of a wealthy art student who wants to slum it with the working classes, and its furious, witty chorus became one of the defining moments of the Britpop era, while 'Sorted for E's & Wizz' captured the comedown of rave culture and 'Disco 2000' and 'Something Changed' showed his gift for melancholy pop. The album went to number one, won the Mercury Prize and made Cocker a national treasure, a shy, bespectacled man whose songs about longing and humiliation somehow made everyone feel less alone. It remains one of the great British albums about class and desire.

name: Suede
teaser: Suede 1993 — the fastest-selling debut album in British history until Oasis broke the record a year later. Brett Anderson's androgynous vocals and Bernard Butler's fluid guitar lines created a glam-rock revival filtered through British miserabilism. The cover photo of two women kissing was considered shocking for a major-label release in 1993.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Animal Nitrate' — Butler's guitar solo is a single sustained note fed through a wah-wah pedal. Then 'The Drowners' — the opening riff sounds like it was beamed in from a 1973 David Bowie session. Butler recorded the album's guitar parts in a closet to capture a claustrophobic, radio-unfriendly ambience.

synopsis: Suede (1993) is the album that launched the Britpop era, a record of such glamorous, androgynous confidence that it made the rest of British guitar music look instantly dated. The band had been hailed as the saviors of British rock on the strength of a single, and their debut, the fastest-selling in British history at the time, delivered on every promise. Brett Anderson's vocals swooped and snarled, sometimes in a single line, while Bernard Butler's guitar work mixed glam rock riffs with the shimmer of classic pop, and Matt Osman's bass and Simon Gilbert's drums provided the drive. Songs like 'So Young', 'Animal Nitrate', a tale of seedy glamour that became their biggest hit, and 'The Drowners' captured a world of suburban longing, sexual ambiguity and glamorous desperation. The album went to number one and made Suede the leaders of a new British rock movement, and though they would be eclipsed by Oasis and Blur, their debut remains a landmark, the record that made it cool to be British again.

name: The Holy Bible
teaser: Manic Street Preachers 1994 — the most harrowing album of the Britpop era. Richey Edwards wrote lyrics about anorexia, the Holocaust, capital punishment, and self-harm while in the grip of severe depression. Four months after the album's release, Edwards disappeared; his car was found near the Severn Bridge. He has never been found.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to '4st 7lb' — the title is the weight at which an anorexic person is at risk of death. Edwards hospitalised himself during the writing. Then 'Faster' — the opening line is 'I am an architect, they call me a butcher.' The album's references range from Primo Levi to Sylvia Plath to the Hungerford massacre.

synopsis: The Holy Bible (1994) is the most harrowing album of the Britpop era, a record of such intellectual fury and personal anguish that it still sounds like nothing else from its time. Manic Street Preachers had been making loud, slogan-heavy rock, but on their third album, guitarist Richey Edwards, who was struggling with severe depression and self-harm, poured his obsessions into the lyrics: the Holocaust, anorexia, prostitution, the dehumanization of modern warfare, the horror of consumer culture. The music, produced by Steve Brown, matches the intensity, all jagged guitars, martial drums and Nicky Wire's driving bass, with James Dean Bradfield's voice, one of the finest in British rock, giving the despair an almost anthemic power. Songs like 'Archives of Pain', 'Die in the Summertime' and the devastating '4st 7lb', about anorexia, are among the most disturbing lyrics ever set to pop music. Six months after the album's release, Edwards disappeared and was never found. The Holy Bible stands as his monument, a brilliant, terrifying record.

name: Urban Hymns
teaser: The Verve 1997 — the album that broke up the band. Richard Ashcroft wrote the songs after a three-year heroin detox. The string arrangement on 'Bitter Sweet Symphony' used a sample from an orchestral version of a Rolling Stones song, leading to a lawsuit that gave Mick Jagger and Keith Richards 100% of the royalties. Ashcroft earned nothing from his most famous song for 22 years.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Bitter Sweet Symphony' — the strings were recorded at Olympic Studios. Then 'The Drugs Don't Work' — Ashcroft wrote it watching his father die of cancer. The song's devastating chorus was sung in a single take. The album broke up the band literally: they split during the tour, reunited briefly, and split again.

synopsis: Urban Hymns (1997) is the album where The Verve, a band who had spent years making sprawling psychedelic rock, suddenly found themselves with the biggest song in the world. Richard Ashcroft wrote the album's songs after coming out of a period of addiction, and the record is full of a hard-won sense of hope and wonder. 'Bitter Sweet Symphony', built on a string sample from an orchestral version of a Rolling Stones song, became an international phenomenon and one of the defining songs of the decade, though a legal battle over the sample meant that the Rolling Stones, not The Verve, ended up owning the royalties. The album around it is just as strong: 'The Drugs Don't Work', written as Ashcroft's father was dying, is one of the most heartbreaking songs of the era, while 'Lucky Man' and 'Sonnet' show the band's gift for soaring, anthemic melody. The album went to number one, but the band broke up shortly after, making Urban Hymns a beautiful, bittersweet farewell.

name: The Lonesome Crowded West
teaser: Modest Mouse 1997 — Isaac Brock's blistering indictment of suburban sprawl, strip malls, and spiritual emptiness. Recorded in a makeshift studio in a house in Seattle. Brock's guitar was tuned to an open chord he'd invented so he could play while drinking. The album was recorded for $10,000 and sounds like it cost ten times that.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Trailer Trash' — Brock's vocal cracks are real; he was drinking whiskey during the session. Then 'Cowboy Dan' — the song starts as a whisper, becomes a scream about a man who 'moves to the city' and 'shoots his rifle in the air.' Brock intentionally recorded the vocals too close to the microphone so you can hear the spit.

tracks.title: Jesus Christ Was an Only Child
Styrofoam Boots/It's All Nice on Ice, Alright

synopsis: The Lonesome Crowded West (1997) is Modest Mouse's furious, sprawling masterpiece, an album about the spiritual emptiness of modern America that sounds like a road trip through a nightmare. Isaac Brock wrote the songs while touring the vast, monotonous spaces of the American West, and the album is full of disgust at suburban sprawl, strip malls, highway culture and the loneliness of life in a country too big to feel like home. 'Teeth Like God's Shoeshine' opens the record with a barrage of noise and fury, 'Cowboy Dan' is a terrifying portrait of violence and despair, and 'Trailer Trash' is a heartbreaking ballad of poverty and resignation, while 'Doin' the Cockroach' and 'Shit Luck' show the band's punk energy. The music, recorded in a makeshift studio with jerry-rigged equipment, is loose and raw, built on Brock's strange, lurching guitar lines and the rhythm section's propulsive drive. It sold modestly at first but has become one of the most influential indie rock albums of the decade.

name: Crooked Rain, Crooked Rain
teaser: Pavement 1994 — the slacker-rock masterpiece that almost made them famous. Stephen Malkmus wrote the lyrics by cutting up newspapers and rearranging the words. The album was recorded in a studio that was also a working horse barn in rural Virginia. The single 'Cut Your Hair' was their attempt at a hit; it nearly worked.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Cut Your Hair' — the melody sounds like a nursery rhyme filtered through guitar fuzz. Then 'Range Life' — Malkmus's gentle mockery of the Smashing Pumpkins and Stone Temple Pilots apparently made Billy Corgan refuse to play festivals with them. The album's charm is its refusal to try too hard.

synopsis: Crooked Rain, Crooked Rain (1994) is the album where Pavement, the kings of slacker rock, almost accidentally made a record that sounded like a hit. After the lo-fi murk of their debut Slanted and Enchanted, the band recorded their second album in a real studio, and the greater clarity revealed how brilliant Stephen Malkmus's songs actually were. 'Cut Your Hair', a sardonic take on the music industry, became an alternative radio hit, and the record is full of songs that seem effortless and tossed off yet are packed with invention: 'Gold Soundz', a perfect pop song about nostalgia, 'Range Life', a lazy, funny diss track aimed at bigger bands, and 'Stop Breathin', a haunting piece of guitar beauty. The album was hailed as a masterpiece of indie rock, and it captured a moment when the underground was about to break into the mainstream. It remains the definitive statement of 1990s indie, a record that made sloppiness, wit and intelligence sound like the future of rock.

name: Keep It Like a Secret
teaser: Built to Spill 1999 — Doug Martsch's guitar meditation disguised as an indie rock album. Recorded piece by piece over a year, with Martsch playing most of the instruments and layering guitars like Brian Wilson on a budget. The album title describes Martsch's philosophy: hold something back, don't give it all away.

exploreAction.targetName: Keep It Like a Secret (1999) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Carry the Zero' — the song starts as a simple chord progression and builds into a three-guitar tapestry that peaks at 4:12 but keeps going. Then 'Else' — Martsch's guitar solo is played through a rotating Leslie speaker, making it sound like it's orbiting the rest of the song. The album rewards headphones: every listen reveals a new guitar line.

synopsis: Keep It Like a Secret (1999) is Built to Spill's greatest record, the album where Doug Martsch's obsession with the possibilities of the guitar produced a set of songs that are both intimate and enormous. The band recorded the album piece by piece over nearly a year, with Martsch layering guitars until they became vast, interlocking structures, and the result sounds both painstaking and effortless. 'The Plan' opens the album with a driving, optimistic rush, 'Carry the Zero' is one of the great lost indie anthems, building to a soaring climax, and 'Else' and 'You Were Right' show Martsch's gift for melody and wry, self-lacerating lyrics. The record is a meditation on memory, regret and the passage of time, wrapped in guitar lines that spiral and sing like nothing else in indie rock. It has become the band's most beloved album, the record that proves that guitar rock, in the right hands, could still sound like a new language.

name: Turn On the Bright Lights
teaser: Interpol 2002 — the album that made post-punk revival a thing. Recorded in a converted church in Connecticut over a bleak winter. Paul Banks' baritone and Daniel Kessler's angular guitar lines drew constant Joy Division comparisons. The album captured post-9/11 New York anxiety without explicitly mentioning it.

exploreAction.targetName: Turn On the Bright Lights (2002) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Obstacle 1' — the opening guitar riff was Kessler trying to play a Joy Division song from memory. Then 'NYC' — the chorus 'New York cares' was written before September 11; after, it sounded like an elegy. The album's atmosphere is so consistent that it sounds like it was recorded in a single room at 3 AM.

tracks.title: Stella Was a Diver and She Was Always Down

synopsis: Turn On the Bright Lights (2002) is the album that launched the post-punk revival, a record of such brooding, icy grandeur that it made New York the center of the rock world again. Interpol recorded the album in a converted church in Connecticut over a bleak winter, and the cold atmosphere seeped into the music: the songs are built on Paul Banks's detached, baritone vocals, Daniel Kessler's chiming, angular guitar lines, and the rhythm section of Carlos Dengler and Sam Fogarino, who gave the band their distinctive, motorik drive. 'PDA' and 'Obstacle 1' are brooding, epic songs of romantic paranoia, while 'NYC' and 'Untitled' show the band's more atmospheric side, and the closing 'Leif Erikson' is a masterpiece of slow-burning tension. The album was hailed as a return to the sounds of Joy Division and the Chameleons, but it had its own identity, and it became one of the most influential records of the decade, the template for a thousand imitators who never matched its icy perfection.

name: Is This It
teaser: The Strokes 2001 — 36 minutes that made rock music feel dangerous again. Recorded in 6 weeks at a studio on Manhattan's Lower East Side. Julian Casablancas recorded his vocals through a small guitar amp to get the right amount of distortion. The album's original cover featured a black-and-white photo of a naked bottom; the US release replaced it with a more abstract image.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Last Nite' — the riff was Casablancas trying to write a song in the style of Tom Petty. Then 'Someday' — Albert Hammond Jr.'s guitar solo is two notes repeated for 10 seconds while the rhythm section carries the song. The album's brevity is a statement: leave before they want more.

synopsis: Is This It (2001) is the album that made rock music feel dangerous and exciting again, a 36-minute record that changed the course of popular music. The Strokes were five friends from New York who had spent years perfecting their sound in tiny clubs, and their debut album, recorded in six weeks with producer Gordon Raphael, captured the ragged, glamorous energy of their live shows. Julian Casablancas's bored, slurred vocals, Albert Hammond Jr. and Nick Valensi's interlocking, minimalist guitar riffs, Nikolai Fraiture's melodic bass and Fabrizio Moretti's tight drums added up to a sound that referenced the Velvet Underground and Television while feeling completely fresh. 'Last Nite', 'Someday', 'Hard to Explain' and the title track became instant classics, songs about urban alienation and romantic confusion delivered with effortless cool. The album was released just after 9/11, and its New York sensibility took on extra weight. It became the blueprint for the garage rock revival, and its influence is still everywhere in rock music.

name: Up the Bracket
teaser: The Libertines 2002 — recorded in 2 weeks with Mick Jones of The Clash producing. Pete Doherty and Carl Barât wrote the songs in a flat on the Caledonian Road they called 'The Albion Rooms'. Doherty was already using heroin heavily. The album sounds like a party that's about to be broken up by the police — which it was, several times.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Doherty's vocal is slurred but the melody is perfect. Then 'Time for Heroes' — the lyrics are a snapshot of the 2000 May Day riots in London, which Barât and Doherty attended together. The album captured a specific moment of British youth culture: pre-smartphone, post-Thatcher, fuelled by cheap lager and idealism.

synopsis: Up the Bracket (2002) is the ragged, romantic debut album from The Libertines, the band that brought a new kind of chaos and poetry to British rock. Pete Doherty and Carl Barât were the band's two songwriters and two stars, a partnership so intense and destructive that it defined the group's legend, and their debut, produced by Mick Jones of the Clash, captured their sound at its most raw and thrilling. The band's music mixed punk energy with music hall singalongs, Kinks-style storytelling and the romance of old London, and songs like 'Time for Heroes', 'Boys in the Band' and the title track are full of wit, violence and desperate friendship. 'Up the Bracket' became a top 30 hit and the album was hailed as the beginning of a new British rock movement, paving the way for the Arctic Monkeys and the rest of the garage rock wave. It is the sound of a band who were brilliant, self-destructive and completely alive, and it remains a classic.

name: Hot Fuss
teaser: The Killers 2004 — a Las Vegas band that sounded more British than most British bands. Recorded in Berkeley, California after the band's van broke down there. Brandon Flowers wrote densely narrative lyrics influenced by growing up Mormon in Sin City. The album's synth-heavy sound was a deliberate rejection of the garage-rock revival happening around them.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Mr. Brightside' — written in one night after Flowers caught his girlfriend cheating. The guitar riff was played by Dave Keuning on an Ibanez through a delay pedal. Then 'All These Things That I've Done' — the 'I got soul but I'm not a soldier' bridge was improvised in the studio. The gospel choir was a local Berkeley church group.

tracks.title: Jenny Was a Friend of Mine
All These Things That I've Done

synopsis: Hot Fuss (2004) is the album where four young men from Las Vegas invented a British band in their heads and then became bigger than most actual British bands. The Killers had barely played live when they recorded their debut in California, and the songs were written by Brandon Flowers with a love of New Order, the Cure and Duran Duran that gave their music a glossy, anthemic quality far removed from their desert hometown. 'Mr. Brightside', a song about jealousy and betrayal that Flowers wrote after catching his girlfriend cheating, became one of the defining rock songs of the decade, and 'Somebody Told Me' and 'All These Things That I've Done' made the album a global smash. The record went to number one in Britain, where the band were embraced as honorary Brits, and it sold over seven million copies worldwide. Hot Fuss announced the Killers as one of the biggest rock bands of their generation, and it remains their most loved record.

name: Franz Ferdinand
teaser: Franz Ferdinand 2004 — the album that made art-school dance-rock a global phenomenon. Recorded in a former church in Glasgow. Alex Kapranos wrote lyrics about dinner parties, jealousy, and the Scottish art scene. The band's tight, clipped guitar style was inspired by the idea of making music that sounded like it was wearing a slim-fit suit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Take Me Out' — the song famously changes tempo and feel at 0:55, a deliberate misdirection. Then 'Michael' — a disco-rock song about a male crush, sung without irony. The band's secret weapon was drummer Paul Thomson, whose hi-hat work on every song turns standard rock rhythms into dance beats.

synopsis: Franz Ferdinand (2004) is the album that made art-school dance rock the sound of the year, a record of such sharp, witty, instantly memorable songs that it seemed to have been beamed in from a smarter, more stylish world. The Glasgow band, led by Alex Kapranos, set out to make music that girls could dance to, and they succeeded beyond their wildest dreams: 'Take Me Out', with its sudden shift from tense verse to explosive chorus, became one of the biggest hits of the decade, while 'Michael', 'This Fire' and 'The Dark of the Matinée' showed the band's gift for combining disco rhythms with angular guitar riffs. The album was recorded in a former church in Glasgow, and its production gives the songs a bright, immediate sound that makes them irresistible. It won the Mercury Prize, went to number three in Britain and launched a worldwide wave of similar bands. Franz Ferdinand remains one of the most confident and enjoyable debuts of the 2000s, proof that intelligence and pop music could be the same thing.

name: Elephant
teaser: The White Stripes 2003 — recorded in 2 weeks at Toe Rag Studios in London, using only pre-1963 analog equipment. Jack White insisted on no computers, no Pro Tools. The album was recorded on 8-track tape. Meg White played a drum kit with only a kick, snare, and one cymbal. The limitations became the sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Seven Nation Army' — the riff was played on a guitar tuned down an octave through a DigiTech Whammy pedal, creating a bass-like tone. Then 'Ball and Biscuit' — Jack's 7-minute blues solo was his attempt to play like Blind Willie McTell through three Marshall stacks. The album proved that restrictions breed creativity.

tracks.title: There's No Home for You Here
I Just Don't Know What to Do with Myself
I Want to Be the Boy to Warm Your Mother's Heart
You've Got Her in Your Pocket
Girl, You Have No Faith in Medicine
It's True That We Love One Another

synopsis: Elephant (2003) is the album where the White Stripes, Detroit's most fiercely minimal band, became global stars without changing a thing about how they sounded. Jack and Meg White recorded the album in two weeks at Toe Rag Studios in London, a tiny studio full of vintage equipment, and insisted on using only pre-1963 analog gear, recording live to tape with no computers. The result is a record of enormous, raw power: 'Seven Nation Army', built on a bass riff Jack White played on a guitar through a pitch-shifting pedal, became one of the most recognizable riffs in rock history and an anthem at stadiums around the world, while 'The Hardest Button to Button', 'There's No Home for You Here' and the eerie 'I Want to Be the Boy to Warm Your Mother's Heart' showed the band's range from punk to blues to balladry. The album went to number one in Britain and won two Grammys. It proved that a two-piece band with limited tools could make one of the biggest rock records of the decade.

name: Fever to Tell
teaser: Yeah Yeah Yeahs 2003 — Karen O's debut as a frontwoman possessed. Recorded in a converted church in Brooklyn. Nick Zinner's guitar was run through so many effects pedals that his pedalboard looked like a small city. The album was produced by David Andrew Sitek of TV on the Radio, who layered ambient noise under every track.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Maps' — Karen O wrote it about her then-boyfriend Angus Andrew of Liars, who was leaving for tour. She cried during the recording; the 'they don't love you like I love you' is addressed directly to him. Then 'Y Control' — Zinner's guitar sounds like a malfunctioning fire alarm in the best possible way.

synopsis: Fever to Tell (2003) is the debut album that turned Yeah Yeah Yeahs from a tiny New York art-punk act into one of the most exciting bands in the world, almost entirely on the strength of Karen O's stage presence and voice. Recorded in a converted church in Brooklyn, the album captures the raw, live energy of the band's early shows: Karen O yelps, moans and screams her way through songs of lust and unease, while Nick Zinner's guitar, often played through a bass amp, provides the jagged, distorted backdrop and Brian Chase's drums keep everything teetering on the edge of collapse. 'Date with the Night' and 'Pin' are all jagged energy, 'Maps', written about Karen O's boyfriend being away on tour, became their breakthrough single and one of the most tender rock songs of the decade, and the closer 'Y Control' showed a band learning to be vulnerable. The album was a critical and commercial success, and it announced Karen O as one of the great rock frontwomen of her generation.

name: Sound of Silver
teaser: LCD Soundsystem 2007 — James Murphy's meditation on getting older, losing friends, and the redemptive power of dance music. Recorded in a converted barn in upstate New York. Murphy was 37, newly married, and questioning whether he should still be making dance-punk.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'All My Friends' — a 7-minute build around a single piano figure. The lyrics catalog a lifetime of parties, friendships, and regrets. Then 'Someone Great' — written after Murphy's therapist died suddenly. The song uses the structure of dance music — repetition, build, release — to process grief. Murphy later said it was the most personal thing he'd ever written.

tracks.title: New York, I Love You but You're Bringing Me Down

synopsis: Sound of Silver (2007) is the album where LCD Soundsystem's James Murphy stopped writing jokes about the music business and started writing about his own life, and the result was his masterpiece. Murphy had made his name with arch, danceable critiques of hipster culture, but on this record he turned inward, writing about getting older, losing friends and the strange comfort of dancing through it all. The title track is a meditation on the consolations of music itself, 'Someone Great' is a devastating account of grief disguised as a disco song, written after a friend and mentor died, and 'All My Friends', the album's centerpiece, is a seven-minute epic about the passage of time built on a repeating piano figure that eventually became an anthem for a generation. The album was recorded in Murphy's own studio in New York, and its blend of punk energy, disco pulse and genuine emotion made it one of the most acclaimed records of the decade, the sound of dance music growing up and finding its heart.

name: Boxer
teaser: The National 2007 — the album where they stopped trying to be a rock band and became The National. Recorded in a house in Bridgeport, Connecticut. Matt Berninger's baritone was recorded in a closet filled with blankets for soundproofing. The album's characters are lonely, drunk, anxious professionals navigating dinner parties and office politics.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Fake Empire' — the song's odd time signature (4/4 over a waltzing 3/4 piano) creates a constant sense of unease. The horn arrangement was written by Padma Newsome, who also played viola. Then 'Mistaken for Strangers' — Berninger wrote it about running into a friend who didn't recognize him, which became a metaphor for his relationship with himself.

synopsis: Boxer (2007) is the album where The National stopped being an interesting cult band and became one of the most beloved rock groups in the world. Recorded in a house in Bridgeport, Connecticut, with long-time producer Peter Katis, the album found the band abandoning the louder sounds of their earlier records for something quieter and more patient: Matt Berninger's deep, weary baritone, now front and center, singing about failed relationships, middle age and quiet desperation, backed by the band's meticulous, brooding arrangements and the Dessner brothers' intricate guitar work. 'Fake Empire' opens the album with a stately, off-kilter march, 'Mistaken for Strangers' and 'Squalor Victoria' are taut, anxious rock songs, and 'Slow Show', 'Apartment Story' and the closing 'Gospel' are among the most tender songs the band has ever written. The album was a critical triumph, and it established the template, elegant, melancholic, increasingly grand, that has defined The National ever since. It remains their most loved record.

name: Lonerism
teaser: Kevin Parker 2012 — recorded entirely alone in a rented house in Perth, Australia, on a laptop. Parker played every instrument, sang every vocal, produced every track. The album is about social isolation from someone who turned isolation into a creative method. The drums were recorded first, then everything else was built around them.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Feels Like We Only Go Backwards' — the swirling synth was a Korg MS-20 routed through a phaser pedal. Then 'Apocalypse Dreams' — the song's mid-point key change was Parker accidentally hitting the wrong chord and deciding it sounded better. The album's drums sound like they're recorded in a room the size of a cathedral.

tracks.title: Why Won't They Talk to Me?
Feels Like We Only Go Backwards
Nothing That Has Happened So Far Has Been Anything We Could Control

synopsis: Lonerism (2012) is the album where Kevin Parker, recording entirely alone under the name Tame Impala, turned his isolation into something radiant. Parker wrote, performed and produced the entire record himself, working on a laptop in a rented house in Perth, Australia, and the album is full of the feeling of that solitude: it is about the loneliness of being in your own head, of feeling disconnected from other people, but it is wrapped in some of the most lush, euphoric psychedelic pop of the decade. 'Elephant' became a surprise hit with its heavy, distorted riff, 'Feels Like We Only Go Backwards' is a gorgeous song of romantic frustration, and 'Endors Toi' and 'Apocalypse Dreams' show Parker's gift for building songs into towering, melodic climaxes. The album was recorded almost entirely alone, which makes its warmth even more remarkable, and it was hailed as a modern psychedelic classic, cementing Parker's reputation as one of the most talented figures in contemporary rock.

name: Total Life Forever
teaser: Foals 2010 — the Oxford band's pivot from math-rock to something more expansive and emotional. Recorded in a church in Gothenburg, Sweden during the coldest winter in decades. Yannis Philippakis wrote the lyrics after devouring books on futurism and transhumanism. The album's aquatic themes were inspired by the Swedish archipelago.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Spanish Sahara' — the song builds for 6 minutes from a single quiet guitar note to a wall of noise, then retreats. Then 'Blue Blood' — the interlocking guitar lines were recorded separately without either guitarist hearing the other's part. Philippakis said the album was about 'what happens when we upload our consciousness.'

synopsis: Total Life Forever (2010) is the album where Foals grew up, trading the jerky, math-rock energy of their debut for something more expansive, atmospheric and emotional. The Oxford band recorded the album in a church in Gothenburg, Sweden, with producer Luke Smith, and the change of scenery and pace is audible in every song: the record is built on echo-laden guitars, Yam's propulsive, intricate drumming and Yannis Philippakis's increasingly confident voice, which moves from hushed croon to desperate shout. 'Spanish Sahara', the album's centerpiece, is a slow-building epic about loss that became one of the defining indie songs of the decade, while 'This Orient' and 'Miami' show the band's new love of texture and space. The album was shortlisted for the Mercury Prize and established Foals as one of the most ambitious British bands of their generation, the record where they stopped being a cult concern and started making music for arenas.

name: Songs for the Deaf
teaser: Queens of the Stone Age 2002 — a concept album structured as a drive through the California desert, with fake radio station interludes between tracks. Dave Grohl played drums as a session musician, recording his parts in 3 days. Josh Homme tuned his guitar down to C-standard, creating the low, heavy 'robot rock' sound that defined the band.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'No One Knows' — the riff was Homme trying to write a polka. Grohl's drum fill at 2:14 is one of the most-emulated in rock. Then 'Go with the Flow' — the distorted piano was played by Homme through a guitar amp. The entire album sounds like a car radio at full volume crossing the Mojave at midnight.

tracks.title: The Real Song for the Deaf
You Think I Ain't Worth a Dollar, But I Feel Like a Millionaire

synopsis: Songs for the Deaf (2002) is Queens of the Stone Age's masterpiece, a concept album structured as a drive through the California desert with the radio scanning between stations. Every few songs, the record cuts to a fake radio interlude, from a hard rock station to a Spanish-language broadcast to a preacher, and the conceit lets Josh Homme and his band, which now included the drummer Dave Grohl of Nirvana and Foo Fighters fame, move between crushing hard rock, blues, stoner metal and radio pop with total freedom. 'No One Knows', with its instantly recognizable opening riff, became the band's biggest hit, 'Go with the Flow' is a propulsive rocker, and the closing 'A Song for the Dead', with a drum intro that Grohl has called the hardest thing he ever recorded, is a ten-minute epic of doom and release. The album was recorded in Los Angeles and made Queens of the Stone Age the leaders of the hard rock revival of the early 2000s, the record that proved heavy music could be smart, funny and massive.

name: Welcome to Sky Valley
teaser: Kyuss 1994 — the album that invented stoner rock. Recorded in a remote studio in the California desert called Rancho De La Luna. The band recorded at night because the daytime heat made the equipment malfunction. Guitarist Josh Homme tuned down to C-standard and played through bass amps to create tones that sound like a truck engine idling.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Gardenia' — the opening riff was played through a bass amp with all the dials turned to 10. Then 'Demon Cleaner' — the slowed-down groove was achieved by recording at a faster tempo and pitching the tape down. The album is three suites of connected tracks, meant to be listened to as movements, not individual songs.

synopsis: Welcome to Sky Valley (1994) is the album that defined stoner rock, the sound of a band from the California desert playing music so slow, heavy and hypnotic that it felt like the earth itself was moving. Kyuss, led by guitarist Josh Homme, had been perfecting their sound for years in the desert parties of Palm Springs, running their amplifiers on generators in the middle of nowhere, and on this, their third album, they captured it perfectly. Recorded at the desert studio Rancho De La Luna, the album is a series of massive, riff-driven tracks, played with a looseness that makes them feel improvised, and the band's secret weapon was vocalist John Garcia, whose soaring voice floated over the sludge like a desert wind. The album's three long suites, each divided into numbered parts, show the band's ambition, and songs like 'Demon Cleaner', 'Space Cadet' and 'Gardenia' have become genre classics. The band broke up a year later, but their influence on everything from Queens of the Stone Age to modern metal is enormous.

name: Dopesmoker
teaser: Sleep 2003 — a single 63-minute song about a caravan of weed priests crossing the desert. The band's label refused to release it; they spent years fighting over the master tapes. Originally recorded in 1996, it wasn't officially released until 2003. The album has since become the most legendary stoner metal record ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the whole thing in one sitting. The riff doesn't change for the first 12 minutes — bassist/vocalist Al Cisneros's mantra-like delivery treats the riff as a meditation object. Then notice how the tempo gradually, almost imperceptibly slows across the full 63 minutes, like a machine running out of fuel. The album was the sole reason Sleep were dropped from London Records.

synopsis: Dopesmoker (2003) is the ultimate statement of stoner metal: one single 63-minute song about a caravan of weed-priests crossing the desert toward a mythical city where they will smoke the sacred herb. Sleep, the California trio behind it, had been building toward this record for years, and when they presented the hour-long track to their label, the label refused to release it, leading to a legal battle that broke the band up. The song was finally released years later, and it has become a legend: a single, colossal riff, played with glacial patience, that slowly shifts and evolves over the full hour, with Matt Pike's guitar and Al Cisneros's bass locked in a hypnotic trance while Cisneros chants lyrics about the 'weedian' quest. It is music that demands total surrender, and its reputation has only grown with time. Dopesmoker is now regarded as one of the greatest achievements of heavy music, the sound of a band pushing an idea to its absolute limit and refusing to compromise.

name: Diary
teaser: Sunny Day Real Estate 1994 — the album that invented emo as an art form rather than a punchline. Recorded in a basement in Seattle for $5,000. Jeremy Enigk's lyrics were written after he converted to Christianity, though the album is more spiritual questioning than religious. The album's emotional directness influenced an entire genre.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Seven' — the opening riff is in an unusual time signature that shifts between 4/4 and 6/8. Then 'In Circles' — Enigk's vocal jumps from a whisper to a scream in the space of a single syllable. The band broke up shortly after the album because the emotional intensity of the songs was too much to sustain live night after night.

synopsis: Diary (1994) is the album that turned emo from a punchline into an art form, a record of such raw emotional intensity that it invented a whole genre by accident. Sunny Day Real Estate were a band from Seattle who played loud, dynamic rock in the post-grunge era, but singer Jeremy Enigk's soaring, desperately sincere voice and the band's intricate, shifting song structures set them apart from everything around them. The album was recorded in a basement in Seattle for almost nothing, and its songs, like the opener 'Seven', 'In Circles' and the epic 'Guitar and Video Games', move between quiet introspection and cathartic explosions with a precision that most bands twice their age never achieved. The band had no idea they were starting a movement, and they broke up almost immediately after the album's release, but Diary became the blueprint for the emotional, mathematically precise rock that dominated the underground for the next decade. It remains the definitive document of emo's first, purest wave.

name: American Football
teaser: American Football 1999 — a single album recorded by University of Illinois students in a college dorm, then the band broke up. Over the next 15 years, the album grew from obscurity into the definitive Midwest emo record. The house on the cover became a pilgrimage site for fans; the band eventually bought it.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Never Meant' — the opening guitar line is in an alternate tuning (FACGCe) that Mike Kinsella invented. Then 'The Summer Ends' — the trumpet solo at the end was played by a friend who happened to be visiting the dorm during recording. The album's math-rock time signatures make the emotional content feel even more exposed.

tracks.title: You Know I Should Be Leaving Soon
But the Regrets Are Killing Me
I'll See You When We're Both Not So Emotional

synopsis: American Football (1999) is the album that became one of the most beloved cult records in indie rock, a quiet, intricate masterpiece made by college students who had no idea anyone was listening. The band were University of Illinois students who recorded the album in a house in Champaign-Urbana, and its sound was completely unlike the loud, aggressive emo of the time: the songs were built around clean, interlocking guitars, played in odd, twinkling patterns, with Mike Kinsella's hushed, hesitant vocals floating above them. 'Never Meant', the opening track, became a slow-burning anthem over the following decades, and songs like 'The Summer Ends' and 'Stay Home' showed the band's gift for melancholy, nostalgic melody. The band broke up shortly after the album's release, and for years it was a secret shared between music obsessives, before the internet turned it into a phenomenon, with the house on its cover becoming a pilgrimage site for fans. The album's influence on the emo and indie revivals of the 2010s is incalculable, and it has been reissued and rerecorded many times since.

name: White Pony
teaser: Deftones 2000 — the album that proved a nu-metal band could make art. Recorded in Sausalito at the Record Plant, where Fleetwood Mac made Rumours. Chino Moreno brought in influences from The Cure, Depeche Mode, and My Bloody Valentine. The album's atmosphere is equal parts violence and sensuality.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Change (In the House of Flies)' — the whispered verses give way to a chorus that feels like drowning. Then 'Passenger' — Maynard James Keenan of Tool trades vocals with Moreno, each trying to out-menace the other. The album's secret is DJ Frank Delgado's turntable work: subtle scratches and samples add texture without ever sounding like a gimmick.

synopsis: White Pony (2000) is the album where Deftones proved that a band from the nu-metal scene could make art that would outlive the whole movement. The Sacramento band had always been more adventurous than their peers, and for their third album they pushed their sound into strange, beautiful new territory, mixing heavy, downtuned riffs with shoegaze textures, trip-hop beats and Chino Moreno's voice, which could move from a scream to a seductive croon in a single line. The album was recorded in Sausalito at the Record Plant, the same studio where Fleetwood Mac had made Rumours, and its songs, from the crushing 'Feiticeira' and 'Elite' to the dreamy 'Digital Bath' and 'Change (In the House of Flies)', which became their biggest hit, show a band operating on a level none of their contemporaries could reach. The title refers to the idea of a white whale, the unattainable thing every artist chases. White Pony won a Grammy and is now regarded as the album that elevated its whole genre, the record where heavy rock met art and won.

name: Ænima
teaser: Tool 1996 — 77 minutes of mathematically precise progressive metal. The album opens with a Bill Hicks sample about fear-based media. The songs are built from Fibonacci sequences, polyrhythms, and shifting time signatures that music students still diagram. Despite the complexity, the album went triple platinum.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Forty Six & 2' — the song is about Jungian shadow integration. The bassline by Justin Chancellor is in 7/8 while the drums are in 4/4, creating a relentless forward momentum. Then 'Eulogy' — the song's structure mirrors the five stages of grief. Tool wrote the album as a single continuous arc, not a collection of songs.

synopsis: Ænima (1996) is the album where Tool turned their mathematically precise progressive metal into something truly monumental, a 77-minute meditation on anger, transformation and the end of the world. The album opens with a sample of the comedian Bill Hicks railing against fear-based media, and his spirit hangs over the whole record, which is full of fury at complacency and a longing for change. The band's sound is built on the locked-in grooves of Danny Carey's drumming and Justin Chancellor's bass, Maynard James Keenan's voice, which moves from a whisper to a roar, and Adam Jones's churning, textural guitar, and songs like 'Stinkfist', 'Forty Six & 2' and the epic title track, which is built on the sound of a flushing toilet, became anthems for a generation of fans who treated the band like a religion. The album won a Grammy and sold millions, and its combination of intellectual ambition, visual artistry and crushing heaviness made Tool the most important progressive metal band of their era.

name: Rage Against the Machine
teaser: Rage Against the Machine 1992 — recorded in 3 months at a warehouse in North Hollywood. Tom Morello played guitar through a Whammy pedal, a DigiTech delay, and a wah-wah in ways no manufacturer intended, creating sounds that people initially assumed were synths. Zack de la Rocha's rap-delivery made radical leftist politics radio-friendly.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Killing in the Name' — the famous 'Fuck you, I won't do what you tell me' closing chant was improvised. Then 'Know Your Enemy' — Morello's 'guitar solo' at 2:30 is him unplugging and re-plugging his guitar cable at specific intervals to create a rhythmic pulse. The album was produced by Garth Richardson, who had to learn Morello's self-invented techniques on the fly.

synopsis: Rage Against the Machine's self-titled debut (1992) is the sound of revolution set to music, an album that fused the politics of the Black Panthers with the aggression of punk and the virtuosity of metal, and it has never sounded dated. The band, fronted by the charismatic Zack de la Rocha, whose lyrics were full of rage at racism, police brutality and corporate greed, were built around the extraordinary guitar playing of Tom Morello, a Harvard graduate who played his guitar through a Whammy pedal and used it to make sounds no one had heard before, from record scratches to helicopter blades. 'Killing in the Name', with its explosive final command, became one of the most iconic protest songs ever recorded, while 'Bombtrack', 'Bullet in the Head' and 'Know Your Enemy' are relentless attacks on the American system. The album was recorded in three months in a warehouse in North Hollywood, and it sold millions, turning the band into one of the most politically potent forces in music and influencing everyone from System of a Down to countless metal and hip-hop artists.

name: Toxicity
teaser: System of a Down 2001 — recorded in Hollywood just before 9/11. The album was accidentally released a week early; tower records in New York sold copies before street date. The band's Armenian heritage infused the music with Middle Eastern scales and rhythms no metal band had used before. Serj Tankian's operatic delivery made political songs about prison reform and the Armenian genocide feel like anthems.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Chop Suey!' — the song's title came from the way a dead body looks after autopsy. The 'father, father' bridge was Tankian quoting a Bible verse. Then 'Aerials' — the time signature shifts from 4/4 to 3/4 to 6/8 without the listener noticing. Daron Malakian wrote most of the music on an acoustic guitar in his bedroom.

synopsis: Toxicity (2001) is the album that made System of a Down one of the biggest bands in the world, a record that somehow contained Armenian folk melodies, operatic vocals, thrash metal riffs and absurdist humor in every single song. The band, four Armenian-Americans from Los Angeles, were unlike anything else in the nu-metal scene: Serj Tankian's voice could shift from a soaring, classically trained wail to a primal scream, Daron Malakian's riffs were jagged and unpredictable, and their songs moved through more changes in three minutes than most bands managed in a whole album. 'Chop Suey!', with its sudden shifts and unforgettable chorus, became a global hit, and the title track, 'Toxicity', and 'Aerials' made the band stadium headliners. The album was recorded in Hollywood just before the September 11 attacks, and its paranoid, political lyrics, about censorship, war and the erosion of freedom, took on a new resonance. It sold over twelve million copies and remains the band's defining statement.

name: Illmatic
teaser: Nas's 1994 Queensbridge debut — 10 tracks, 5 producers, 39 minutes. The watershed East Coast record. Q-Tip, Large Professor, Pete Rock, DJ Premier, and L.E.S. all produced tracks. Nas was 19 and had been writing verses for 5 years before the album came out.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening of 'N.Y. State of Mind' — Nas recorded the first verse in one take, chain-smoking in the booth. DJ Premier built the beat from a Joe Chambers piano sample. The album is a 39-minute mural of Queensbridge projects — every line is a photograph.

synopsis: Illmatic (1994) is the most revered album in hip-hop history, a flawless 39-minute record made by a teenager from Queensbridge who was determined to be the greatest rapper alive. Nas was nineteen when he recorded it, and he assembled a dream team of the era's greatest producers, Q-Tip, Large Professor, Pete Rock, DJ Premier and L.E.S., each of whom gave him a track that became a classic. Over ten songs, Nas painted a portrait of life in the Queensbridge housing projects that was more vivid and literate than anything hip-hop had heard: 'N.Y. State of Mind' and 'Represent' are street narratives of stunning detail, 'The World Is Yours' and 'Halftime' are full of jazz samples and quiet confidence, and 'Life's a Bitch' features a verse from the veteran AZ that rivals Nas's own. The album sold modestly at first but its reputation grew instantly, and it is now universally regarded as one of the greatest records ever made, the benchmark against which every rapper since has been measured.

name: Ready to Die
teaser: Notorious B.I.G.'s 1994 debut — the only album released in his lifetime. Recorded at Puff Daddy's house in New Jersey between court dates. The album's last track 'Suicidal Thoughts' was recorded at 4 AM with Biggie barely able to get through it.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Juicy' — the famous opening line was a last-minute replacement; Puffy wanted a hook they could sample from Mtume's 'Juicy Fruit'. Then 'Warning' — Biggie narrates an entire crime drama in 3 minutes. The album's arc mirrors his life: from birth ('Intro') to self-destruction ('Suicidal Thoughts').

tracks.title: Fuck Me (Interlude) (censored #!*@ Me (Interlude) on the back cover)

synopsis: Ready to Die (1994) is the debut album of The Notorious B.I.G., and it made the 22-year-old from Brooklyn, born Christopher Wallace, the biggest star in hip-hop. Biggie's genius was his voice and his flow: he rapped with a relaxed, conversational ease over the sparse, menacing beats that Sean 'Puffy' Combs and a team of producers built for him, and his lyrics moved effortlessly between boasts of unparalleled confidence and confessions of desperate vulnerability. 'Juicy', built on a sample of a song about rising from poverty, became his signature anthem, 'Big Poppa' was a smooth, seductive hit, and 'One More Chance' showed his commercial power, while 'Suicidal Thoughts', the album's closing track, is one of the darkest and most honest songs ever recorded. The album made Biggie the king of New York hip-hop just as the East Coast-West Coast rivalry was beginning to consume the genre. He would release only one more album before his murder in 1997, making Ready to Die a singular, towering document of his genius.

name: Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers)
teaser: Wu-Tang Clan 1993 — recorded in RZA's basement studio in Staten Island for $36,000. Nine MCs, one producer. The kung-fu movie samples came from RZA's personal VHS collection. The album invented a new sound: gritty, lo-fi, with minor-key piano loops and off-kilter drums.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'C.R.E.A.M.' — the piano loop is from The Charmels' 'As Long As I've Got You', sped up and pitched up. Raekwon wrote his verse in 15 minutes. Then 'Protect Ya Neck' — every member gets a verse, and they recorded it in one night with the lights dimmed.

tracks.title: Can It Be All So Simple / Intermission
Wu-Tang Clan Ain't Nuthing ta F' Wit

synopsis: Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers) (1993) is the album that changed hip-hop forever, the sound of nine MCs from Staten Island, unified by the vision of their producer, the RZA, into a single, fearsome force. The RZA produced the entire record in his basement studio, building beats from dusty soul samples and, most memorably, samples of kung-fu movies, which gave the album its martial atmosphere and its philosophy of clan warfare. The group's lineup was staggering: Method Man, Ol' Dirty Bastard, Raekwon, Ghostface Killah, GZA, Inspectah Deck, U-God, Masta Killa and the RZA himself, each with a distinct voice and style, trading verses with a chemistry that has never been matched. 'C.R.E.A.M.', with its iconic hook about money, 'Protect Ya Neck', 'Shame on a Nigga' and 'Wu-Tang Clan Ain't Nuthing ta F' Wit' became instant classics. The album was raw, funny, violent and brilliant, and it turned the Wu-Tang Clan into the most influential crew in hip-hop, spawning solo careers that defined the rest of the decade.

name: To Pimp a Butterfly
teaser: Kendrick Lamar's 2015 album — recorded over 9 months at a Compton studio with a live jazz band. The album's closing single 'Alright' became a Black Lives Matter anthem. Kamasi Washington, Thundercat, and Flying Lotus all contributed.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Wesley's Theory' — the opening groove samples Parliament-Funkadelic, then Kendrick's voice cracks like a radio tuning between stations. Then 'For Free?' — Kendrick raps over his own trumpet practice tape. The album's last track reveals the whole thing was a letter to Tupac.

synopsis: To Pimp a Butterfly (2015) is Kendrick Lamar's magnum opus, a sprawling, ambitious album that fused hip-hop with jazz, funk, soul and spoken word to create a portrait of black America that felt both deeply personal and historically vast. Kendrick recorded the album over nine months in a studio in his hometown of Compton, working with a live band that included members of the legendary jazz group Kamasi Washington's ensemble, and the result sounds like nothing else in hip-hop: songs shift from funk workouts to jazz ballads to furious political rants, with Kendrick's voice, which can move from a whisper to a preacher's shout, holding it all together. 'Alright', with its defiant chorus, became an anthem of the Black Lives Matter movement, 'King Kunta' is a brilliant funk workout, 'The Blacker the Berry' is a furious meditation on race, and the title track is a stunning spoken-word dialogue with the ghost of Tupac. The album won the Pulitzer Prize, the first hip-hop album to do so, and it is now regarded as one of the greatest records of all time.

name: The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill
teaser: Lauryn Hill's 1998 debut solo album — the first hip-hop album to win Album of the Year at the Grammys. She was 23, pregnant, and had just left the Fugees. The album sold 15 million copies in its first year; she has never released a proper follow-up.

exploreAction.targetName: The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill (1998) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Doo Wop (That Thing)' — it's 4 minutes of two voices debating economic materialism across a 1950s doo-wop sample. Then 'Ex-Factor' — the song that killed her next album, because the raw emotion was impossible to reproduce. The skit near the end is Lauryn talking to her unborn son.

tracks.title: Can't Take My Eyes Off You

synopsis: The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill (1998) is one of the most remarkable debuts in music history, an album that fused hip-hop, R&B, reggae and soul into something entirely new, and it made Lauryn Hill one of the most celebrated artists of her generation. Hill was 23 when she recorded it, having just left the Fugees at the height of their fame, and the album is a deeply personal document of heartbreak, self-discovery and spiritual searching, narrated by a fictional teacher's lessons between songs. 'Doo Wop (That Thing)' became her biggest hit, 'Ex-Factor' and 'Lost Ones' are masterpieces of relationship drama, and 'To Zion', written about her decision to have her first child, is one of the most moving songs of the decade. The album was the first hip-hop record to win Album of the Year at the Grammys, and it sold millions. Hill would release no proper follow-up, which only added to the album's legend, and it remains a singular, untouchable classic.

name: My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy
teaser: Kanye West's 2010 album — recorded in a Hawaii studio over a year with dozens of collaborators. Made after the Taylor Swift incident when the world turned on him. The album becomes a maximalist fever dream of self-examination and self-aggrandizement.

exploreAction.targetName: My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy (2010) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Runaway' — 9 minutes, a single verse, and a 4-minute vocoder outro. The line 'let's have a toast for the douchebags' is delivered without apology. Then 'All of the Lights' — 14 vocalists including Rihanna, Elton John, and Alicia Keys. The horns were played by a marching band Kanye hired for a single session.

synopsis: My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy (2010) is Kanye West's grandest statement, a maximalist masterpiece that he made after months of public disgrace, and it stands as the most ambitious hip-hop album of its era. In 2009, West had interrupted Taylor Swift at the MTV Video Music Awards, and the backlash was so severe that he retreated to Hawaii, where he spent months recording with an ever-changing cast of collaborators, including Jay-Z, Kid Cudi, Nicki Minaj, Bon Iver, RZA and many more. The album that emerged is a towering, operatic exploration of fame, ego, love and self-destruction, full of symphonic strings, psychedelic production and some of the most extravagant beats ever made. 'Power' and 'Monster' are statements of intent, 'Runaway', a nine-minute piano epic with an extended auto-tuned outro, became his most personal song, and 'All of the Lights' is a masterpiece of maximalist pop. The album was hailed as a masterpiece on release and is now widely regarded as Kanye's greatest work and one of the best albums of the 2010s.

name: The Low End Theory
teaser: A Tribe Called Quest 1991 — the album that proved jazz and hip-hop could be the same thing. Q-Tip and Phife Dawg traded verses over Ron Carter's upright bass. The cover art is a painted nude that the label almost refused.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Scenario' — the posse cut that introduced Busta Rhymes to the world. His verse at the end was improvised in one take. Then 'Jazz (We've Got)' — the beat is built from a 4-bar Jimmy Smith organ loop that Q-Tip found on a dollar-bin record.

synopsis: The Low End Theory (1991) is the album that proved jazz and hip-hop belonged together, a record of such effortless cool that it made A Tribe Called Quest the most respected group in rap. Q-Tip and Phife Dawg traded verses with a chemistry that was part friendship, part rivalry, their playful, intelligent rhymes floating over Q-Tip's production, which was built on jazz bass lines, sparse drums and samples that sounded like the most beautiful music imaginable.
