Ellison said the album was shaped by grief, the death of his mother, and that sense of loss rises through the celestial titles and the gospel-piano close of 'Table of the Elements'. It was his breakthrough, the record that moved him from LA beat scene cult figure to the front rank of experimental electronic music, and its ambition is still startling.

name: OIL OF EVERY PEARL'S UN-INSIDES
teaser: SOPHIE 2018 — the only studio album from the Scottish producer who reshaped pop music's relationship with synthesized sound. Recorded between Los Angeles and Berlin. The songs use industrial noise, bubblegum hyperpop, and ambient drift to explore identity, transformation, and the body. SOPHIE died in 2021 at age 34.

exploreAction.targetName: OIL OF EVERY PEARL'S UN-INSIDES (2018) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Faceshopping' — the synth bass sounds like skin stretching. The video was shot in a mirrored room with SOPHIE's face projected onto a morphing sculpture. Then 'It's Okay to Cry' — the first song where SOPHIE used her own unaltered voice. The song is a ballad over a single piano chord, and it's the most radical thing on the album.

tracks.title: Is It Cold in the Water?

synopsis: SOPHIE's debut album arrived after years of producing rubbery, hyperpop singles for artists like Madonna and Charli XCX, and it is the fullest statement of her vision: pop music rebuilt from synthetic materials, where every sound seems to be made of plastic, latex or liquid metal. The album runs from the brutal industrial crunch of 'It's Okay to Cry' into the glossy surrealism of 'Immaterial', and its lyrics circle themes of transformation and becoming, fitting for a producer who came out as a trans woman while making it. There is real warmth buried under the metallic surfaces, and the record was hailed as a landmark for electronic pop. It was SOPHIE's only studio album; she died in 2021, leaving it as her monument.

name: In a Silent Way
teaser: Miles Davis 1969 — the album where he abandoned jazz structure entirely, recorded with three keyboardists (including a 22-year-old Herbie Hancock) and edited into continuous 18-minute sides by producer Teo Macero. The album is considered the birthplace of ambient jazz and directly influenced Brian Eno's ambient series.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Shhh / Peaceful' — the title is literally the entire musical instruction Davis gave the band. The track was assembled from several hours of improvisation. Then the title track — Macero spliced together three separate sessions recorded on different days into a single piece. The musicians didn't know their sessions would be combined.

tracks.title: In a Silent Way" / "It's About That Time

synopsis: After years of pushing his band through ever faster and more complex post-bop, Miles Davis cut the knot on this record, which abandons head-solos-head structure entirely. He assembled a rare supergroup, with John McLaughlin, Joe Zawinul, Chick Corea, Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter, Tony Williams and Jack DeJohnette all present, and let them drift: the two side-long pieces unfold as slow, luminous vamps over which the soloists float instead of improvising choruses. Davis and producer Teo Macero then edited the tapes heavily in the studio, looping and splicing sections, which made this one of the first jazz records built like a studio artifact. Its quiet revolution pointed straight at the fusion movement that followed, even though Davis reportedly disliked the final mix of his own album.

name: Pastel Blues
teaser: Nina Simone 1965 — recorded in a single day at a New York studio with a small jazz ensemble. The album opens with five short songs and closes with a 10-minute transformation of the traditional 'Sinnerman' into a spiritual that builds like a storm. Simone's piano playing on the album is almost as expressive as her voice.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Sinnerman' — based on an old African-American spiritual Simone first heard at a revival meeting as a child. The 10-minute track has no verse or chorus, just waves of intensity. Then 'Strange Fruit' — her version of the Billie Holiday anti-lynching song strips away the strings and leaves only Simone's voice and a single piano. It's more terrifying without the orchestration.

tracks.title: Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out
Tell Me More and More and Then Some

synopsis: Nina Simone recorded this in a single day at a New York studio with a small band, and the speed shows in the directness of the performances. The set is a mix of jazz standards, blues and folk, but Simone makes everything hers: her version of 'Sinnerman' turns a traditional spiritual into a ten-minute gospel-house firestorm, while 'Strange Fruit' and the title track are delivered with the controlled fury that made her voice a political instrument. She was already a cult figure, and this album, recorded at the height of the civil rights movement, sharpened the politics that would come to define her later work. The songs she chose and the way she sang them made it one of the great statements of mid-60s soul.

name: Chet Baker Sings
teaser: Chet Baker 1956 — the West Coast trumpeter's first vocal album, recorded at 26 when he had never sung professionally. His voice is untrained, fragile, occasionally off-key, and absolutely devastating. The album established the template for every jazz vocalist who prioritized intimacy over technical perfection. Baker hated his own singing voice.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'My Funny Valentine' — Baker's trumpet solo and vocal take were recorded on the same mic, facing each other, with no overdubs. Then 'I Fall in Love Too Easily' — the song is 3 minutes long and Baker sounds like he's about to stop singing at any moment. He was addicted to heroin during the recording; you can hear a tremor in his voice at 1:45.

tracks.title: I've Never Been in Love Before
I Get Along Without You Very Well (Except Sometimes)
There Will Never Be Another You
I Fall in Love Too Easily

synopsis: Chet Baker was already the most photographed face in jazz, a trumpeter in his mid-twenties with a matinee idol look, when he began singing, against the advice of nearly everyone around him. His voice was light, untrained and vulnerable, and on standards like 'My Funny Valentine' and 'But Not for Me' he turned that fragility into a style: he sang the way he played trumpet, behind the beat, barely above a whisper. The album made him a star beyond jazz, with teenage girls mobbing him in Europe, and it effectively created the template for the sensitive crooner jazzman. Critics at the time dismissed it, but it proved astonishingly durable, and Baker's singing became as influential as his horn playing on a generation of musicians.

name: Let's Get It On
teaser: Marvin Gaye 1973 — recorded in Los Angeles and Detroit with the Funk Brothers after the political intensity of 'What's Going On.' Gaye wanted to make an album purely about love and sex. The title track was written in 20 minutes; Gaye recorded his vocal while lying on the studio floor because he wanted to sound relaxed.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the opening guitar riff was played by session guitarist Melvin Ragin on a Fender Telecaster through a Leslie speaker. Gaye's vocal was triple-tracked with himself singing different harmonies. Then 'Distant Lover' — recorded live at a concert where Gaye had a panic attack and walked off stage immediately after.

tracks.title: Please Don’t Stay (Once You Go Away)

synopsis: After the towering social statements of What's Going On, Marvin Gaye turned inward for this record, which he described as an album about sex, an exploration of the force he felt drove everything. The title track, built on a rolling groove Gaye recorded with the Funk Brothers in Detroit, became one of the most-played slow jams in history. The rest of the album mixes that carnality with spiritual searching, particularly on 'Distant Lover' and the closing 'Just to Keep You Satisfied', a pleading ballad sung to his soon-to-be-ex-wife Anna Gordy. It was a commercial triumph that cemented Gaye's second act as a sex symbol, though the marriage crumbling behind the sessions gave the record's joy a melancholy undertow.

name: Mama's Gun
teaser: Erykah Badu 2000 — recorded at Electric Lady with the Soulquarians. The album expands on Baduizm's jazzy neo-soul with psychedelic rock and hip-hop influences. Questlove's drumming is at its most inventive. The album's cover, inspired by a Fela Kuti album, shows Badu as a mythical warrior queen.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Didn't Cha Know' — the beat was built from a sample of Tarika Blue's 'Dreamflower,' which J Dilla found on a dollar-bin record. Badu wrote the lyric about not knowing which direction to take in life. Then 'Green Eyes' — a 10-minute song that changes style three times. The string section was arranged by the late Roy Hargrove.

synopsis: Erykah Badu recorded this at Electric Lady Studios in New York as part of the loose collective of neo-soul musicians known as the Soulquarians, with producer James Poyser and drummer Questlove at the center of the sessions. Where her debut Baduizm was cool and minimal, this record stretches out: 'Penitentiary Philosophy' rides a lazy funk groove, 'Didn't Cha Know' floats over a sample of Donald Byrd, and 'Orange Moon' is pure cosmic balladry. The album is a meditation on love, self-respect and survival that gets deeper the closer you listen. It took a while to find its audience but is now regarded as the peak of her catalog, and its unhurried confidence helped define what neo-soul could be.

name: There's a Riot Goin' On
teaser: Sly and the Family Stone 1971 — the darkest funk album ever made. Sly Stone recorded it at home on a four-track, layering instruments and vocals at all hours while sinking into cocaine addiction. The album's sound is muddy, paranoid, and deliberately out of tune. The title was a response to Marvin Gaye's 'What's Going On.' There was no riot — just Sly, alone, unravelling.

exploreAction.targetName: There's a Riot Goin' On (1971) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Family Affair' — the drum machine was a Maestro Rhythm King MRK-2, one of the first drum machines on a hit record. Sly programmed it himself at half-speed. Then 'Thank You for Talkin' to Me Africa' — a 7-minute noise jam built from tape loops and feedback. The song is Sly and his drug dealer yelling at each other.

tracks.title: Africa Talks to You 'The Asphalt Jungle'
Thank You for Talkin' to Me Africa

synopsis: Sly Stone recorded this album at his home studio in Los Angeles during 1970, holed up with a growing drug habit while the country convulsed around him, and the music reflects every bit of that tension. Gone are the sunny horns of 'Everyday People'; in their place is a murky, slowed-down funk built on drum machines and clavinet, with Sly's voice buried in the mix. The album came out the same week as the Attica prison uprising, and its weary, paranoid grooves, from the title track to the shocking finale 'Thank You for Talkin' to Me Africa', seemed to speak directly to the collapse of the 60s dream. It was a commercial hit and an enormous influence on the funk and hip-hop that followed, though it also marked the beginning of the long unraveling of its maker.

name: Legend
teaser: Bob Marley and the Wailers 1984 — the greatest-hits compilation released 3 years after Marley's death from cancer at 36. It's the best-selling reggae album of all time. Every song on it was written, performed, and recorded before Marley turned 33. The album has never left the Billboard 200 — over 800 weeks and counting.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Redemption Song' — recorded with just Marley's voice and an acoustic guitar. It was the last song he recorded before his death. The line 'emancipate yourselves from mental slavery' was taken from a speech by Marcus Garvey. Then 'No Woman, No Cry' — the live version is from the Lyceum Theatre in London, 1975. The crowd joins the chorus unprompted.

synopsis: This greatest-hits collection, assembled three years after Bob Marley's death, is the album that turned reggae into a global language. Compiled by Island Records founder Chris Blackwell, it draws mostly from Marley's late-70s Island albums, and every song is a standard: 'No Woman, No Cry', 'Is This Love', 'Three Little Birds', 'Buffalo Soldier'. The sequencing moves between love songs, protest songs and faith, which gives the record a shape that feels like a statement of Marley's whole vision rather than a random hits pile. It has sold over 25 million copies worldwide, one of the best-selling reggae albums ever, and for most listeners outside Jamaica it remains the doorway into Marley's music.

name: King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown
teaser: Augustus Pablo 1976 — a dub album where the mixing board became the lead instrument. Recorded at King Tubby's tiny studio in the Waterhouse district of Kingston, Jamaica. Tubby's dub technique — dropping instruments in and out, adding reverb, phasing, and delay — invented remix culture. The album has almost no vocals; the melodies are carried by Pablo's melodica.

exploreAction.targetName: King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown (1976) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown' — the track is a dub of a Jacob Miller song, but Tubby stripped the vocal and added so much reverb that the bass becomes the melody. Then 'Keep on Dubbing' — you can hear the mixing board squeak at 2:15 because Tubby's equipment was held together with tape. The imperfections are the art.

synopsis: Augustus Pablo, the teenager who made the melodica a reggae instrument, recorded the rhythm tracks for this album, but the star of the record is King Tubby, the Kingston sound engineer who remixed them into something entirely new. Tubby treated the mixing board as an instrument, muting vocals into ghostly echoes, dropping instruments out and back in, and drowning the tracks in reverb and delay. The result is dub as a complete language: 'Babylon Rocker' and the title track sound like reggae heard through a wall of water. It is the rare album that both defined a genre and remains its purest example, and it made the dub remix a form that musicians in London and New York would spend the next decade building on.

name: Three Ragas
teaser: Ravi Shankar 1956 — the album that introduced Indian classical music to the West. Recorded in London and produced by George Martin (who would later produce the Beatles). Shankar plays sitar with Alla Rakha on tabla. The ragas are organized by time of day; each one is meant to be heard at a specific hour.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Raga Jog' — it's an evening raga that unfolds in three movements: the alap (slow, unmetered exploration), the jor (rhythm enters), and the gat (the tabla joins and the tempo accelerates). Shankar's fingers move so fast during the gat that individual notes blur into a single continuous sound.

synopsis: Ravi Shankar recorded this in 1956 in London, and the album is exactly what its title promises: three long ragas, each an extended improvisation that unfolds over a drone, with tabla player Chatur Lal answering Shankar's sitar. It was one of the first Indian classical records widely heard in the West, and its unhurried structure, where the music builds from slow meditative lines into dazzling rhythmic fireworks, fascinated listeners raised on three-minute pop songs. Shankar's virtuosity is on full display, especially on the closing fast section of the final raga, and the record helped set the stage for the Indian music craze of the late 60s. It remains the classic introduction to a tradition most of its original listeners knew nothing about.

name: Woyaya
teaser: Osibisa 1971 — a Ghanaian-British band that fused highlife, rock, and funk into a sound that anticipated afrobeats by decades. Recorded at AIR Studios in London. The title means 'we are going' in Ga. The album was produced by Tony Visconti, who was simultaneously producing David Bowie. The cover art by Roger Dean is pure 1970s fantasy.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Woyaya' — the dual percussionists create a polyrhythm that never repeats exactly. The horn section sounds like a Ghanaian funeral brass band. Then 'Beautiful Seven' — a 7-minute instrumental that starts as highlife and ends as psychedelic rock, with saxophone and guitar soloing simultaneously in different keys.

synopsis: Osibisa, a band of Ghanaian and Caribbean musicians based in London, spent the late 60s building a sound that mixed West African highlife with calypso, funk and rock, and this second album is where it all clicked. The songs, led by Teddy Osei's saxophone and the group's vocal harmonies, are warm and rhythmically intricate, celebrating the band's name, which means 'crossing' in the Ga language. 'Music for Gong Gong' and the title track became live favorites, and the band's joyful pan-African sound made them pioneers of what would later be called world music. They were a huge live draw in Britain and toured with rock bands, winning over audiences who had never heard highlife before.

name: obZen
teaser: Meshuggah 2008 — the Swedish band that treats time signatures like a physics experiment. The album's opener 'Combustion' is Meshuggah's only song in 4/4, and it feels wrong because everything else is polyrhythmic. The album's drumming was performed by Tomas Haake, who programmed the patterns on a computer first to confirm they were humanly possible.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Bleed' — the kick drum pattern is four hits, but the pattern shifts over a 4/4 pulse so that the accent lands on a different beat every bar. Haake described playing it as 'meditation through physical pain.' Then 'Dancers to a Discordant System' — the song's riff repeats but never in the same time signature twice.

synopsis: Meshuggah spent the 90s and 2000s perfecting a sound based on polymeters and machine-gun riffing, and this album is the clearest statement of it. The band locks into grooves that constantly shift against the implied beat, with drummer Tomas Haake playing parts that feel like they were designed by algorithm, which, in a sense, they were, since he programmed many of them. Tracks like 'Bleed' demand inhuman stamina and have become a rite of passage for metal drummers. The album's title and artwork point to a Buddhist meditation on anger, and the songs are as punishing mentally as physically. It is widely regarded as the band's masterpiece and a high-water mark for extreme metal in the 2000s.

name: From Mars to Sirius
teaser: Gojira 2005 — a metal album about environmental collapse, whales, and interstellar travel. The French band recorded it in their own studio in a Basque farmhouse. Joe Duplantier's guitar tone makes the riffs sound like they're being played by the ocean itself. The album's environmental themes predate the mainstream climate conversation by a decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Flying Whales' — the song literally musically depicts whales breaching. The riff at 2:40 sounds like a pod of whales communicating through sonar. Then 'The Heaviest Matter of the Universe' — the verse riff is played entirely on one string at 220 BPM with palm muting so tight the guitar sounds like a jackhammer.

tracks.title: The Heaviest Matter of the Universe

synopsis: Gojira's third album tells a story: a whale takes a human on a journey through space to confront the damage humanity has done to the earth. It sounds like a concept album designed by a nature documentary, which is fitting, since frontman Joe Duplantier wrote much of it after watching a film about whaling. The band's sound is massive and precise, shifting from crushing grooves to soaring clean passages, and the title track's rolling, oceanic riffs make the environmental theme feel physical. Songs like 'Flying Whales' and 'Backbone' turned them into the biggest metal band to come out of France, and the album's message of ecological grief has only grown more relevant since it appeared.

name: The Number of the Beast
teaser: Iron Maiden 1982 — the first album with vocalist Bruce Dickinson, recorded over 5 weeks in London. The band was accused of being Satanists due to the artwork and title track. The album's galloping basslines (played by Steve Harris with three fingers, not a pick) became the band's sonic signature.

exploreAction.targetName: The Number of the Beast (1982) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Hallowed Be Thy Name' — the 7-minute closer was written in 15 minutes by Steve Harris. The song has 5 distinct sections and Bruce Dickinson's vocal reaches a high B at the climax. Then 'Run to the Hills' — the song is about the genocide of Native Americans, written from both the colonizer's and the colonized's perspectives.

synopsis: Iron Maiden's third album was the first with new vocalist Bruce Dickinson, an operatically trained singer whose range finally matched the band's galloping ambition. Recorded over five weeks in a London studio, the record opens with the apocalyptic title track, built on a spoken passage from the Book of Revelation, and also carries 'Run to the Hills' and the epic 'Hallowed Be Thy Name', which became a concert centerpiece for decades. Despite accusations of Satanism from some quarters, the album topped the UK charts and broke the band in America. It set the template for British heavy metal's commercial peak in the 80s.

name: Lateralus
teaser: Tool 2001 — an album structured around the Fibonacci sequence. The title track's time signatures follow the sequence (1-1-2-3-5-8-13) and the syllables in the verses match it. The album was recorded in singer Maynard James Keenan's home studio over a year of obsessive refinement. The album art by Alex Grey depicts layers of the human body dissolving into energy.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Schism' — the bassline by Justin Chancellor alternates between bars of 5/8 and 7/8, creating a constant sense of shifting ground. Then 'Parabol' into 'Parabola' — the quiet intro is exactly the same chords as the explosive song that follows, slowed to 1/4 speed. Keenan said the album was designed to be listened to in one sitting in darkness.

synopsis: Tool's third album is structured around the Fibonacci sequence: the song 'Lateralus' arranges its verses in syllables that count 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and the album's themes spiral outward from there. The band spent five years writing it, emerging with their most ambitious and complex music, built on Maynard James Keenan's cryptic vocals and drummer Danny Carey's mathematically precise playing. The title track's time signatures shift constantly while remaining hypnotically groovy, and the album explores spirituality, sacred geometry and the mind's limits. It debuted at number one in the US and is widely considered the band's masterpiece, the moment where their prog-metal experimentation and their pop sense of dynamics perfectly aligned.

name: American Recordings
teaser: Johnny Cash 1994 — a 62-year-old man with a failing career recording acoustic covers in Rick Rubin's living room. No band, no overdubs. Cash sings songs by Tom Waits, Leonard Cohen, Glenn Danzig, and his own 'Delia's Gone.' Rubin had to convince Cash's label that one man and a guitar was a commercial proposition.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Delia's Gone' — Cash begins 'Delia, oh Delia, Delia all my life / If I hadn't shot poor Delia, I'd have had her for my wife.' There is no apology in his voice. Then 'The Beast in Me' — written by Nick Lowe about his own alcoholism. Cash had been sober for 6 years when he recorded it; he chose it because he recognized the monster.

tracks.title: Let the Train Blow the Whistle

synopsis: In 1993, producer Rick Rubin signed Johnny Cash, then a 61-year-old country star whose career had stalled, and suggested he record a set of acoustic covers in his living room. Cash picked songs by artists as varied as Leonard Cohen, Tom Waits, Nick Cave, and Soundgarden, and sang them in a voice stripped of every production trick, accompanied by little more than his own guitar. The title track's stark reading of Waits' 'Delia's Gone' and the gospel-soaked 'Redemption' announced a new, elemental Cash. The album was a surprise hit, won a Grammy, and launched the American Recordings series that would define the final decade of his life, rehabilitating him as an artist of almost mythic gravity.

name: Moanin' the Blues
teaser: Hank Williams 1952 — recordings from the last year of his life, compiled after his death at 29. Williams wrote or co-wrote most of the songs in hotel rooms while touring between shows. His voice sounds decades older than a man in his 20s; the pain isn't performance. 'Cold, Cold Heart' was inspired by his wife Audrey, who'd recently left him.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Cold, Cold Heart' — the song was written in 30 minutes in a Nashville hotel room after Williams saw his wife at a party with another man. Then 'I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry' — the lyric 'the silence of a falling star lights up a purple sky' was Williams's favorite line he ever wrote. The yodel in the bridge was his mother's technique.

tracks.title: I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry

synopsis: Put together in 1952 as Hank Williams' first album, this set gathers the singles from the last years of his life, recorded with his touring band the Drifting Cowboys. His voice is in full command, singing about the pain, drinking and restlessness that were killing him, and the title track and 'I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry' had already become standards. Williams died within months of its release at 29, and the album's rawer, country-blues side helped cement the legend of a singer who defined country music's emotional vocabulary.

name: Golden Hour
teaser: Kacey Musgraves 2018 — a country album that sounds like a sunrise in slow motion. Recorded in Nashville with producers Ian Fitchuk and Daniel Tashian, who had never made a country album before. The production incorporates vocoders, drum machines, and disco strings. Musgraves wrote the album while falling in love with her then-husband.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Slow Burn' — the song begins with only Musgraves's voice and one acoustic guitar, then a banjo enters at 1:15 that sounds like a synthesizer. Then 'High Horse' — a disco-country hybrid with a Bee Gees-style falsetto chorus. Musgraves's label told her it was 'not a country song' and she released it anyway.

synopsis: Kacey Musgraves wrote this album with producers Ian Fischel, Daniel Tashian and Shane McAnally, and together they built a country record that sounds like a warm evening: pedal steel, disco strings, and lyrics about love that actually feel good. Musgraves pushes back against country's small-mindedness throughout, from the disco strut of the kiss-off 'High Horse' to 'Space Cowboy''s quiet dismissal, but the album's secret weapon is its tenderness, especially on 'Slow Burn' and the title track. It won Album of the Year at the Grammys, a rare victory for a country artist at the general awards, and its crossover appeal introduced a new audience to a genre they'd written off.

name: Blood on the Tracks
teaser: Bob Dylan 1975 — a divorce album recorded mostly in New York with a group of session musicians Dylan had never met. Five of the tracks were re-recorded in Minneapolis with his brother's band because Dylan decided the originals were 'too cold.' The album's songs follow a dissolving marriage from multiple angles.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Tangled Up in Blue' — Dylan later claimed he wrote it after spending an afternoon studying Cubist painting and applied the same approach to time in lyrics. Then 'Idiot Wind' — the New York version was angry; the Minneapolis version is sad. Dylan re-recorded it because he thought the first version was too cruel to the subject.

tracks.title: You're Gonna Make Me Lonesome When You Go
Lily, Rosemary and the Jack of Hearts
If You See Her, Say Hello

synopsis: Bob Dylan returned to New York in the fall of 1974, separated from his wife Sara, and wrote a set of songs that dealt in heartbreak with a directness he had rarely allowed himself. The album's core tracks, 'Tangled Up in Blue', 'Simple Twist of Fate', 'Shelter from the Storm', were recorded in New York with a group of session musicians, then largely re-recorded in Minneapolis with a younger band after Dylan decided the originals sounded too rushed. The result is an album of intricate, haunting narratives about love and loss, sung in a voice that sounds older than its years. Many critics call it his finest work, and its emotional honesty made it one of his best-selling records.

name: Songs of Love and Hate
teaser: Leonard Cohen 1971 — recorded in a converted barn in Tennessee with a children's choir and a producer who'd never made a folk album. The album's 8 songs are arranged like a therapy session: confession, anger, bargaining, acceptance. Cohen was 36 and considered himself a failed novelist making a last attempt at music.

exploreAction.targetName: Songs of Love and Hate (1971) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Famous Blue Raincoat' — the song is a letter to a man who slept with Cohen's wife, written in the voice of a husband who can't bring himself to be angry. Cohen later said he never liked the song because 'the lyric was never finished.' Then 'Joan of Arc' — a dialogue between Joan and the fire, where the fire is a lover.

tracks.title: Love Calls You by Your Name

synopsis: Leonard Cohen's third album deepens the baritone gloom of his early work, but the record is stranger than his reputation suggests. Recorded in Nashville with rich string and choral arrangements, it features one of his most harrowing songs, 'Dress Rehearsal Rag', a portrait of a man on the edge, alongside the epistolary heartbreak of 'Famous Blue Raincoat' and the stern invocation of the opening 'Avalanche'. The title is a fair summary: the songs swing between devotion and despair, often in the same verse. It was a modest seller at the time but has grown in stature, and its unflinching look at the mechanics of love made it essential to understanding Cohen's whole catalog.

name: Déjà Vu
teaser: Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young 1970 — the first album where all four members of the supergroup recorded together. Sessions were famously tense: each member recorded their songs separately, the mixing took 800 hours, and the final cost was astronomical for 1970. The album's cover photo was the first album cover to use a brown-toned sepia effect.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Helpless' — Neil Young's vocal was recorded at a different studio from the backing track because he refused to be in the same room as the others. Then 'Woodstock' — Joni Mitchell wrote it from her hotel room while watching the festival on TV; CSNY recorded it before Mitchell released her version. Stephen Stills's guitar solo swallowed 50 tracks of tape.

tracks.title: Country Girl" / a. "Whiskey Boot Hill" / b. "Down, Down, Down" / c. "Country Girl (I Think You're Pretty)

synopsis: After Crosby, Stills and Nash's debut established the supergroup, Neil Young joined full-time, and the four of them spent months in the studio, cutting over a hundred songs to make this record. The album's centerpiece is Young's 'Helpless', with its ache of northern Ontario winters, and the title track, a sprawling meditation on the failures of the 60s counterculture. Graham Nash's 'Our House' and Stephen Stills' 'Carry On' show the pop side, while David Crosby's 'Almost Cut My Hair' captures the era's paranoia. The friction between the four big egos is audible in the music's tension, but that friction also produced one of the defining albums of the California sound.

name: Bridge Over Troubled Water
teaser: Simon and Garfunkel 1970 — their final studio album, recorded while their partnership was disintegrating. Art Garfunkel was simultaneously filming Catch-22 in Mexico; Paul Simon wrote most of the songs alone. The title track's arrangement by Larry Knechtel built from a single piano to a full orchestra and choir, echoing Phil Spector.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Garfunkel's vocal was recorded in a single take, piano-only. The orchestra and choir were added later without Garfunkel's knowledge. Then 'The Boxer' — the 'lie-la-lie' refrain was Paul Simon's placeholder lyric that he never replaced. The snare drum explosion at 3:15 was a real gunshot, recorded in a church lobby.

tracks.title: The Only Living Boy in New York

synopsis: Simon and Garfunkel's final studio album was recorded while their partnership was already dissolving, and the tension is audible throughout. Paul Simon wrote most of the songs, many of them during the sessions, and the pair's harmonies, never more intricate, sound like two people trying to hold a conversation across a widening gap. The title track, with its swelling arrangement, became one of the best-selling singles of the decade. The record topped charts worldwide and won Album of the Year at the Grammys, yet the duo broke up before its release, and the album stands as a farewell that sounds like it was always meant to be one.

name: Tracy Chapman
teaser: Tracy Chapman 1988 — a debut album of ten political folk songs recorded in 8 weeks. The album reached #1 in 7 countries. Chapman performed 'Fast Car' at Nelson Mandela's 70th birthday concert at Wembley, and the song climbed the charts globally on the strength of that one TV appearance. The album's simplicity — mostly voice and acoustic guitar — was a rebuke to the excess of 80s production.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Fast Car' — Chapman wrote it at 22 while busking in Harvard Square. The song's narrative arc — hope, escape, disappointment, resignation — unfolds over 5 minutes without a chorus. Then 'Talkin' 'Bout a Revolution' — the song became an anthem of the anti-apartheid movement. The guitar is tuned a half-step down to match Chapman's vocal range.

synopsis: Tracy Chapman recorded her debut in eight weeks with producer David Kershenbaum, and the album arrived fully formed, ten songs of folk and protest written by a woman in her mid-twenties. 'Fast Car' tells the story of a young woman trying to escape poverty with heartbreaking economy, and 'Talkin' Bout a Revolution' became an anthem at a time when political folk was thought to be dead. Chapman's voice, a warm alto that could turn fierce, carried the songs with no adornment. The album made her an instant star, winning three Grammys, and its quiet insistence that a singer with just a guitar could still move millions changed the industry's math.

name: Tapestry
teaser: Carole King 1971 — recorded in three weeks at A&M Studios with James Taylor's backing band. King had spent the 1960s writing hits for other artists in the Brill Building; this was her declaring herself as a performer. The album won four Grammys and spent 15 weeks at #1, a record for a female artist that stood for 25 years.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'It's Too Late' — the electric piano riff was improvised by King in the studio during the first take. Then 'You've Got a Friend' — King and James Taylor recorded their versions simultaneously in different studios. King's version is quieter; Taylor's became the hit. King later said she preferred Taylor's because 'his was happier.'

tracks.title: (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman

synopsis: Carole King had been one of pop's most successful songwriters, co-writing hits with Gerry Goffin, before she moved to Laurel Canyon and recorded her own songs with James Taylor's band. The album came together in a matter of weeks at A&M Studios, and its homespun intimacy, King playing piano and singing in a voice full of grain, felt like a revelation next to the orchestral pop of the era. 'It's Too Late', 'You've Got a Friend' and 'I Feel the Earth Move' became standards, and the record spent six years on the charts. It sold over 25 million copies and made King the first woman to win Album of the Year at the Grammys, redefining what a singer-songwriter could be.

name: Dummy
teaser: Portishead 1994 — recorded in a disused basement in Bristol on an 8-track. Geoff Barrow sampled snippets of film scores and spy-movie soundtracks from charity-shop vinyl; Beth Gibbons wrote lyrics that read like noir film scripts. The album's sound is so cohesive that bands are still trying to replicate it 30 years later.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Glory Box' — the Isaac Hayes sample was cleared only after the album's release, narrowly avoiding a lawsuit. Gibbons's vocal wavers on the word 'tired' at 3:22 because she was actually exhausted from recording all night. Then 'Sour Times' — the sample is from Lalo Schifrin's 'Danube Incident,' a song from a 1960s spy movie.

synopsis: Portishead formed in Bristol in the early 90s, and this debut, recorded in a basement on an 8-track tape machine, created a genre out of whole cloth: trip hop with a film noir heart. Geoff Barrow's production is built on cracked samples of 60s soul and spy soundtracks, while Beth Gibbons sings like a torch singer from a movie that never existed. Songs like 'Sour Times' and 'Glory Box' are built on loops that feel broken and beautiful, and the album's gloom is both seductive and unsettling. It won the Mercury Prize in 1995, and its sound, dubbed 'Bristol blues', spawned a thousand imitators.

name: The Cold Vein
teaser: Cannibal Ox 2001 — a defining album of underground hip-hop, produced entirely by El-P before Run the Jewels. Recorded in a Brooklyn basement over 6 months. Vast Aire and Vordul Mega trade verses about poverty, surveillance, and survival in New York City over El-P's industrial-symphonic beats. The album sounds like the subway at 3 AM.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Iron Galaxy' — El-P built the beat from a sample of a 1970s sci-fi movie score with distorted synth bass underneath. Vast Aire's opening line 'You were a stillborn baby / Mother didn't want you but you were still born' is one of the most quoted bars in underground hip-hop. Then 'Pigeon' — the song is about watching a pigeon and seeing yourself.

synopsis: Cannibal Ox, a duo of Harlem rappers Vast Aire and Vordul Mega, made this album with producer El-P, before he became famous with Run the Jewels, and it is a landmark of underground hip-hop. El-P's production is a dark, dusty mosaic of orchestral samples and static, and the duo's dense, sci-fi soaked rhymes paint New York as a city of cold apartments and colder streets. Songs like 'Iron Galaxy' and 'Pigeon' are both haunting and funny, full of deadpan observations about poverty and paranoia. It is a record that rewards the patient listener, and its influence on the next decade of experimental rap is incalculable.

name: That's the Way of the World
teaser: Earth, Wind & Fire 1975 — conceived as the soundtrack to a film of the same name (which flopped; the album became a classic). Recorded in Denver and Los Angeles with a 10-piece horn section. The album's philosophy of cosmic positivity is embedded in every horn line and vocal harmony. Maurice White had been a session drummer for Chess Records before forming the band.

exploreAction.targetName: That's the Way of the World (1975) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Shining Star' — the song was written in 15 minutes during a soundcheck. Then 'Reasons' — Philip Bailey's falsetto reaches a high C at 4:05, a note most operatic tenors struggle with. The live version is even higher. Bailey had never taken a voice lesson.

tracks.title: That's the Way of the World

synopsis: Earth, Wind & Fire conceived this album as the soundtrack to a film of the same name, a Hollywood production that flopped, but the music outlived the movie. Recorded with producer Charles Stepney and the band's full horn and string sections, the record is a summit of 70s funk and soul, with 'Shining Star' becoming the band's first number one single. The title track and 'Reasons' showed Maurice White's ambition to make music that uplifted spiritually as well as physically, blending Afrocentric mysticism with tightly choreographed pop-funk. It was a huge commercial success and remains the band's most beloved album.

name: Spirit of Eden
teaser: Talk Talk 1988 — recorded in a converted church over a year of near-total darkness. The band improvised for hours, and producer Tim Friese-Greene stitched the results into six tracks. EMI demanded a commercial album; Talk Talk delivered this — 41 minutes of free-form art-rock with jazz and ambient passages. EMI sued them.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Rainbow' — the harmonica solo by Mark Feltham was recorded in a cathedral with 17 seconds of natural reverb. Then 'I Believe in You' — Mark Hollis's vocal was recorded at 3 AM in total darkness. The choir enters one voice at a time. EMI lost the lawsuit but dropped the band. Hollis later retired from music entirely.

synopsis: Talk Talk had been a synth-pop band, but by the late 80s Mark Hollis had stripped the group down to its core and retreated into long, costly studio sessions with producer Tim Friese-Greene and a rotating cast of improvisers. The sessions, held in a room kept almost completely dark, produced an album that abandons conventional song structure for slow, luminous collages of organ, guitar, trumpet and found sound. 'The Rainbow' and 'Desire' unfold like dawn breaking, and the record sounds like nothing else made in 1988. It is now regarded as a foundational document of post-rock, though it took years for its reputation to catch up with its influence.

name: Takk...
teaser: Sigur Rós 2005 — the Icelandic band's most accessible album, recorded in their converted swimming-pool studio outside Reykjavík. Jónsi Birgisson sings in a mixture of Icelandic and 'Hopelandic,' a made-up language of nonsense syllables. The album is bookended by a countdown and a countup, framing the listening experience as a single journey.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Hoppípolla' — the title means 'jumping in puddles' in Icelandic. The strings were recorded by a youth orchestra in a Reykjavík school hall. Then 'Sæglópur' — the song sounds like drowning — a slow piano intro, then a massive distorted bass drop at 4:00 that changes the song's language from Hopelandic to actual Icelandic.

synopsis: Sigur Rós's fourth album found the Icelandic band making their most melodic and accessible music, though 'accessible' is relative: the songs are sung in a mix of Icelandic and the band's invented 'Hopelandic' language, and they build from hushed whispers to orchestral crescendos. Recorded in a converted swimming pool in Reykjavik, the album's title means 'thanks' in Icelandic, and the music carries a gratitude for the natural world, with song titles like 'Glósóli' (glowing sun) and 'Hoppípolla' (hopping into puddles). 'Hoppípolla' became a global hit after being used in television and film, and the album remains the clearest entry point into the band's vast, glacier-like sound.

name: Pirate's Choice
teaser: Orchestra Baobab 1982 — the Senegalese band's masterpiece, blending Cuban son, Wolof rhythms, and Congolese rumba into a sound that defined West African nightlife. The band was named after the Baobab Club in Dakar where they were the house band. The album was recorded in two days and promptly went out of print for 20 years.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Utrus Horas' — the title is Wolof for 'the same hours.' The guitar solo by Barthelemy Attisso was improvised in one take. Then 'Mouhamadou Bamba' — a tribute to the Senegalese Sufi saint, with the full horn section playing a melody that sounds like a New Orleans funeral march transposed to the Sahel.

synopsis: Orchestra Baobab spent the 70s as Senegal's most beloved dance band, playing Cuban-influenced music at the club they were named after in Dakar, and this 1982 record is their crowning achievement. By then the Cuban sound that had shaped West African pop for decades was being pushed aside by faster, newer styles, and the band responded by leaning into their roots, mixing son and rumba with Wolof and Manding melodies. The result is a set of slow-burning, intricately arranged songs, led by guitarist Barthelemy Attisso, that are utterly danceable and deeply melancholic at once. The album disappeared for years after the band broke up, and when it was reissued in the 90s it was hailed as a lost classic of African music.

name: Éthiopiques Vol. 4: Mulatu Astatke
teaser: Mulatu Astatke 1998 — a compilation of the Ethiopian vibraphonist's 1969-1974 recordings, the first Ethiopian musician to study at Berklee. Astatke invented Ethio-jazz by fusing traditional Ethiopian scales with American jazz harmony and Latin rhythms. He was the first African student at Berklee College of Music in Boston.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Yèkèrmo Sèw' — the title means 'a man of experience and knowledge.' The melody uses a pentatonic scale that exists in both Ethiopian and Japanese traditional music. Then 'Tezeta' — the title means 'memory' or 'nostalgia' in Amharic. Astatke's vibraphone floats over a rhythm section playing in 6/8 while the horns play in 4/4.

synopsis: Mulatu Astatke trained as a jazz musician in Boston and London before returning to Ethiopia in the late 60s, where he built a new sound that fused jazz harmony and Latin rhythms with the five-note scales of Ethiopian music, a style he named Ethio-jazz. This collection gathers his recordings from the early 70s, when he was backed by Ethiopian funk and soul bands and played vibraphone, keyboards and percussion over grooves that sounded unlike anything else in jazz. The music is unhurried and hypnotic, built on repeating vamps with Astatke's vibes floating on top. Rediscovered in the late 90s when the Éthiopiques series brought Ethiopian music to Western ears, his work became a touchstone for a new generation of DJs and producers.

name: Soro
teaser: Salif Keita 1987 — the 'Golden Voice of Africa' recording in Paris after being exiled from Mali for his albinism (considered a curse by some). Produced by Ibrahima Sylla, who brought in synthesizers and drum machines to modernize Keita's traditional Mande griot music. The result was Afro-pop before the term existed.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Soro (Afriki)' — Keita's voice enters at full volume with no buildup, as is traditional in Mande praise-singing. Then 'Sina (Soumbouya)' — the kora player is Toumani Diabaté, then 21 years old, from a family of griots going back 71 generations. The drum programming was done on a Roland TR-808.

synopsis: After being exiled from Guinea in 1984 following a coup, Salif Keita, a singer of royal Malian descent known as the Golden Voice of Africa, settled in Paris and set out to make an album that could reach the world without watering down his sound. Soro was recorded with a group of French session players who helped him weave his griot heritage into a slicker, synthesizer-heavy production, and the title track became a hit across Europe and Africa. Keita's voice, an extraordinary tenor that can leap from a whisper to a roar, carries songs about exile, love and the struggles of his continent. The album made him an international star and opened the door for a wave of African artists on the world music circuit.

name: Moussolou
teaser: Oumou Sangaré 1991 — the debut album from the Malian singer that sold 200,000 copies in West Africa on cassette. Sangaré was 21 and singing Wasulu music, traditionally women's music from southern Mali, amplified by electric guitar and trap drums. The lyrics advocate for women's rights in a polygamous society.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Diaraby Nene' — the title means 'the sweetness of love.' Sangaré's vocal line is doubled by a single violin played by a member of the National Orchestra of Mali. Then 'Moussolou' — the title track is a direct address to women, telling them to stand up against forced marriage. Sangaré wrote it after her mother was abandoned by her polygamous husband.

synopsis: Oumou Sangaré was in her early twenties and already a celebrated voice in Mali when she recorded this debut, and it turned her into a star across West Africa. The songs, sung in the Wassoulou tradition of her region, are direct and modern in their concerns: she sings about arranged marriage, women's independence and the right to choose a partner, themes that made her a hero to women who had never heard those words in pop music. Her voice is huge and joyful, riding on the kamalen ngoni, a traditional hunter's harp, with a rhythm section that makes the record feel both ancient and contemporary. It sold hundreds of thousands of copies in West Africa, an almost unheard-of number for a woman singer at the time.

name: Franco et le TP OK Jazz — 20ème Anniversaire
teaser: Franco Luambo Makiadi 1976 — a 6-LP set recorded live over 6 nights in Kinshasa, celebrating 20 years of Congo's greatest band. Franco's guitar style, known as 'mi-solo,' blends rhythm and lead into a single endlessly flowing line. The band included 30 musicians, and the lineup changed every night.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Mario' — a 14-minute song about a gigolo that became a pan-African anthem. Franco narrates the story over a two-chord groove that never changes. Then 'AZDA' — a tribute to a bus company. Congolese rumba is built on a guitar pattern that cycles forever; the listener's job is to find the micro-variations.

tracks.title: Matata Ya Muasi Na Mobali Ekoki Kosila Te
Tosambi Bapeji Yo Raison Na Quartier
Bokolo Bana Ya Mbanda Na Yo Malamu

synopsis: To celebrate two decades of the TP OK Jazz band he led, Franco, the most important guitarist and bandleader in Congolese music, organized this six-record set, recorded live over six nights in Kinshasa. The marathon format suited Franco's style perfectly: his songs were known for their length, with solos and call-and-response sections that could stretch past ten minutes as he sermonized in Lingala about love, money, politics and gossip. The set captures the full glory of the band's Cuban-derived soukous sound at its peak, with Franco's chiming lead guitar weaving through horn charts and a dozen voices. It stands as a monument to the man who dominated African popular music for three decades.

name: África Brasil
teaser: Jorge Ben 1976 — a Brazilian samba-rock album that linked Black Brazilian identity to African roots. Ben played a custom guitar with only four strings because he preferred the sound. The album was recorded during Brazil's military dictatorship; the Black pride messaging was a coded form of political resistance.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Ponta de Lança Africano (Umbabarauma)' — the title refers to an African football striker. The rhythm is a samba beat played by a rock band. Then 'Xica da Silva' — a celebration of the 18th-century enslaved woman who became the wealthiest person in colonial Brazil. Ben sings her name like an incantation.

synopsis: Jorge Ben had spent the 60s as one of Brazil's most inventive pop stars, but on this 1976 album he pulled together the threads of his music into a statement of Black Brazilian identity. The record mixes samba with rock, funk and soul, and its lyrics celebrate Afro-Brazilian culture, history and religion with a warmth and humor that make the politics go down easy. Songs like 'Taj Mahal' and 'Xica da Silva' are built on Ben's signature guitar style, a percussive strumming that sounds like a rhythm section by itself. It was a huge hit in Brazil and has been celebrated ever since as one of the key documents of the Black movement in Brazilian popular music.

name: Clube da Esquina
teaser: Milton Nascimento & Lô Borges 1972 — a double album recorded in a rented house in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, that invented a new Brazilian sound: Beatles-inspired songwriting filtered through Minas Gerais folk traditions and Catholic church music. Borges was 19 when he co-wrote half the songs.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Tudo Que Você Podia Ser' — the song's melody was written on a piano that was out of tune. Then 'Nada Será Como Antes' — the title means 'nothing will be as it was before.' The vocal harmonies between Nascimento and Borges were recorded with both singers sharing a single microphone in an untreated room.

tracks.title: Um Girassol Da Cor De Seu Cabelo

synopsis: Milton Nascimento and Lô Borges, two young songwriters from Belo Horizonte, spent months in 1971 writing songs together in a rented house with a group of friends, and the double album that came out of those sessions became a landmark of Brazilian music. The record's songs, many co-written across the whole group, move between delicate acoustic meditations and soaring, orchestral pop, all built around Nascimento's extraordinary voice, which floats above the arrangements like an instrument of its own. The lyrics are full of references to the mountains and highways of Minas Gerais, giving the album a deep sense of place. It is one of the most beloved records in the Brazilian canon, endlessly influential on later generations of musicians.

name: Construção
teaser: Chico Buarque 1971 — a concept album about a construction worker who falls to his death from a building, recorded under Brazil's military dictatorship. Every song is a coded protest. Buarque's lyrics were so cleverly disguised that censors approved the album; only later did they realize every song was political.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — every line ends with a proparoxytone word (a word stressed on the antepenultimate syllable), a formal constraint that makes the song feel like it's constantly off-balance. Then 'Deus Lhe Pague' — the title means 'God repay you,' a phrase beggars use. The song lists everything the narrator paid for and was never given.

synopsis: Chico Buarque, Brazil's most celebrated songwriter, had been fighting the military dictatorship's censors for years when he wrote this, his most ambitious record. The title track tells the story of a construction worker who dies in a fall, and Buarque set it to music that builds relentlessly, an ascending melody that mirrors the building of the tower and the man's fatal climb. The rest of the album explores similar themes of ordinary people crushed by power, wrapped in arrangements that mix samba, bossa nova and theatrical flourishes. It was released at the height of the dictatorship's repression and became an anthem of quiet resistance, widely considered the greatest album in the history of Brazilian popular music.

name: Elis & Tom
teaser: Elis Regina and Tom Jobim 1974 — the greatest Brazilian singer and the greatest Brazilian songwriter meeting in a Los Angeles studio. The sessions were tense: Jobim wanted total control, Regina wanted to interpret. At one point Regina said 'I hate you, Tom' and Jobim replied 'I hate you too.' Then they recorded 'Águas de Março' in a single flawless take.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Águas de Março' — the song lists everyday objects, each one a fragment of a larger mosaic. Jobim's English translation uses completely different objects from the Portuguese original. Then 'Corcovado' — recorded with the lights dimmed and Jobim at the piano. Regina's vocal at the final 'quiet nights of quiet stars' is a single breath held for 20 seconds.

tracks.title: Só Tinha de Ser com Você

synopsis: By 1974 Elis Regina was Brazil's most powerful singer and Tom Jobim its greatest songwriter, and the two had never recorded together. Producer Aloysio de Oliveira arranged a meeting in Los Angeles, where they spent days choosing songs and two weeks recording them in a rented house, with Jobim on piano and Regina's voice pushed to the front. The album is a relaxed, intimate set of Jobim's classics, including 'Águas de Março' and 'Corcovado', sung with a freedom and joy that captures two masters enjoying each other. Regina later said she was terrified of singing with Jobim, but the record sounds like pure pleasure, and it is regarded as one of the finest bossa nova albums ever made.

name: Éthiopiques Vol. 7: Mahmoud Ahmed
teaser: Mahmoud Ahmed 1975 — the golden voice of Ethiopian music. Recorded in Addis Ababa with the Ibex Band, a group of musicians from the Imperial Police Orchestra. Ahmed's melismatic style, stretching single syllables across multiple notes, comes from Ethiopian Orthodox church chanting. The albums were recorded during the last years of Emperor Haile Selassie's reign.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Ere Mela Mela' — the 16-minute title track is built on a single pentatonic scale that repeats for the entire duration. Ahmed's voice rises and falls in waves. Then 'Atawurulign Lela' — the horn section plays in parallel fifths, a harmonic choice derived from Ethiopian church music. The rhythm section plays a 6/8 groove that never repeats.

synopsis: Mahmoud Ahmed was one of the most popular singers in Addis Ababa in the 1970s, and these recordings, made for the city's Kaifa label, capture the golden age of Ethiopian popular music before the revolution silenced it. Ahmed's voice is a remarkable instrument, a high, keeling tenor that slides around the melody in ways that sound almost like Arabic or Indian singing, over arrangements built on electric guitar, horns and the pentatonic scales of Ethiopian tradition. The music is danceable but strange to Western ears, with its shifting rhythms and bent notes. When the album was reissued in the West decades later, it became one of the best-selling records in the influential Éthiopiques series and introduced a lost world of music to a new audience.

name: Buscando América
teaser: Rubén Blades 1984 — the Panamanian singer-composer's salsa album about Latin American identity, politics, and the disappeared. Recorded with the Seis del Solar band, who played salsa without the traditional horn section: just vibraphone, bass, piano, and percussion. Blades has a Harvard Law degree and ran for president of Panama.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Desapariciones' — a song about people 'disappeared' by Latin American dictatorships. The chorus lists the names and descriptions of the missing. Then 'El Padre Antonio y el Monaguillo Andrés' — a priest is assassinated during Mass while his altar boy watches. Blades wrote it after Archbishop Oscar Romero was murdered in El Salvador.

tracks.title: El Padre Antonio y el Monaguillo Andrés

synopsis: Rubén Blades, a Panamanian lawyer turned singer-songwriter, had already made waves in New York salsa by writing literate lyrics about the lives of ordinary Latin Americans, and this album with his band Seis del Solar made the case whole. The title means 'searching for America', and the songs examine the idea of Latin American identity from every angle: politics, exile, the immigrant's double life, the region's dictators and its hopes. Blades sings with a storyteller's urgency over arrangements that mix salsa with rock and jazz, and the record is as much a work of journalism as of music. It is widely considered the most important salsa album of the 80s for proving the genre could carry serious ideas.

name: Clandestino
teaser: Manu Chao 1998 — the former Mano Negra frontman recording alone with a laptop, a guitar, and a portable studio while traveling through Latin America. The album was recorded in hotel rooms, train stations, and at a Zapatista camp in Chiapas. It's sung in Spanish, French, English, Portuguese, and Arabic. The album sold 5 million copies without mainstream radio play.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Clandestino' — the song is about being an undocumented immigrant: 'I'm a clandestine, I'm illegal.' The radio broadcast at the end is an actual Mexican border radio transmission. Then 'Desaparecido' — a song about being a person without papers, traveling without a destination. Chao recorded his vocal in a bathroom for natural reverb.

synopsis: After leading the raucous Franco-Spanish band Mano Negra through the late 80s, Manu Chao dropped out of the rock circus, traveled through Latin America, and returned to record alone in his home studio with a laptop and a crate of found sounds. The album he made is a collage of styles and languages, mostly Spanish, mixing reggae, salsa, punk and hip-hop over homemade beats, with street noises and radio fragments woven through. Its songs about borders, migrants and the dispossessed of the global south made it an unlikely worldwide hit, selling millions without a major label push. It turned Chao into a one-man ambassador of a rootless, multilingual pop music that belonged to no single country.

name: Amassakoul
teaser: Tinariwen 2004 — a band of Tuareg nomads from the Sahara whose music is called 'desert blues.' Formed in Libyan refugee camps where the members received military training and electric guitars. The songs are about exile, rebellion, and the longing for the desert homeland. Many members fought in Tuareg rebellions before becoming full-time musicians.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Amassakoul 'N' Ténéré' — the title means 'traveler in the desert.' The guitar riff cycles through three chords while the call-and-response vocals are traditional Tuareg poetry. Then 'Chet Boghassa' — a tribute to a Tuareg heroine who fought against French colonization. The rhythm is a camel's walking pace.

synopsis: Tinariwen grew out of a group of Tuareg rebels who took up guitars alongside their weapons in the Libyan desert camps of the 1980s, and by the time they recorded this debut they had become the voice of the Saharan people. The band's music is built on interlocking guitar lines that imitate the rhythms of the camel caravans and the Tuareg drum traditions, played over hypnotic, trance-like grooves with vocals that call and answer across the mix. It is rock music in the loosest sense, closer to a desert meditation than to anything on Western radio. The album announced a whole new genre, dubbed desert blues, and its mixture of rebellion, poetry and ancient culture made Tinariwen festival stars and spokespeople for their people.

name: Shahen-Shah
teaser: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan 1989 — the Pakistani Qawwali master's first international release on Peter Gabriel's Real World label. Recorded in one session with his 10-member party, which included his brothers and nephews. Khan's voice could sustain a note for over a minute; he used circular breathing techniques developed from years of practice.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Allah Hoo Allah Hoo' — a 12-minute praise song that starts as a whisper and becomes a storm. Khan's voice climbs through at least four octaves. Then the title track — the harmonium and tabla build a drone over which Khan improvises for minutes at a stretch. The audience shouts 'Wah!' (an expression of ecstasy) throughout.

tracks.title: Kali Kali Zulfon Ke Phande Nah Dalo
Meri Ankhon Ko Bakhshe Hain Aansoo
Nit Khair Mansan Sohnia Main Teri
Kehna Ghalat Ghalat To Chhupana Sahi Sahi

synopsis: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan had been the most celebrated performer of qawwali, the devotional Sufi music of Pakistan, since inheriting his family's tradition as a young man, but this was the album that brought his extraordinary voice to the wider world. Recorded with his ensemble and released in the West, it presents the ecstatic core of qawwali: long, building songs of praise and longing in which Khan's voice, one of the most powerful and flexible ever recorded, leaps and soars through ornaments that seem to defy the physics of singing. The call-and-response with his chorus, the handclaps, the accelerating climaxes, all of it is aimed at inducing spiritual transport. It opened the door to his later collaborations with Western musicians and made him a global ambassador for Sufi music.

name: Heartwork
teaser: Carcass 1993 — the album where the grindcore pioneers pivoted to melodic death metal and invented the template that dozens of bands would follow. The cover art is an H.R. Giger sculpture of a human figure made of welded metal. The lyrics were written by Jeff Walker, a former pathology student, using genuine medical terminology.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the riff at 2:10 is a harmonized twin-guitar line that sounds more like Iron Maiden than any death metal band before it. Then 'No Love Lost' — the opening riff was Bill Steer's attempt to write a song in the style of a ZZ Top boogie, played at double-speed through a distortion pedal.

synopsis: Carcass had spent the late 80s as the most extreme band in extreme metal, writing songs with clinical precision about disease and decay, but on this record they took their musicianship to a new level. Guitarist Bill Steer and bassist Jeff Walker, who also sang, learned to play melodies that cut through the blast beats, and the album's title track and 'No Love Lost' showed that death metal could be both brutal and tuneful. The lyrics kept their surgical obsessions, now turned on the corruption of the human heart rather than the body. It is the record that built the bridge between grindcore and melodic death metal, and its influence on the next decade of European metal is immense.

name: Bergtatt
teaser: Ulver 1995 — a Norwegian album that fused black metal with Norwegian folk music. The title means 'spellbound' or 'taken into the mountain' in archaic Norwegian, referring to a folk tale about a maiden lured into a mountain by a supernatural being. Garm's vocals alternate between black metal screams and clean folk singing.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Capitel I: I Troldskog faren vild' — the title means 'lost in the troll forest.' The song shifts from acoustic folk to black metal without a transition, as if the music itself has been kidnapped. Then 'Capitel III: Graablick blev hun vaer' — the clean vocal sections are sung in a style derived from Norwegian folk hymns.

tracks.title: Capitel I: I Troldskog faren vild
Capitel II: Soelen gaaer bag Aase need
Capitel III: Graablick blev hun vaer
Capitel V: Bergtatt - Ind i Fjeldkamrene

synopsis: Ulver, a young Norwegian band whose name means 'wolf', recorded this debut in the winter of 1993-94, when the black metal scene of their country was at its most notorious, and they set themselves apart immediately. The album mixes the raw, tremolo-picked guitars and shrieked vocals of black metal with passages of clear, ancient-sounding folk song, sung in Norwegian over acoustic instruments, telling a story of a man lost in the wilderness who meets his fate. The production is cold and distant, like the record was recorded in a forest, which it partly was. It is regarded as one of the first and best albums to fuse black metal with folk, and it set Ulver on a path of constant reinvention that has never stopped surprising.

name: Autumn Aurora
teaser: Drudkh 2004 — Ukrainian black metal inspired by the landscapes of Eastern Europe. The band is anonymous by choice. The lyrics are Ukrainian poetry by authors like Oleksandr Oles and Oleh Olzhych, both suppressed during the Soviet era. The album's title and sound evoke the Ukrainian steppe in late autumn: barren, beautiful, and cold.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Summoning the Rain' — the opening blast beat is so fast it becomes texture rather than rhythm. Then the keyboards enter like a fog rolling across a field. The guitar melodies are in a minor scale that sounds like Ukrainian folk music slowed to 1/4 speed.

tracks.title: Вітер нічних лісів (Wind of the Night Forests)

synopsis: Drudkh, a Ukrainian band that emerged in the early 2000s, make black metal that sounds like weather: slow, vast, and shaped by the landscape of their homeland. This, their second album, is built on long, hypnotic songs with titles drawn from Ukrainian poetry, and the music unfolds like the changing of seasons, from the frozen opening to the thaw of the final track. The guitars are layered into shimmering walls of sound, the vocals buried and distant, and the drums move between trance-like patterns and bursts of fury. It is a record that rewards patience, and it helped establish the Eastern European school of atmospheric black metal, in which nature and national history replace the satanic posturing of the genre's Scandinavian founders.

name: Dopethrone
teaser: Electric Wizard 2000 — the heaviest album ever made, according to its own press release. Recorded in a disused church in Dorset, UK, with the volume turned up to levels that damaged the band's hearing permanently. The riffs are played so slowly that the gaps between notes become the music. The lyrics are about Lovecraft, Satan, weed, and the apocalypse.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Funeralopolis' — the opening riff drops to a frequency that vibrates your chest rather than your ears. The bass and guitar are tuned down to B-standard. Then 'We Hate You' — the lyrics are a list of things the band hates, screamed through a distortion pedal. The album was mixed at a volume so high the studio monitors caught fire.

synopsis: Electric Wizard's third album is a monument of doom metal, an hour of music played at the slowest possible tempo and the heaviest possible volume, soaked in horror films, weed smoke and occult imagery. Guitarist and singer Jus Oborn writes riffs that sound like they are being played by a band drowning in molasses, and the record's three long songs and several shorter ones grind forward with a weight that feels physical. The album's press release famously called it the heaviest record ever made, and while that is arguable, its commitment to pure, crushing slowness set the template for an entire generation of doom and stoner metal bands. It has become the cult record of its scene.

name: Colors
teaser: Between the Buried and Me 2007 — a single continuous 64-minute song broken into 8 tracks, recorded in one take. The album cycles through death metal, jazz fusion, surf rock, polka, and country in a single unbroken performance. The band rehearsed the entire album for two months before recording.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Sun of Nothing' — the song shifts from death metal blast beats to a lounge-jazz piano solo at 5:00, then to a country hoedown at 7:30, all without a break. Then 'White Walls' — the closing 14-minute track has a guitar solo that quotes the opening track's melody, bringing the album full circle. The final note hangs for 30 seconds.

synopsis: Between the Buried and Me's fourth album is one long piece of music, broken into eight sections, that runs over an hour without a pause. The band had been building toward this ambition for years, and on Colors they let all of their influences fight it out in the same songs: death metal blast beats, jazz fusion guitar, carnival organ, delicate clean singing, even a cappella passages, all stitched together into a single seamless flow. The result is exhausting and exhilarating, a record that demands full attention and rewards repeated listens with new connections between its parts. It is the album that made the band the standard bearers of progressive metalcore, and it remains a benchmark of technical ambition in heavy music.

name: Jane Doe
teaser: Converge 2001 — 45 minutes of pure aggression about a failed relationship, recorded in three weeks. Jacob Bannon's vocals are unintelligible; the lyrics were printed separately because no one could understand them. The cover art is a distorted photograph of a woman's face that Bannon took himself. Every metalcore band since has tried and failed to match this.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Concubine' — the opening track is 1:19 long and opens with a scream that sounds like someone being thrown from a window. Then the title track — 11 minutes that starts as a ballad, becomes a thrash assault, and ends in feedback. Bannon's cat can be heard meowing in the pause at 7:12.

synopsis: Converge's fourth album is one of the defining documents of hardcore punk's metallic evolution, forty-five minutes of music built on the collapse of a relationship that singer Jacob Bannon and guitarist Kurt Ballou were living through as they made it. The songs are short and devastating, built on Ballou's jagged, dissonant riffs and drummer Ben Koller's wrecking-ball rhythms, with Bannon screaming lyrics that read like poetry torn out of a private diary. The album's closing title track is an eleven-minute epic that moves from pure rage into a strange, exhausted calm. Recorded in Ballou's basement studio, it became the most influential hardcore record of its decade and a touchstone for the entire genre.

name: Sunbather
teaser: Deafheaven 2013 — a black metal album that alienated black metal fans by being beautiful. Named after frontman George Clarke's experience watching a sunbather in his apartment complex while struggling financially. The album cover is a photograph by Clarke of a sunset in the San Francisco Bay area, printed with the letters in hot pink.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Dream House' — the opening guitar riff is in a major key and sounds like My Bloody Valentine playing black metal. Then 'Vertigo' — the blast beats enter at 2:00 and don't stop for 10 minutes, but the tremolo-picked chords underneath stay beautiful. The album was mixed without bass guitar, so the guitars dominate everything.

synopsis: Deafheaven came out of the San Francisco underground with a debut EP and then this album, which took the blast beats and shrieked vocals of black metal and set them inside bright, soaring melodies and clean, arena-sized guitar tones. The music is named for the way sunlight feels on the skin, and its songs move between passages of pure aggression and passages of shoegaze beauty that black metal purists found sacrilegious. The record was greeted with fury and acclaim in equal measure, and its crossover appeal, praised by publications that never reviewed metal, turned it into one of the most discussed heavy albums of the decade. It opened black metal to a new audience and spawned a thousand imitators.

name: Lowgazers
teaser: Plebeian Grandstand 2014 — French dissonant blackened hardcore that sounds like a building collapsing. The band tuned their guitars to such low frequencies that the notes became percussive rather than melodic. The album's production is intentionally suffocating: there is no space between the instruments.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Thick Jar of Hallucinations' — the track opens with a single dissonant chord sustained for 30 seconds before the drums shatter it. Then 'Lowgazers' — the title track layers three vocals: a scream, a growl, and a chant, all at the same time, saying different things. The album cover is a painting of a head with no face.

synopsis: Plebeian Grandstand make music that sounds like a machine breaking down, and on this, their second album, they perfected the noise. The French quartet plays a kind of blackened hardcore that lurches between blast beats and grinding slowdowns, with vocals that are less sung than spat, and the production is raw and suffocating. The songs are short and dense, built on dissonant riffs that never resolve into anything comfortable, and the record's twenty-two minutes pass like a car crash in slow motion. It is difficult, confrontational music for a small audience, but within the underground it is regarded as a high point of the dissonant metal scene of the 2010s.

name: Mirror Reaper
teaser: Bell Witch 2017 — a single 83-minute song for two members: bass and drums. Written as a memorial for their former drummer Adrian Guerra, who died a year before the album's release. The song contains sections of complete silence, and at one point the bass and drums trade roles. The album art is a painting by Mariusz Lewandowski.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the first 20 minutes: the bassline cycles through four notes while the drums roll like distant thunder. Then skip to minute 50: a vocal sample of their deceased drummer can be heard, his voice pulled from an old demo. The album's final 10 minutes are just bass feedback fading into silence.

synopsis: Bell Witch's third album is a single song, eighty-three minutes long, played by two people on bass guitar and drums. The band had already made a name with slow, crushing funeral doom, but on Mirror Reaper they outdid themselves, composing a piece that moves through many moods across its length, from funereal crawl to passages of almost peaceful beauty, with the bass carrying both the riffs and the melody. The song was written in part as a memorial to the band's former drummer, who died while they were working on it, and his vocals appear on the recording, which gives the music an unbearable weight. It is a demanding listen and one of the most extraordinary achievements in extreme metal's history.

name: Painkiller
teaser: Judas Priest 1990 — recorded after the band fired their drummer and brought in Scott Travis, whose double-bass drumming completely rewired the band's sound. Rob Halford was dealing with the end of a relationship and channeled the pain into a vocal performance that set a new standard for heavy metal singing. The album is about a cyborg messiah.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the opening drum fill by Travis was his audition piece. Halford recorded the chorus in a single breath, hitting a high C. Then 'A Touch of Evil' — the most atmospheric song Priest ever wrote, with synthesized orchestration and Halford singing about a serial killer in a whisper before the full band detonates.

synopsis: Judas Priest had spent the 80s becoming one of the biggest metal bands in the world, and for this 1990 album they responded to the rise of thrash by turning their own sound up to maximum. New drummer Scott Travis, recruited from a glam metal band, gave the group a power and speed they had never had, and the title track and 'Hell Patrol' are among the fastest and heaviest songs they ever recorded. The album is a pure, unapologetic statement of what Priest did best, and it arrived just as the band was facing legal trouble in America over allegations of hidden messages in their music. It was both a commercial peak and a defiant answer to their critics, and it remains one of the great metal albums of its year.

name: Rust in Peace
teaser: Megadeth 1990 — Dave Mustaine's fourth album, recorded after firing the entire band and hiring new members. Marty Friedman, the new guitarist, had never played thrash metal before; his exotic-scale solos came from his background in Japanese pop and flamenco. Mustaine was in and out of rehab during recording.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Holy Wars... The Punishment Due' — the song was originally two separate tracks that Mustaine stitched together after a fan at a concert in Northern Ireland asked him to play something about 'the Cause.' Friedman's solo at 3:30 uses the Phrygian dominant scale, a Middle Eastern mode that sounds like a snake charmer at high speed.

synopsis: Megadeth's fourth album was recorded under the shadow of frontman Dave Mustaine's drug problems, which were so bad that he fired the entire band and started over with a new lineup, including guitarist Marty Friedman and drummer Nick Menza. The new group rehearsed for months and then recorded what is widely considered the peak of technical thrash metal. The album's opening one-two punch of 'Holy Wars... The Punishment Due' and 'Hangar 18' set a standard for speed and precision that few bands have matched, and Friedman's exotic, classically influenced leads gave the music a dimension that pure aggression could not reach.
