It was nominated for a Grammy and is still regarded as the band's masterpiece.

name: Vulgar Display of Power
teaser: Pantera 1992 — the album where groove metal was born. Recorded at Pantego Sound Studio in Texas, a converted garage. Dimebag Darrell recorded his guitar solos in a single day, one after another, without referencing the songs. The album's title came from a line in the film The Exorcist. The cover photo is a fan being punched in the face.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Walk' — the opening riff is one note played with Dimebag's signature 'squeal' pinch harmonic. Phil Anselmo's vocal is a barked command. Then 'This Love' — the ballad starts as a clean arpeggio and becomes a scream of betrayal. Anselmo wrote the lyrics about a girlfriend who left him while he was in rehab.

synopsis: Pantera had spent the 80s as a glam metal band in their native Texas before reinvented themselves as the heaviest thing in American metal, and this album, their sixth, is where they completed the transformation. Singer Phil Anselmo, guitarist Dimebag Darrell, bassist Rex Brown and drummer Vinnie Paul locked into a groove so powerful it created a new subgenre, later named groove metal. Songs like 'Mouth for War' and 'Walk' are built on riffs that seem to swing even at full speed, and Anselmo's roar became the template for a generation of metal vocalists. Recorded at Pantego Sound in their hometown of Arlington, the album broke the band worldwide and stands as the sound of American metal in the early 90s.

name: Chaos A.D.
teaser: Sepultura 1993 — the Brazilian band's pivot from death metal to groove metal, recorded in Rockfield Studios in Wales. The album was influenced by the band's visit to indigenous communities in the Amazon, and the title reflects that: the chaos after Christ. The album closes with a cover of New Model Army's 'The Hunt.'.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Refuse/Resist' — the opening drumbeat is a heartbeat played on a floor tom. The lyrics are about standing up to authority. Then 'Kaiowas' — recorded in an empty hall with the band playing only percussion instruments they built themselves. The song is named after an indigenous Brazilian tribe, the Kaiowá, who were being displaced from their land.

tracks.title: We Who Are Not as Others

synopsis: Sepultura had spent the late 80s as one of the fastest and most brutal bands in death metal, but by 1993 the Brazilian quartet had begun to widen their sound, and this album made the break complete. The songs are slower and groovier than their earlier work, built on riffs informed by the street rhythms of their native São Paulo, and the band drew on the anger and violence of Brazilian life for their lyrics. 'Refuse/Resist' and 'Territory' became anthems for the disenfranchised, and the album's politics were made concrete by the cover art, a photo of a boy facing down a tank. It was their commercial breakthrough in America and Europe, and its fusion of metal with world music influences opened a door that many bands would follow through.

name: Bloody Kisses
teaser: Type O Negative 1993 — a gothic doom metal album from Brooklyn that sounds like the Addams Family formed a rock band. Peter Steele's bass-baritone voice goes subsonic. The album's themes of death, sex, and Catholicism are filtered through a humor so dark it's often mistaken for sincerity. Steele was 6 feet 8 inches tall and his bass was custom-built to match.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Christian Woman' — the song is 9 minutes of whispered seduction over funeral-paced riffs. Steele's vocal drops to a basso profundo C2 at 5:30. Then 'Black No. 1' — an 11-minute song about a goth girl who dyes her hair black. The title is a hair color code. The song takes 3 minutes to get to the first verse.

tracks.title: Christian Woman" * A) "Body of Christ (Corpus Christi)" * B) "To Love God" * C) "J.C. Looks Like Me
Fay Wray Come Out and Play
Bloody Kisses (A Death in the Family)

synopsis: Type O Negative came out of the Brooklyn metal scene in the early 90s with a sound all their own: doom metal slowed to a crawl and played with a black humor that set them apart from the genre's solemnity. Singer and bassist Peter Steele, a towering figure with a deep baritone, wrote songs about heartbreak, sex and death that were equally sincere and ridiculous, and the band wrapped them in layers of gothic atmosphere, female backing vocals, and even samples of horror movies. The album was a slow-burning hit, helped by the single 'Christian Woman', and it turned the band into goth-metal stars. It is the record that defined their sound and made Brooklyn gothic a thing.

name: At San Quentin
teaser: Johnny Cash 1969 — a live album recorded at San Quentin State Prison in California. Cash performed 'A Boy Named Sue' for the first time, reading the lyrics off a sheet of paper because Shel Silverstein had handed them to him that morning. The prisoners' cheers on the recording are genuine: Cash performed a song called 'San Quentin' that said they should burn the place down.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'San Quentin' — Cash sings 'San Quentin, may you rot and burn in hell' and 1,000 inmates roar approval. The song was banned by the California Department of Corrections. Then 'A Boy Named Sue' — recorded without rehearsal. Cash flubs the lyrics twice; the band stops and restarts. The version you hear is the second attempt.

synopsis: Johnny Cash had spent the late 60s playing to prison audiences, and this live album, recorded at San Quentin State Prison in California in February 1969, captures him at the height of his powers as a performer for the incarcerated. The record opens with his reading of 'Wanted Man' and includes the notorious moment when Cash, asked by the warden to behave, responds with a cheerful insult and then plays a song whose lyrics thumb their nose at authority. The centerpiece is 'A Boy Named Sue', a comic epic written by Shel Silverstein that Cash delivers with full theatrical relish. The album topped the charts and outsold even his earlier Folsom Prison record, cementing the image of Cash as the outlaw's singer.

name: Showcase
teaser: Patsy Cline 1961 — recorded in five sessions over nine months at Bradley's Barn in Nashville with producer Owen Bradley. The album features 'I Fall to Pieces' and 'Crazy,' the latter written by Willie Nelson. Cline was skeptical about 'Crazy' because Nelson's demo was 'too jazzy.' Bradley convinced her by slowing the tempo and adding strings.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Crazy' — Cline recorded the vocal while on crutches after a car accident. She had to be helped to the microphone. Then 'I Fall to Pieces' — the song was her first #1 country hit. Cline's vocal was overdubbed because the session musicians had recorded the backing track in the wrong key. She found the correct key without rehearsal.

tracks.title: South of the Border (Down Mexico Way)
I Love You So Much It Hurts
A Poor Man's Roses (or a Rich Man's Gold)
Have You Ever Been Lonely (Have You Ever Been Blue)

synopsis: Patsy Cline's second album was recorded over several sessions in 1961 at Bradley's Barn in Nashville, with producer Owen Bradley surrounding her voice with the lush, string-heavy countrypolitan sound he was inventing. Cline had already scored with 'I Fall to Pieces', and this record consolidated her transformation from a honky-tonk singer into a crossover star, with her version of the standard 'Crazy', written by a young Willie Nelson, becoming one of the best-selling country singles of the era. Her voice, full of ache and steel, carried songs of heartbreak and resilience that appealed far beyond the country audience. She died two years later in a plane crash, which gave this album an extra weight as one of the last documents of her prime.

name: Coal Miner's Daughter
teaser: Loretta Lynn 1971 — named after her autobiographical song about growing up in Butcher Holler, Kentucky, in a cabin with no electricity or running water. Lynn was married at 15, had four children by 18, and taught herself guitar while her husband was working. The album was recorded in Nashville with Owen Bradley producing.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Lynn wrote it in 20 minutes while doing dishes. Every detail is factual: her father washing coal dust off his back, her mother reading the Bible by coal-oil light. Then 'You're Lookin' at Country' — a statement of identity from a woman who was told she was 'too country' for country radio. She was right and they were wrong.

tracks.title: Any One, Any Worse, Any Where
Another Man Loved Me Last Night
It'll Be Open Season on You

synopsis: Loretta Lynn wrote the title song of this album as a memoir of growing up in a coal mining family in Butcher Holler, Kentucky, and it became the biggest hit of her career and the basis for a film about her life. The album around it is a full statement of her voice as a songwriter, mixing songs about the hard lives of working women with love songs and a few covers, all sung in her clear, direct Kentucky accent. By 1971 Lynn was the most famous woman in country music, and this record shows why: she sang about marriage, money and independence with a frankness that no one else in Nashville would touch. It remains one of the essential albums of country music's classic era.

name: Grievous Angel
teaser: Gram Parsons 1974 — released 4 months after his death from a morphine overdose at age 26. Parsons invented 'cosmic American music,' fusing country, rock, soul, and gospel into a sound that no one at the time knew how to categorize. Emmylou Harris, 26, sings harmony on every track; it was her first major recording and launched her career.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Return of the Grievous Angel' — Parson's voice cracks on the word 'angel' at 3:10 because he was recording at 4 AM after a night of drinking. Then 'In My Hour of Darkness' — Parsons recorded the vocal in his living room on a 4-track while dying of drug addiction and grief. His body was stolen by his manager and burned in Joshua Tree.

tracks.title: Medley Live from Northern Quebec" * "Cash on the Barrelhead" * "Hickory Wind

synopsis: Gram Parsons had spent his short career trying to marry country music with rock, first with the Byrds and then with the Flying Burrito Brothers, and this, his second solo album, completed the project. Recorded in Los Angeles with a band that included his partner Emmylou Harris, who duets on several songs, the album moves from the aching country soul of 'Love Hurts' to the rollicking 'Ooh Las Vegas', with Parsons' plaintive tenor and Harris's harmonies floating over steel guitar and piano. The songs are steeped in the country music he had loved since childhood, sung with a rock singer's feeling for dynamics. He died of an overdose before the album was released, and it has since been recognized as the founding document of country rock.

name: Live at the Old Quarter, Houston, Texas
teaser: Townes Van Zandt 1977 — recorded over two nights at a 150-seat club in Houston, just Van Zandt's voice and a guitar. The audience is so quiet you can hear the ice cubes in glasses. Van Zandt tells stories between songs that are as gripping as the songs themselves. He was 33 and already sounded ancient.

exploreAction.targetName: Live at the Old Quarter (1977) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Pancho and Lefty' — the definitive version of his most famous song, with an introduction where he explains he's 'a songwriter, not a performer.' Then 'For the Sake of the Song' — he flubs a chord and mutters 'sorry' to himself. Van Zandt died at 52 on New Year's Day. His tombstone reads 'To Live Is to Fly.'

tracks.title: Don't You Take It Too Bad
She Came and She Touched Me
For the Sake of the Song

synopsis: Townes Van Zandt was known as a songwriter's songwriter, admired by the likes of Willie Nelson and Bob Dylan for songs that cut to the bone, and this live album, recorded over two nights at a small club in Houston in 1973, is the essential document of his art. It captures him alone with his guitar, between songs trading jokes and stories with the tiny audience, then delivering devastating performances of his own material, from the aching 'Pancho and Lefty' to the unbearably direct 'Waiting Around to Die'. The intimacy of the setting lets the songs breathe, and his between-song patter reveals the warm, funny man behind the bleak poetry. It is the best introduction to one of America's greatest songwriters.

name: Time (The Revelator)
teaser: Gillian Welch 2001 — recorded in Nashville with David Rawlings on archtop guitar and harmony vocals. The album's sound is so authentically old-time that critics assumed it was recorded in the 1930s. Welch wrote the songs over 4 years, inspired by the Carter Family, the Stanley Brothers, and a deep reading of American history.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Elvis Presley Blues' — written the day after Welch watched a documentary about Presley's final years. Then 'I Dream a Highway' — a 14-minute meditation that repeats the same five chords for its entire duration. Welch's vocal is so intimate that it sounds like she's singing from the next room. The song is about the impossibility of going home.

tracks.title: I Want to Sing That Rock and Roll

synopsis: Gillian Welch and her musical partner David Rawlings recorded this, their second album, in Nashville with almost no production, just two voices, Rawlings' archtop guitar and Welch's banjo and guitar, captured in a room. The result sounds like it could have been recorded in 1930 rather than 2001, which is exactly the point: the duo had built their sound on a deep study of old-time and bluegrass music, and their original songs fit seamlessly into that tradition. 'Revelator' and 'I Want to Sing That Rock and Roll' are timeless and strange at once, full of death, faith and redemption, sung in Welch's plain, luminous voice. It is regarded as the masterpiece of the duo's catalog and a high point of modern roots music.

name: Car Wheels on a Gravel Road
teaser: Lucinda Williams 1998 — recorded over 6 years in 5 different studios with 3 different producers. Williams fired two producers because she wanted a sound that existed only in her head. The album cost $300,000 — extravagant for a folk album — and it won a Grammy for Best Contemporary Folk Album.

exploreAction.targetName: Car Wheels on a Gravel Road (1998) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the song is a list of Southern childhood images: car wheels on gravel, Loretta Lynn on the radio, a child in the back seat. Then 'Joy' — produced by Steve Earle, who kept urging her to sing louder until she was shouting. The song's title is ironic: 'You got no right to take my joy, I want it back.'

tracks.title: Car Wheels on a Gravel Road
Still I Long for Your Kiss

synopsis: Lucinda Williams spent six years and enormous sums of money trying to record this album, her fifth, cycling through producers, studios and musicians before she got it right, and the struggle is audible in the perfection of the result. The songs are built on her gift for capturing the texture of a place and a moment, from the title track's memory of riding in a car with her father to the cracked love songs and character sketches that fill the record. Her voice, a Southern drawl that can turn from a whisper to a snarl, carries lyrics that read like the best short stories. Released in 1998 to near-universal acclaim, it won a Grammy and made her, after two decades of cult status, a star of American roots music.

name: Copperhead Road
teaser: Steve Earle 1988 — an album that fused country songwriting with hard rock production, recorded with members of the Pogues and Earle's own backing band the Dukes. The title track, about a Vietnam vet who runs moonshine and then marijuana, was banned by some country radio stations but became a rock-radio staple.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the drum loop was created by sampling a shotgun being cocked. The song follows three generations of Appalachian men: a moonshiner, a bootlegger, and a Vietnam vet growing weed. Then 'Johnny Come Lately' — a collaboration with the Pogues, recorded in Dublin. Earle was heavily addicted to heroin during the sessions.

synopsis: Steve Earle had spent years as a Nashville songwriter before getting his own shot, and by the time he recorded this, his third album, he had decided to stop apologizing for loving rock and roll. The title track, about a moonshiner who turns to growing marijuana, is built on a hard electric riff and a drum sound borrowed from arena rock, and it became his biggest hit. The rest of the album follows the same path, mixing his unflinching country storytelling with the volume and swagger of a rock band, including the Vietnam ballad 'Johnny Come Lately' and the working class lament 'The Devil's Right Hand'. It made Earle a star and pointed the way for the whole genre of insurgent country that followed.

name: Wrecking Ball
teaser: Emmylou Harris 1995 — produced by Daniel Lanois in a New Orleans church, using the building's natural reverb as an instrument. Harris was 48 and had spent her career in traditional country. This album completely reinvented her sound with atmospheric production and songs by young songwriters like Gillian Welch, Steve Earle, and Lucinda Williams.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Where Will I Be' — the opening track, with Larry Mullen Jr. of U2 playing drums in a New Orleans church while Harris's voice floats through 7 seconds of natural reverb. Then 'Goodbye' — a Steve Earle song recorded at 2 AM with Lanois playing a dobro. Harris's vocal was the first take; Lanois refused to let her do a second.

synopsis: By the mid-90s Emmylou Harris had spent two decades as the most respected voice in country and folk music, but she was ready to leave Nashville's polish behind. She turned to producer Daniel Lanois, who recorded her in a converted church in New Orleans with a band that included U2 guitarist the Edge, and the album that resulted sounds like nothing she had made before: murky, atmospheric, full of echo and space, with her voice, still achingly pure, floating over music that owed more to rock and ambient music than to country. The title track, written by Neil Young, became her signature song of the decade. It won a Grammy and reinvented her for a new generation.

name: The Grand Tour
teaser: George Jones 1974 — recorded during the most turbulent period of his marriage to Tammy Wynette. The title track is a guided tour of an empty house after a wife has left, with each room representing a stage of grief. Jones was drunk for most of the sessions; producer Billy Sherrill would record Jones's vocals one line at a time because he couldn't remember full songs.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Jones recorded it at 10 AM while hungover. His vocal catches on 'the chair where she'd bring the bottle to me' because the line was too personal. Then 'Once You've Had the Best' — Sherrill had to tape Jones's lyric sheet to the microphone stand. Jones is considered the greatest country singer who ever lived, and he would tell you his life was the reason.

tracks.title: The Grand Tour (Norro Wilson, George Richey, Carmol Taylor)
Pass Me By (If You're Only Passing Through) (H. B. Hall)
She'll Love the One She's With (Hank Cochran, Grady Martin)
Once You've Had the Best (Johnny Paycheck)
The Weatherman (Norro Wilson, George Richey, Carmol Taylor)
Mary Don't Go 'Round (Earl Montgomery, J. R. Richards)
Who Will I Be Loving Now (Carmol Taylor, Agnes Wilson)
Our Private Life (George Jones, Tammy Wynette)

synopsis: George Jones was at the absolute peak of his vocal powers when he recorded this album, but he was also in the middle of the stormiest period of his life, newly married to Tammy Wynette and fighting the drinking that would nearly kill him. The title song, a devastating portrait of a man showing a friend through the empty house his wife has left, became one of the greatest country singles ever recorded, and his reading of it is a masterclass in heartbreak. The rest of the album is nearly as strong, full of the honky-tonk and balladry that made him the greatest pure singer in country music history, a voice that could break your heart and then grin at you.

name: Basket of Light
teaser: Pentangle 1969 — the British folk supergroup at their peak. John Renbourn and Bert Jansch on guitars, Jacqui McShee on vocals, Danny Thompson on bass, and Terry Cox on drums. The band fused traditional English ballads with jazz improvisation. Thompson's upright bass was so virtuosic that he was later hired by Nick Drake and John Martyn.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Light Flight' — the song was used as the theme for the BBC drama Take Three Girls. The guitar interplay between Renbourn and Jansch is so intertwined you can't tell who's playing what. Then 'Once I Had a Sweetheart' — an old English ballad that McShee sings without accompaniment for the first 90 seconds. The silence is as important as the notes.

synopsis: Pentangle brought together two of the finest guitarists in British folk, John Renbourn and Bert Jansch, with the jazz-influenced rhythm section of Danny Thompson and Terry Cox and the soaring voice of Jacqui McShee. This, their third album, is where the group's alchemy worked perfectly, mixing traditional British ballads with original songs and jazz-tinged arrangements that let the guitars weave and sparkle around McShee's clear vocals. The record was a surprise hit, reaching the top five in Britain on the strength of the medieval-flavored 'Light Flight', and it remains the finest hour of the folk-jazz sound that the band had essentially invented. It captures the brief moment when British folk was the most adventurous music around.

name: I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight
teaser: Richard and Linda Thompson 1974 — the first album by the married couple, recorded in 10 days for £2,500. Richard's guitar playing draws from British folk, rock, and Arabic modes (he later became a Sufi Muslim). Linda's voice, untrained and pure, carries songs about death, despair, and the occasional night out.

exploreAction.targetName: I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight (1974) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Great Valerio' — a song about a tightrope walker that's really about the fragility of performance. Then 'The End of the Rainbow' — a lullaby for a newborn baby that tells the baby life will be miserable. Richard played the accordion part on a cheap instrument that could only play in one key. Linda was pregnant during the recording.

tracks.title: When I Get to the Border
I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight
Has He Got a Friend for Me

synopsis: Richard Thompson had spent the late 60s as the teenage guitar hero of Fairport Convention, then left to make music with his new wife Linda, and this debut by the duo is one of the great first albums in British music. Recorded in a few days with Sandy Denny's producer Joe Boyd, the record is built around Richard's extraordinary guitar playing and Linda's warm, plain voice, singing songs of faith, temptation and domestic life that were far stranger and more honest than the folk-rock of the time. Songs like 'The Calvary Cross' and 'I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight' swing between medieval balladry and rock and roll. It made the couple stars in Britain and set the course for Richard's long, idiosyncratic career.

name: Just Another Diamond Day
teaser: Vashti Bunyan 1970 — recorded in a London studio over 6 months with contributions from members of Fairport Convention and the Incredible String Band. Bunyan had spent 2 years traveling by horse and wagon from London to the Outer Hebrides. The album sold fewer than 100 copies and she quit music for 30 years. Rediscovered in 2000, it's now considered a lost masterpiece.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Diamond Day' — the song was written on the back of a horse-drawn wagon during a rainstorm in Scotland. Then 'Where I Like to Stand' — the only recording where you can hear the sound of Bunyan's horse, Bess, neighing in the background. The album is so gentle it barely touches the ground.

synopsis: Vashti Bunyan made this, her only album of the 60s, after a journey across England in a horse-drawn wagon with a dog and a dream of a pastoral commune, and the record sounds exactly like that trip: gentle, rambling, full of wide-open spaces. Produced by Joe Boyd with contributions from musicians who would soon form Fairport Convention, the album is built on Bunyan's small, childlike voice and simple fingerpicked guitar, singing songs of nature, travel and quiet hope. It sold almost nothing on release and Bunyan gave up music for decades, but in the 2000s the album was rediscovered and became a cult treasure, its innocence and fragility speaking to a new generation of listeners and musicians.

name: Parsley, Sage, Rosemary and Thyme
teaser: Simon and Garfunkel 1966 — the album where Paul Simon took over production from the label's house producer. He insisted on recording his guitar and vocals at the same time, then layering Art Garfunkel's harmonies. The album was recorded over 7 months in 6 different studios. 'Scarborough Fair' was their first song to use a folk-rock arrangement.

exploreAction.targetName: Parsley, Sage, Rosemary and Thyme (1966) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Scarborough Fair/Canticle' — the song is two different compositions sung simultaneously. The main melody is a traditional English ballad; the counter-melody is a reworked anti-war song by Simon. Then '7 O'Clock News/Silent Night' — the duo sing 'Silent Night' over a news broadcast listing the day's deaths in Vietnam.

tracks.title: The Big Bright Green Pleasure Machine
Flowers Never Bend with the Rainfall
A Simple Desultory Philippic (or How I Was Robert McNamara'd into Submission)
For Emily, Whenever I May Find Her
A Poem on the Underground Wall

synopsis: After their debut album was dismissed as a Beatles knockoff, Simon and Garfunkel took control of their own recording and came back with a set of songs that proved Paul Simon had become one of the finest songwriters of his generation. The album's centerpiece is 'The Sound of Silence', re-recorded with electric instruments against the duo's wishes, which became their first number one single, and it also includes the darkly gorgeous 'Scarborough Fair/Canticle' and the bitter 'The Big Bright Green Pleasure Machine'. The arrangements, largely by Simon with the producer he trusted, mix folk intimacy with baroque pop ambition. It was the record that turned the duo from folkies into one of the biggest acts in the world.

name: Music from Big Pink
teaser: The Band 1968 — recorded in a pink house in West Saugerties, New York, that the band shared. The album rejected psychedelia and returned American music to its roots: folk, country, gospel, and R&B. Bob Dylan, who lived nearby, contributed three songs. Eric Clapton quit Cream after hearing this album because he felt his own music was pointless.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Weight' — Levon Helm sings the lead on the choruses and Rick Danko on the verses, each playing a different character in the story. Then 'I Shall Be Released' — Dylan's song, but Richard Manuel's falsetto at the climax makes it his. The album was recorded in a basement with the microphones clustered around a single spot on the floor.

synopsis: The Band had spent the mid-60s backing Bob Dylan on his legendary world tour, and when they retreated to a pink house in upstate New York to write their own music, they came up with something that changed rock history. Recorded in the basement of that house and in New York studios, Music from Big Pink is a record of songs that sounded ancient and American, drawing on country, gospel, blues and the rural South, which none of the band members, all Canadians, had ever lived in. 'The Weight' became an instant standard, and the album's ragged, soulful ensemble sound, built on Robbie Robertson's guitar and three singers, turned the tide against psychedelia and toward the rootsy rock that dominated the next decade.

name: Liege & Lief
teaser: Fairport Convention 1969 — the album that invented British folk-rock. Recorded after their drummer died in a van accident at 19, the band salvaged their grief by recording traditional British ballads with electric instruments. Sandy Denny's voice — simultaneously ancient and modern — sounds like she's channeling every British folk singer who ever lived.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Matty Groves' — an 8-minute telling of a 400-year-old murder ballad where a lord's wife sleeps with a servant and the lord kills him. Then 'Tam Lin' — the longest song on the album, telling the story of a woman who rescues her lover from the Queen of the Fairies. Dave Swarbrick's fiddle solo at 5:00 is a single take.

tracks.title: Medley" *I. "The Lark in the Morning" *II. "Rakish Paddy" *III. "Foxhunter's Jig" *IV. "Toss the Feathers

synopsis: Fairport Convention had spent their early years as Britain's answer to American folk-rock, but on this, their fourth album, they dug into the old songs of the British Isles and rewired them with electric guitars and rock rhythms, inventing an entire genre in the process. Recorded after the tragic death of their drummer in a road accident, the album is full of life and invention, from the medley of reels and jigs that opens it to Sandy Denny's transcendent reading of the traditional ballad 'Matty Groves'. Singer and guitarist Richard Thompson, only twenty, plays with a ferocity that belies his age. It is the founding document of British folk-rock, and its influence on everything from Led Zeppelin to modern indie music is incalculable.

name: Live at Monterey
teaser: Ravi Shankar 1967 — an 18-minute afternoon set at the Monterey Pop Festival that introduced Indian classical music to a Western audience. Shankar's sitar and Alla Rakha's tabla held a crowd of hippies in complete silence. The recording captures a single dhun (a light raga) performed with the intensity of a full concert.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Dhun' — Shankar begins with a 4-minute alap, exploring the raga without rhythm. Then the tabla enters and Shankar's fingers move so fast that the sitar sounds like it's generating multiple melodies from a single string. The encore is captured, with the audience—stoned and silent—erupting at the final note.

synopsis: Ravi Shankar had been performing in the West for a decade, but it was this set at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967 that made him a star to the rock generation. His afternoon performance, which stretched to nearly an hour with tabla player Alla Rakha, was one of the festival's most talked-about moments, a spellbinding demonstration of Indian classical music's depth and fire that held a crowd of hippies in total silence and then brought them roaring to their feet. The album preserves the full arc of the performance, from the slow, meditative opening to the dazzling rhythmic fireworks of the closing section. It introduced Indian music to millions and sent a generation of musicians, including the Beatles, running to buy sitars.

name: Folk Singer
teaser: Muddy Waters 1964 — an acoustic album recorded when Chess Records was trying to market Waters to the folk revival audience. Stripped of his electric band, Waters is alone with his guitar, Willie Dixon on upright bass, and Buddy Guy on second guitar. The recording engineer was so careful that Waters later said it was the best-sounding album he ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'My Home Is in the Delta' — Waters recounts his childhood in Mississippi over a single repeated guitar riff. Then 'Feel Like Going Home' — the song is about a longing that has no specific object. The microphone was placed so close to Waters's guitar that you can hear his thumb slide on the strings between chords.

tracks.title: My Home Is in the Delta

synopsis: By 1964 Muddy Waters was the most famous bluesman in the world, the man who had electrified the Delta blues in Chicago and inspired the British bands who were then outselling him, but his label decided the future was in folk and sent him into the studio with just an acoustic guitar. The result is a revelation: with no band to hide behind, Waters' voice, huge and grainy, carries songs like 'My Home Is in the Delta' and a devastating version of 'Good Morning Little Schoolgirl' with a power that makes the electric records sound tame. It is the album that proved the acoustic blues he had grown up with was still the core of his art, and it is regarded as one of the great blues records of the decade.

name: The Rockin' Chair Album
teaser: Howlin' Wolf 1962 — a compilation of Chess singles by the man with the most terrifying voice in American music. Wolf was 6 foot 3, 275 pounds, and his voice sounded like a gravel truck downshifting. He learned guitar from Charley Patton and harmonica from Sonny Boy Williamson. The album's cover, of a rocking chair and a guitar, is misleadingly peaceful.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Smokestack Lightning' — the song was recorded in one take at 3 AM. Wolf sings the opening line a cappella, then his band enters one by one. Then 'Spoonful' — a song about how a spoonful of love/drugs/anything can kill you, delivered over a single-chord drone. Wolf's producer said the sessions were 'like a hurricane' and he stayed in the control room.

tracks.title: Going Down Slow (St. Louis Jimmy Oden)

synopsis: Howlin' Wolf was the most fearsome presence in the Chicago blues, a giant of a man with a voice that sounded like it came from the bottom of a coal mine, and this collection of his Chess singles shows why he was revered. The album gathers the sides he cut in the early 60s with guitarist Hubert Sumlin, whose stinging, unpredictable leads were the perfect foil for the Wolf's booming delivery, including 'Wang Dang Doodle', 'Back Door Man' and 'Spoonful'. The songs, many written by Willie Dixon, are full of menace and humor, and the Wolf's growl, which could drop to a whisper and then explode, made every one of them sound like a threat or a promise. It is the essential document of one of the blues' true originals.

name: Live at the Regal
teaser: B.B. King 1965 — the definitive live blues album, recorded at the Regal Theater in Chicago with a full horn section. King's guitar, Lucille, sings and cries between every vocal line. The audience screams for every note. King was 39 and had been touring for 15 years; this was the album where everything clicked.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'How Blue Can You Get' — B.B. sings 'I gave you seven children, and now you want to give them back' and the audience loses their minds. Then 'Sweet Little Angel' — he holds a single note on Lucille for 15 seconds while the crowd screams louder and louder. B.B. King said he sang through Lucille because his voice couldn't do what the guitar could.

tracks.title: Every Day I Have the Blues (Memphis Slim)
Sweet Little Angel (Riley King, Jules Taub)
It's My Own Fault (John Lee Hooker)
How Blue Can You Get (Jane Feather)
You Upset Me Baby (Joe Josea, Maxwell Davis)
You Done Lost Your Good Thing Now (King, Josea)

synopsis: B.B. King had been a star in the black community for over a decade, but this album, recorded live at the Regal Theater on Chicago's South Side in November 1964, caught him at the moment his fame was about to explode to a white audience. King's guitar, which he named Lucille, sings and cries through the set, answering his own vocal lines with stinging phrases, and the crowd's roar of recognition at the opening notes of each song shows how beloved he was to his home audience. The set list is a greatest hits of his early classics, including 'Every Day I Have the Blues' and 'How Blue Can You Get?'. It is regarded as the definitive live blues album, the record that taught generations of guitarists how the blues was supposed to feel.

name: Born Under a Bad Sign
teaser: Albert King 1967 — recorded with Booker T. & the M.G.'s as the backing band. King played guitar upside-down and left-handed, bending strings so far they sounded like they were being tortured. The title track was written by William Bell and Booker T. Jones, but King's version became definitive. The album was recorded in a single day.

exploreAction.targetName: Born Under a Bad Sign (1967) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the opening riff was played by Steve Cropper on a Telecaster, but King's response bends a single note through three pitches. Then 'Personal Manager' — King plays a 2-minute solo that hits the same bent note 8 times, each one slightly different. Eric Clapton later said King's bends sounded like 'a man crying.'

tracks.title: As the Years Go Passing By

synopsis: Albert King, the hulking guitarist who played a right-handed guitar upside down and tuned it to a strange open tuning, had been a cult figure on the West Coast blues scene for years when this album brought him to a wider audience. Recorded in Memphis with Booker T. and the M.G.'s, the city's finest session band, the album captures King's huge, horn-like guitar sound and his laconic vocals on a set of songs that includes the title track and the immortal 'Crosscut Saw'. The record is the definitive statement of the modern electric blues guitar, and its influence on younger players, from Stevie Ray Vaughan to Eric Clapton, is almost impossible to overstate.

name: The Healer
teaser: John Lee Hooker 1989 — an album of duets recorded when Hooker was 72 and had been largely forgotten by the mainstream. Carlos Santana, Bonnie Raitt, and Los Lobos all appear. The album won Hooker his first Grammy. Hooker's signature style — a single guitar chord repeated over a foot-stomped rhythm — is the sound of the Delta distilled.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track with Carlos Santana — Santana's guitar weeps over Hooker's single chord. Then 'I'm in the Mood' with Bonnie Raitt — the song that made Hooker a star again at 72. Hooker's voice floats behind the beat as if the rhythm is a train he's not sure he wants to catch.

synopsis: John Lee Hooker had spent three decades as a blues legend, but by the late 80s his career had slowed to a crawl, and he was living in a suburb of San Francisco, playing occasional shows. Then a young guitarist named Ry Cooder talked him into recording an album of duets with his admirers, and the result revived him completely. The record pairs Hooker's droning, hypnotic boogie with Carlos Santana, Bonnie Raitt, Robert Cray and others, each duet letting the old master set the pace. The title track, a slow, spoken-sung meditation on healing, became a surprise hit and won a Grammy. Hooker was 72, and the album launched the most successful decade of his long career.

name: Texas Flood
teaser: Stevie Ray Vaughan 1983 — the debut album that brought blues back to rock radio. Recorded in 3 days at Jackson Browne's studio in LA. Vaughan was 28 and had been playing Texas bars for 15 years. His guitar tone was so powerful that the studio monitors kept blowing. The album was nominated for a Grammy and lost, which now seems absurd.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Vaughan recorded it in one take with the lights off because the studio had a power outage. Then 'Pride and Joy' — the guitar part switches between rhythm and lead so seamlessly you don't realize Vaughan is the only guitarist. The band recorded the whole album live with no overdubs.

synopsis: Stevie Ray Vaughan had been playing the clubs of Austin, Texas for years, honing a guitar style that combined the fire of Jimi Hendrix with the deep feeling of the Chicago bluesmen, when this debut album made him an overnight star at 28. Recorded in just a few days with his band Double Trouble, the album leads with a cover of Hendrix's 'Pride and Joy' and Vaughan's own 'Love Struck Baby', then shows its full range across slow blues and hard rockers. Vaughan's playing, all speed, soul and controlled chaos, announced the arrival of the most important guitarist of his generation and single-handedly brought the blues back to rock radio. It remains one of the greatest debut albums in the history of the guitar.

name: Taj Mahal
teaser: Taj Mahal 1968 — the debut that announced a new kind of blues musician: scholarly, omnivorous, and unbound by genre. Mahal studied at UMass Amherst and played with Ry Cooder in a band called the Rising Sons. The album includes songs by Sleepy John Estes, Blind Willie McTell, and Mahal himself, played with a band that included Jesse Ed Davis on slide guitar.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Leaving Trunk' — the opening slide guitar was played on a National resonator guitar that Mahal found in a pawn shop. Then 'Statesboro Blues' — 15 years before the Allman Brothers made it a rock anthem, Mahal plays it as a solo acoustic blues. The album was recorded for $4,000.

tracks.title: Statesboro Blues (Blind Willie McTell, Taj Mahal)
Checkin' Up on My Baby (Sonny Boy Williamson II)
The Celebrated Walkin' Blues (arr. Taj Mahal)

synopsis: Taj Mahal came out of the same Los Angeles folk scene that produced Ry Cooder, but where his peers treated the blues as something to study, he treated it as a living music full of joy. This debut album presents him as a scholar and a partyer at once, mixing Mississippi Delta songs with Caribbean rhythms, ragtime and even a calypso-flavored original, all delivered with his huge, warm voice and virtuoso guitar and banjo playing. The album's freewheeling sense of fun was a rebuke to the solemnity of the folk revival, and it helped open the door for the broader exploration of African American roots music that followed. It made Taj Mahal a star and set the template for a career of joyful genre-mixing.

name: The Bill Broonzy Story
teaser: Big Bill Broonzy 1957 — recorded over two days in Chicago, a few months before Broonzy's death from throat cancer. The album is just Broonzy's voice and acoustic guitar, interspersed with stories about learning guitar from an uncle who made him play for food as a child. Broonzy was one of the crucial links between pre-war country blues and post-war Chicago blues.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Black, Brown, and White' — a protest song about racial discrimination written in 1947, when recording it was professionally dangerous. Broonzy's guitar accompanies his voice like a second conversation partner. He tells a story about being asked to play at a club that wouldn't serve him. Then he plays the song.

tracks.title: Tell Me What Kind of Man Jesus Was (Ananias)
Goin' Down the Road Feelin' Bad
I'm Gonna Move to the Outskirts of Town
In the Evenin' (When the Sun Goes Down)
Bill Bailey, Won't You Please Come Home

synopsis: Big Bill Broonzy was one of the most important figures in the history of the blues, a singer and guitarist who had recorded prolifically since the 1920s, and this album, cut over two days in Chicago in 1956, was his summing up. Working alone with his guitar, Broonzy talks his way through the history of the music he helped create, telling stories and singing the songs of his youth in the Mississippi Delta, and the record is as much a spoken memoir as a musical one. His voice, warm and weathered, and his rolling guitar style are captured with complete intimacy, and the album preserves a direct link to the earliest days of the blues. He died two years later, making this one of the last and most valuable documents of his life.

name: Father of the Delta Blues: The Complete 1965 Sessions
teaser: Son House 1965 — recorded after a 20-year absence from music, when a group of young blues enthusiasts tracked him down in Rochester, New York, where he was working as a railroad porter. House had taught Robert Johnson how to play and was considered the most intense performer in the Delta. His slide guitar sounds like metal scraping against bone.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Death Letter' — a song about receiving the news that a lover has died, played on a National resonator guitar. House's voice breaks on the word 'dead.' Then 'John the Revelator' — an a cappella spiritual where House claps his hands on the offbeats. The recording captures the sound of a 63-year-old man singing songs he learned in church as a boy.

synopsis: Son House had been one of the founding giants of the Delta blues, the man who taught Robert Johnson, but by the 1940s he had quit music for the pulpit and disappeared from view. He was rediscovered in the mid-60s by young blues enthusiasts who found him working as a railroad porter, and these sessions, recorded in 1965 when he was in his sixties, captured the full fury of his style. House's singing is a harrowing, hollering thing, and his bottleneck guitar playing, full of slide and thunder, sounds like a man wrestling with the devil, which, in his songs, he often was. The album is a vital document of a living connection to the blues' earliest era, made all the more precious by House's advanced age.

name: Too Bad Jim
teaser: R.L. Burnside 1994 — raw, droning Mississippi hill country blues recorded in a converted barn in Holly Springs by Fat Possum Records. Burnside's style uses a single chord with a droning bass string, creating a trance-like groove that sounds more like West African music than Chicago blues. He was 67 when this was recorded.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Shake 'Em On Down' — the rhythm is a single guitar riff repeated for 5 minutes while Burnside shouts encouragement to the dancers. Then 'When My First Wife Left Me' — recorded in one take with a 1970s drum machine. Burnside's grandchildren can be heard playing in the next room during the quieter passages.

tracks.title: When My First Wife Left Me

synopsis: R.L. Burnside spent most of his life playing the raw, hypnotic blues of the Mississippi hill country for local audiences, and he was in his sixties when this album, recorded in his own home, introduced him to the world. The music is built on a single droning chord, repeated for minutes at a time while Burnside chants and shouts over the top, a style closer to a trance than to the twelve-bar blues of Chicago. Producer Robert Palmer captured the sound perfectly, raw and unpolished, and the album's relentless groove made Burnside a favorite of the punk and garage rock crowd as well as blues purists. It is the definitive document of hill country blues, a music that sounds ancient and modern at once.

name: Goldberg Variations (1981 Recording)
teaser: Glenn Gould 1981 — a re-recording of the work that made him famous in 1955. The 1955 version was 38 minutes of breathtaking speed. This one is 51 minutes, with tempos so slow that individual notes hang in the air. Gould, who died a year later at 50, said the 1981 recording was the only one he could stand to listen to.

exploreAction.targetName: Goldberg Variations (1981) — Aria and first 5 variations
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the Aria — Gould plays it 40% slower than in 1955. The silence between notes is as important as the notes. Then compare variation 25, the 'black pearl' — Gould called it the saddest piece of music ever written. The aria returns at the end, identical to the opening, but now it sounds completely different.

synopsis: Glenn Gould had shocked the music world in 1955 when, at 22, he recorded Bach's Goldberg Variations with a clarity and speed that made the piece his own, and he shocked it again in 1964 when he walked away from the concert stage forever. This 1981 recording, made near the end of his life, is a completely different performance: slower, deeper, more ruminative, with Gould singing along audibly and treating the music as a private meditation rather than a display of virtuosity. He died the following year, making this the last record he ever made. Listening to the two versions side by side is like watching a brilliant young man become an old sage, and the 1981 recording is regarded as one of the great piano records of the century.

name: Maria Callas: La Divina
teaser: Maria Callas 1992 — a compilation of the Greek-American soprano who redefined opera in the 1950s by insisting that acting mattered as much as singing. Her voice wasn't conventionally beautiful — it cracked, wobbled, and sometimes failed — but no one communicated human emotion through operatic technique like Callas. Her personal life was as dramatic as her roles.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Casta Diva' from Bellini's Norma — Callas holds the opening note for 12 seconds without vibrato. Then 'Vissi d'arte' from Tosca — she sang this at her final concert in 1974. Her voice is diminished but the desperation is real: she knew her career was ending and the aria is about a woman whose entire life has been art.

tracks.title: Madama Butterfly: Act II. Un bel dì vedremo
Carmen: Act I. L'Amour est un oiseau rebelle (Habanera)
La Wally: Act I. Ebben? Ne andrò lontana
Il barbiere di Siviglia: Act I. Una voce poco fa
Samson et Dalila: Act II. Mon cœur s'ouvre à ta voix
La Traviata: Act I. Sempre libera
Roméo et Juliette: Act I. Je veux vivre dans ce rêve
La Bohème: Act I. Sì, mi chiamano Mimì
Don Giovanni: Act II. Mi tradì quell'alma ingrata
Cavalleria rusticana: Voi lo sapete, o mamma
Gianni Schicchi: O mio babbino caro
Turandot: Act II. In questa reggia
Tosca: Act II. Vissi d'arte, vissi d'amore

synopsis: Maria Callas was not just the most famous opera singer of the 20th century, she was a cultural force who changed what it meant to be a diva, and this compilation gathers highlights from across her recording career. Her voice was not conventionally beautiful, with its wide vibrato and cutting edge, but she used it with a dramatic intelligence that made every role she sang feel like a life she was living, from the tragic heroines of Bellini and Donizetti to the fierce women of Verdi and Puccini. The arias collected here, including 'Casta diva' and 'Vissi d'arte', show why audiences and conductors considered her the most compelling singing actress who ever lived. Her recordings remain the standard against which all opera singers are judged.

name: The Rite of Spring
teaser: Igor Stravinsky 1913 — the ballet that caused a riot at its Paris premiere. The dissonant chords and irregular rhythms depicting pagan sacrifice so enraged the audience that dancers couldn't hear the orchestra over the shouting. Stravinsky escaped through a backstage window. The piece is now considered the birth of musical modernism.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Augurs of Spring' — the famous chord that opens the second section repeats 128 times with shifting accents. Then 'Sacrificial Dance' — the chosen victim dances herself to death. The meter changes 47 times in the final movement. Listen for the bassoon solo at the beginning — it plays so high that the original audience thought it was a broken saxophone.

tracks.title: The Augurs of Spring: Dances of the Young Girls
Mystic Circles of the Young Girls

synopsis: Igor Stravinsky's ballet score for The Rite of Spring caused one of the most famous riots in music history at its Paris premiere in 1913, when audiences, shocked by the pounding rhythms and dissonant harmonies depicting a pagan sacrifice, began fighting in the aisles. The music broke every rule of orchestral writing, with its shifting, stamping rhythms and its depiction of primitive ritual, and it changed the course of classical music overnight. The work tells the story of a tribe that dances a young girl to death as an offering to the god of spring, and Stravinsky's score, all brutal energy and glittering color, remains as startling today as it was over a century ago. It is the most influential orchestral work of the modern era.

name: Tabula Rasa
teaser: Arvo Pärt 1984 — the album that introduced the Estonian composer's 'tintinnabuli' style to the world: two notes ringing against each other like bells. After years of silence and study of medieval chant, Pärt emerged with music so sparse that a single note can reduce listeners to tears. The title means 'blank slate' in Latin.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Fratres' — written for violin and piano, though Pärt never specified the instruments. The piece is built from a simple mathematical formula: a melody that expands and contracts over a drone. Then the title track — two violins, prepared piano, and chamber orchestra. The prepared piano has screws placed between its strings, making it sound like a ghost.

tracks.title: Cantus in Memory of Benjamin Britten

synopsis: Arvo Pärt had spent the 1960s writing modernist music in the approved Soviet style before a creative crisis led him to silence, and when he emerged in the mid-70s he had found his own voice, a style he called tintinnabuli, after the Latin for bells. This album introduced that music to the wider world, and its centerpiece, the two-movement 'Tabula Rasa' for violins and prepared piano, is one of the most haunting works of the late 20th century, a slow, tolling meditation that seems to exist outside of time. The music is built on the simplest materials, a single voice and the chiming notes of a triad, and its effect is strangely profound. It made Pärt the most performed living composer in the world.

name: Einstein on the Beach
teaser: Philip Glass 1979 — a 4-hour opera with no plot, no intermission, and no characters except Einstein (who appears as a violinist). Numbers are sung instead of words. The audience was invited to enter and leave as they pleased. Glass performed it with his own ensemble of amplified keyboards and woodwinds because no orchestra would touch it.

exploreAction.targetName: Einstein on the Beach (1979) — first hour
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Knee Play 1' — the opera opens with an actress reading numbers over an electric organ playing two chords. This continues for 3 minutes. The point isn't the words — it's the rhythm of counting. Then 'Building' — the chorus sings solfège syllables for 8 minutes while the orchestra builds the same pattern over and over. Something enormous accumulates.

tracks.title: Act II, Scene 1: Dance 1 (Field with Spaceship)
Act III, Scene 1: Prematurely Air-Conditioned Supermarket

synopsis: Philip Glass spent years developing a minimalist style of music built on slowly shifting patterns of notes, and Einstein on the Beach, made with theater director Robert Wilson, was the work that brought it to the world's attention. The opera has no plot, no intermission and runs over four hours; its scenes show Einstein, a violinist, a trial, a spaceship and a train, all rendered in Glass's pulsing, hypnotic music and Wilson's dreamlike staging. It premiered in 1976 and toured the world to audiences who had never been to an opera in their lives. This recording preserves the full work, and its relentless, ecstatic repetition remains one of the defining achievements of American music in the 20th century.

name: The Blue Notebooks
teaser: Max Richter 2004 — an album composed as a protest against the Iraq War, though you'd never guess it from the music. Fragile piano melodies, string quartets, and typewriter sounds are interspersed with Tilda Swinton reading Kafka. Richter recorded it in a small Berlin studio over 6 months. It's become one of the most-used soundtracks in film and television.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'On the Nature of Daylight' — a 6-minute string piece built on a single descending bassline. The viola enters at 2:00 and the piece never resolves. Then 'Shadow Journal' — the typewriter recording is Richter's own, from a vintage machine he found in a Berlin flea market. The album's quietness is political: Richter said he wanted to make 'a space for reflection in a world of noise.'

tracks.title: This Bitter Earth / On the Nature of Daylight

synopsis: Max Richter composed The Blue Notebooks in 2003 as a protest against the war in Iraq, and the album is full of the unease and grief of that moment, though you would not know it from the music alone, which is mostly quiet, patient and beautiful. Over sparse piano and strings, actress Tilda Swinton reads fragments from Kafka's notebooks and Czeslaw Milosz's poetry, their words of doubt and witness floating over Richter's slowly unfolding melodies. The album's title comes from Kafka, who wrote his dark thoughts in blue notebooks. It sold steadily for years and then exploded in popularity when its opening piece, 'On the Nature of Daylight', was used in films and television, becoming one of the most recognized pieces of modern classical music.

name: La Mer
teaser: Claude Debussy 1905 — three symphonic sketches of the sea, written entirely from memory because Debussy hated boats and composed them in a landlocked French village. The music doesn't describe the ocean — it becomes the ocean. Debussy called it 'three symphonic sketches' rather than a symphony because he hated the word.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'From Dawn to Noon on the Sea' — the opening harp and muted strings create the sensation of light appearing over water. Then 'Dialogue of the Wind and the Sea' — the final movement where two themes collide like waves. Debussy said his goal was to capture 'the sound of the wind and the rhythm of the waves' without literally imitating either.

tracks.title: De l'aube à midi sur la mer
Dialogue du vent et de la mer

synopsis: Claude Debussy spent years composing La Mer, three symphonic sketches of the sea, working from memory and imagination on the coast of France and, mostly, inland in Burgundy, where he had no view of the water at all. The result is not a picture of the sea but a dream of it, full of shimmering orchestral color, shifting light and the sense of vast, indifferent power. The three movements, from the dawn opening to the violent final dialogue between wind and sea, flow into one another like the waves they evoke. The premiere was poorly received, but the work quickly became recognized as one of the supreme achievements of orchestral impressionism, and it has never left the concert repertoire since.

name: Symphony No. 5 in D minor
teaser: Dmitri Shostakovich 1937 — written after Stalin's regime had publicly condemned his previous opera and his friends were being disappeared. Shostakovich subtitled it 'A Soviet Artist's Response to Just Criticism' — a phrase that might be sincere or might be bitter sarcasm. The audience at the premiere cried openly, and the applause lasted 30 minutes.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the third movement, Largo — the strings weep for 15 minutes without relief. Then the finale — the triumphant brass at the end sounds like forced celebration. Shostakovich later said the finale was 'a forced rejoicing, created under threat.' The timpani pounds the same note 252 times, like a heart that won't stop beating.

synopsis: Dmitri Shostakovich was 30 and at the height of his fame when Stalin's regime publicly condemned his opera Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk, and for two years he lived in fear of arrest. His Fifth Symphony was his attempt to win back official favor, and he subtitled it 'a Soviet artist's reply to just criticism', but the music itself is far more ambiguous than that phrase suggests. Its famous slow movement, with its long, searing string melody, and its ambiguous, march-like finale can be heard as either triumphant affirmation or bitter irony, and audiences wept at the premiere. It is the most performed symphony of the 20th century, a work whose public triumph and private anguish remain inseparable.

name: Ascension
teaser: John Coltrane 1966 — a 40-minute free-jazz collective improvisation by an 11-piece band including Pharoah Sanders, Archie Shepp, Freddie Hubbard, and McCoy Tyner. There are no solos — everyone plays simultaneously, creating a wall of sound that was unlike anything recorded before. The album exists in two takes; Coltrane preferred Take 2.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — the band enters together on a single chord and sustains it for nearly a minute before anyone moves. Then the collective improvisation begins, with 11 musicians creating independent melodic lines that somehow cohere. Pharoah Sanders's entrance at 8:00 sounds like someone screaming through a saxophone. Some critics called it noise. Coltrane called it prayer.

synopsis: John Coltrane had spent 1965 pushing his quartet to the limits of what jazz could be, and on Ascension he went further, assembling eleven musicians, including Pharoah Sanders, Archie Shepp and Freddie Hubbard, for a single collective improvisation that fills both sides of the album. The music is built on a simple sequence of chords that the ensemble returns to between waves of free playing, with each soloist given room to scream, moan and shout through their instruments. It is exhausting, ecstatic and confrontational music that divided listeners and critics on release, but it has come to be seen as one of the essential documents of free jazz, the sound of a musician pushing past every boundary he had ever known.

name: We Insist! Freedom Now Suite
teaser: Max Roach 1960 — a jazz album about the Civil Rights movement, written with lyricist Oscar Brown Jr. and featuring Abbey Lincoln's searing vocals. The album traces Black history from slavery to the sit-ins of the 1960s. The cover photo shows three Black men at a lunch counter being served by a white waiter; it was banned in several Southern states.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Triptych: Prayer / Protest / Peace' — the middle section is Abbey Lincoln screaming wordlessly for 3 minutes while Roach's drums build a storm around her. No lyrics were written for this section because Brown said words couldn't capture the emotion. Then 'Tears for Johannesburg' — written in response to the Sharpeville massacre in South Africa.

synopsis: Max Roach had been the most influential drummer in jazz since the 1940s, but in 1960 he made an album that was about something bigger than music. We Insist! was written with lyricist Oscar Brown Jr. as a direct response to the civil rights movement, and its five tracks trace the arc of Black history in America, from the sit-ins of the present to the rebellion of the past to the freedom that had not yet come. The opening 'Driva' Man' imagines the horror of the slave ship from the perspective of the enslaved, and the closing 'Tears for Johannesburg' mourns the Sharpeville massacre. Recorded with a young singer named Abbey Lincoln and an ensemble that included Booker Little, it was the first jazz album to confront racism head on, and it remains one of the most powerful political statements in the history of the music.

name: Cinq Études de Bruits
teaser: Pierre Schaeffer 1948 — the first musique concrète compositions, made entirely from recorded sounds: trains, pots, spinning tops, and a piano played 'prepared' with objects wedged between the strings. Schaeffer composed in a Paris radio studio using only turntables and a disc-cutting lathe. There was no tape yet. This is where sampling began.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Étude aux Chemins de Fer' — it's made entirely from train sounds: whistles, steam, wheels on tracks, all recorded at a Paris train depot. Then 'Étude Pathétique' — made from the sounds of saucepans, a harmonica, and a boat horn. Schaeffer locked grooves on records to create loops, the earliest form of sampling.

synopsis: Pierre Schaeffer was a radio engineer in Paris who, in 1948, began making music by recording everyday sounds and manipulating them on tape, cutting, looping and splicing them into compositions he called musique concrète. The five pieces collected here, made entirely from sounds like train whistles, saucepans and spoken voice, were the first works of electronic music ever composed, and they must have sounded like nothing on earth when they were first broadcast. The pieces are playful and strange, closer in spirit to the avant-garde art of the time than to any music that had come before. Schaeffer's experiments opened the door to all electronic music, and these primitive, charming recordings are where the whole adventure begins.

teaser: John Cage 1952 — a piece in three movements where the performer plays nothing. The 'music' is the ambient sound of the environment: coughing, rain, traffic, the HVAC system. Cage wrote it after visiting an anechoic chamber (a completely silent room) and hearing two sounds: his heartbeat and his nervous system. The lesson: silence doesn't exist.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to a live recording — the first movement is the sound of an audience realizing nothing is happening. People cough, shift in seats, whisper. The second movement: someone laughs nervously. The third movement: most have accepted it. The piece was premiered by pianist David Tudor, who closed and opened the piano lid to mark the movements.

synopsis: John Cage's 4'33" is the most famous piece of silent music ever written, a work in three movements in which the performer plays nothing at all, and the music is whatever sounds happen to fill the hall while they sit there. Cage composed it in 1952 after spending time in an anechoic chamber, where he discovered that true silence does not exist, and the piece forces the audience to listen to the coughs, whispers and traffic that surround every concert. It was greeted with outrage and confusion at its premiere, and it has provoked arguments about the nature of music ever since. Whether you hear it as a joke, a provocation or a profound meditation on listening, it changed the way we think about what music can be.

name: Discreet Music
teaser: Brian Eno 1975 — the album that launched ambient music as a concept. The 30-minute title track was created by feeding two synthesizer melodies through a tape-delay system with such long echoes that the music seemed to generate itself. Eno was bedridden after a car accident when a friend put on a harp record too quietly; Eno couldn't reach the volume knob and realized he liked music he had to strain to hear.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the two melodies enter 3 minutes apart and the delay system repeats them at slightly different intervals, creating patterns that shift without human intervention. Eno called it 'generative music' before the term existed. Then put the album on repeat at low volume while you work. The music only reveals itself when you stop paying attention.

synopsis: Brian Eno had left Roxy Music and made two albums of artful pop before a car accident left him bedridden, and during his recovery he found that he could barely turn the volume of his music up, so he began listening to it quietly and noticing how it interacted with the sounds of the room. That experience led to Discreet Music, an album of slow, generative pieces made by feeding simple melodies into tape delay systems and letting them evolve on their own. The title piece is thirty minutes of gentle, overlapping patterns that drift like clouds. Eno later wrote that this record was the beginning of ambient music as a concept, and its influence on everything from new age to electronic pop to film scores is everywhere you listen.

name: The Drift
teaser: Scott Walker 2006 — the former 1960s pop idol's final masterpiece, recorded over 5 years in a London studio. Walker used a 100-piece orchestra not for beauty but for terror: strings scrape, brass blares, percussionists punch slabs of raw meat. Songs are about Mussolini's mistress, 9/11, and Elvis's stillborn twin. Walker was 63.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Clara' — a song about Mussolini's mistress being executed, set to strings that sound like air-raid sirens. The percussionist was instructed to punch a side of raw pork to create the sound of a fist hitting flesh. Then 'Jesse' — a 6-minute song about Elvis Presley's stillborn twin brother, with Walker's voice dropping to a basso profundo that seems impossible for a 63-year-old.

synopsis: Scott Walker had been a teen idol in the 1960s, singing lush ballads with the Walker Brothers, before he retreated from pop stardom into a decades-long exploration of the darkest corners of avant-garde music. The Drift, his first album in over a decade, is the fullest expression of that journey, a set of songs that sound like nightmares set to an orchestra, full of grinding percussion, ominous brass and Walker's still-magnificent baritone singing cryptic lyrics about dictators, slaughterhouses and his own mortality. The album's centerpiece is a duet between Walker and a slowed-down recording of Elvis Presley's heartbeat. It is harrowing, unclassifiable music, made by a man who had spent his life escaping his own fame, and it is regarded as a masterpiece of the avant-garde.

name: Dolmen Music
teaser: Meredith Monk 1981 — a composition for 6 voices, cello, and percussion that sounds like it was unearthed from a prehistoric ritual. Monk invented her own vocal techniques: ululation, overtone singing, percussive breath patterns. The piece was recorded in a church in New York's Greenwich Village, using the building's 4-second natural reverb.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — a single voice keens over a drone, then other voices join, each one entering at a slightly different pitch. Monk has said she was trying to recreate the feeling of being inside a Neolithic stone circle. Then the climax at 18:00 — all six voices create a chord that sounds like it's coming from every direction at once.

tracks.title: Dolmen Music: Overture and Men's Conclave/Wa-ohs/Rain/Pine Tree Lullaby/Calls/Conclusion

synopsis: Meredith Monk spent the 1970s developing a style of music built entirely around the human voice, using extended techniques, chants, cries and wordless syllables to create music that sounds both ancient and utterly new. Dolmen Music, named for the prehistoric stone monuments, is a work for six voices, cello and percussion that evokes ritual, with the singers moaning, keening and ululating in overlapping patterns that build to a trance-like intensity. Monk described her work as 'the kind of music that existed before language', and that quality is on full display here. The record brought her work to a wider audience and established her as one of the most original composers and performers of her generation, an artist who treats the voice as a complete instrument.

name: The Well-Tuned Piano
teaser: La Monte Young 1987 — a 5-hour solo piano piece in just intonation (a tuning system with intervals that aren't equal, unlike the equal temperament of Western music). Young's piano is tuned to a system of his own invention, and the piece is improvised within that system. He only performs it a few times a decade, and it's never the same twice.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — a single chord is held for over a minute. The intervals are 'pure' in a mathematical sense, creating overtones that shimmer. The piano has been tuned for days before each performance. Young is a student of Indian classical music and conceptual art; the piece is a raga and a Rothko painting happening simultaneously.

tracks.title: The End of the First Movement
The Beginning of the Second Movement

synopsis: La Monte Young had spent two decades developing his theories of just intonation and sustained drones before he began work on this, his magnum opus, in 1964, and he kept refining it for decades. The piece is a solo piano improvisation that can run over five hours, played on a piano tuned to Young's own exacting system, in which the intervals are derived from the natural harmonic series rather than the equal temperament used in Western music. The result is a hypnotic, slowly unfolding world of sound, full of luminous overtones and microtonal shimmers that seem to hang in the air. Recordings of the work have never quite captured its live power, but this version, made in 1981, remains the essential document of one of the most radical and influential composers of the century.

name: Marcus Garvey
teaser: Burning Spear 1975 — Winston Rodney's debut, named after the Jamaican Black nationalist leader. Recorded with the Black Disciples, a band of former studio musicians from Studio One. The album's Rastafarian messaging was so potent that Island Records initially refused to release it, calling it 'too political.'.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Rodney's voice carries the weight of a sermon. The horn arrangement was written by a 21-year-old musician who'd never written for horns before. Then 'Slavery Days' — a direct address to the African diaspora: 'Do you remember the days of slavery?' The album has no guitar solos and no love songs.

tracks.title: The Invasion (W. Rodney, Carl Paisley, Fullwood)
Live Good (Marcus Rodney, Mackba Rodney, Winston Rodney)
Tradition (D. Hines, R. Willington, W. Rodney)
Jordan River (W. Rodney, M. Lawrence, Fullwood)
Red, Gold & Green (A. Folkes, W. Rodney, Fullwood)
Resting Place (W. Rodney) — 3:10 (not on original Jamaican LP release)

synopsis: Burning Spear's Winston Rodney named his group after the Jamaican national hero Marcus Garvey, and this debut album is a full statement of the Rastafarian consciousness that Garvey inspired. Rodney's voice, a deep, keening tenor, sings songs of Black liberation, African return and spiritual awakening over roots reggae rhythms produced by Jack Ruby, with harmonies from Rupert Willington and Delroy Hines. The title track, an imagining of Garvey's voice calling his people home, became an anthem, and the album's serious, militant tone set Burning Spear apart from the more commercial reggae of the time. It is a cornerstone of roots reggae, the sound of a movement as much as a band.

name: Funky Kingston
teaser: Toots and the Maytals 1973 — the album where Frederick 'Toots' Hibbert fused reggae with Memphis soul, recording partly in Kingston and partly in Muscle Shoals, Alabama. The title track was a response to critics who said reggae couldn't be funky. The album contains 'Pressure Drop,' one of the most-covered reggae songs of all time.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Pressure Drop' — Toots' voice sounds like Otis Redding transported to Kingston. The song is about karma catching up with you. Then the title track — a cover of an Isaac Hayes-style funk song that the Maytals transformed into a reggae anthem. The Muscle Shoals horns were recorded separately and flown to Jamaica.

tracks.title: Daddy's Home (James Sheppard, Clarence Bassett, Charles Baskerville)

synopsis: Toots Hibbert had been a star in Jamaica since the early 60s, and his band the Maytals had helped invent ska and rocksteady, but this album, recorded after he got out of prison on a marijuana charge, found him at the peak of his powers. The record is a joyful fusion of reggae, soul and gospel, led by Hibbert's enormous voice, one of the greatest in the history of Jamaican music, capable of shouting, crooning and testifying in the same song. The title track became a worldwide hit after it appeared in the film The Harder They Come, and the album's version of 'Pressure Drop' and the gospel-flavored 'Oh Carolina' showed the range of the Maytals' sound. It is the essential document of early reggae at its most vital.

name: The Harder They Come (Soundtrack)
teaser: Various Artists 1972 — the soundtrack to the film that introduced reggae to the world. Starring Jimmy Cliff as a country boy turned outlaw, the movie and its soundtrack brought Jamaican music to international audiences for the first time. Every major early reggae artist appears: Cliff, Toots and the Maytals, Desmond Dekker, the Melodians.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Jimmy Cliff wrote it in 20 minutes after watching a rough cut of the film. Then 'Many Rivers to Cross' — Cliff was 24 when he recorded it, a gospel-influenced ballad about exhaustion and perseverance. The organ was played by a church musician who had never been in a recording studio before.

synopsis: The film The Harder They Come told the story of a Jamaican outlaw and introduced reggae to the world, and its soundtrack did as much as the movie to spread the music. The album gathers some of the greatest songs in the history of Jamaican music, including Jimmy Cliff's desperate title track and 'Many Rivers to Cross', the Maytals' 'Pressure Drop', Desmond Dekker's '007' and Toots Hibbert's 'Sweet and Dandy'. Cliff, who starred in the film, dominates the set, but the record is really a survey of everything Jamaican music had achieved by 1972, from ska to rocksteady to early roots reggae. It sold millions worldwide and remains the best-selling reggae album of all time, the doorway through which most of the world first heard the music.

name: Two Sevens Clash
teaser: Culture 1977 — named after a prophecy by Marcus Garvey that chaos would erupt on July 7, 1977 (when the sevens clashed). The album was so eagerly anticipated in Jamaica that stores sold out within hours. Joseph Hill's voice is a preacher's instrument. The prophecy didn't come true, but the album predicted the punk-reggae crossover that followed.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Hill sings 'Two sevens clash / And I don't know what's gonna happen to the human race' over a one-drop rhythm that never varies. Then 'Natty Dread Taking Over' — a song of Rastafarian empowerment released when dreadlocks were still illegal in parts of the Caribbean. The album was recorded in 3 days.

tracks.title: Get Ready to Ride the Lion to Zion

synopsis: Culture, a harmony trio led by the great Joseph Hill, named this album after a prophecy attributed to Marcus Garvey that a great reckoning would come on July 7, 1977, when the sevens clashed. The album's title track, released in advance of that date, became one of the biggest hits in Jamaican history, a song of dread and hope that spoke to the millennial mood of the time. The rest of the record is nearly as strong, with Hill's soaring tenor and the group's sweet harmonies riding over roots rhythms produced by Joe Gibbs. It is regarded as one of the greatest roots reggae albums ever made, a record that captures both the spiritual depth and the political urgency of the music at its peak.

name: Scientist Rids the World of the Evil Curse of the Vampires
teaser: Scientist 1981 — a dub album with the best title in recorded music history. Scientist (born Hopeton Brown) was King Tubby's teenage protégé, and at 21 he created this album in a single overnight session at Channel One studio. The album's comic-horror concept was a ploy to sell records, but the dub techniques are jaw-dropping.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Voodoo Curse' — a bassline drops out mid-phrase and returns 4 bars later, as if the mixing board is possessed. Then 'Dance of the Vampires' — Scientist feeds the drums through a phaser pedal and the horns through a spring reverb so deep the notes seem to come from the next room. Every track was mixed in real time with no automation.

synopsis: Scientist, born Hopeton Brown, was the teenage engineer at King Tubby's legendary Kingston studio who learned to treat the mixing board as a musical instrument, and this 1981 album is his masterpiece. The record is a set of dub versions of rhythms played by the Roots Radics, Jamaica's hottest session band, remixed by Scientist into a spooky, spacious soundscape full of echo, reverb and sudden drops into silence. The title, with its comic horror movie imagery, matches the music's unsettling atmosphere: these are reggae songs taken apart and reassembled as ghost music.
