teaser: 2011 The Beastie Boys' final album: 'Make Some Noise', 'Too Many Rappers', and 'Don't Play No Game That I Can't Win' are playful, funky, and defiant. The album was released while Adam Yauch battled cancer. It is a fitting farewell.

exploreAction.targetName: Hot Sauce Committee Part Two (2011) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the energy — the album sounds like three friends having fun. 'Make Some Noise' has a star-studded video.

tracks.title: Don't Play No Game That I Can't Win
Here's a Little Something for Ya

synopsis: The Beastie Boys had spent the 2000s making increasingly political records, and this eighth and final album, released in 2011 after a four-year wait, was a return to pure fun. The record's songs, from the opener 'Make Some Noise', with its star-studded video, to 'Too Many Rappers', a collaboration with Nas, showed the trio at their most playful, and its blend of old-school rap and punk energy recalled their early work. It was released three years before Adam Yauch's death from cancer, making it their last album, and its joyful, life-affirming mood has taken on an elegiac quality. It is a fitting farewell from one of the most beloved groups in hip-hop.

name: License to Ill
teaser: 1986 The Beastie Boys' debut made rap a party: 'Fight for Your Right', 'No Sleep till Brooklyn', and 'Brass Monkey' are bratty, loud, and catchy. The album was the first rap LP to top the Billboard chart. It sold 10 million copies.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — Rick Rubin's beats are minimal and huge. 'Fight for Your Right' became an anthem of teenage rebellion.

synopsis: The Beastie Boys had spent their early career as a punk band before turning to rap, and this debut album, released in 1986, was the record that made them stars. The album is a party record, full of the juvenile humor and heavy beats that defined their early persona, and its centerpiece, 'Fight for Your Right', with its video of a trashed hotel room, became an anthem of teenage rebellion. The record sold over ten million copies, making it the best-selling rap album of the 80s, and its success opened the door for rap's commercial explosion. The band later disowned it, embarrassed by its frat-boy excess, but its influence is undeniable. It is the sound of a revolution made fun.

name: The Blue Album
teaser: 1994 Weezer's debut made nerd-rock mainstream: 'Buddy Holly', 'Undone (The Sweater Song)', and 'Say It Ain't So' are power-pop perfection. The album's video for 'Buddy Holly' spliced the band into Happy Days. It sold 3 million copies and launched Rivers Cuomo's career.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — Ric Ocasek of the Cars produced the album's clean, punchy sound. 'Say It Ain't So' is a dark song about family.

tracks.title: The World Has Turned and Left Me Here

synopsis: Weezer had spent their early years as the cult favorites of the Los Angeles punk scene, and this debut album, released in 1994, was their transformation into stars. The record's songs are built on Rivers Cuomo's gift for writing melodies that stick in your head for days, and its blend of power pop, punk and the geeky, self-deprecating lyrics that would define the band made it an instant classic. 'Buddy Holly', 'Undone (The Sweater Song)' and 'Say It Ain't So' became hits, and the album sold over three million copies. It made nerd-rock mainstream and inspired a generation of bands who had never seen themselves in rock before. It is one of the most beloved debut albums of the decade.

name: Pinkerton
teaser: 1996 Weezer's second album was a commercial flop that became a cult classic: 'El Scorcho', 'Pink Triangle', and 'Across the Sea' are raw, confessional, and awkward. The album's honesty alienated fans at the time. It is now considered a masterpiece.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the rawness — the album was recorded quickly with a heavier sound. 'El Scorcho' is about a crush on someone with different taste.

synopsis: Weezer had spent their debut album becoming the most beloved new band in alternative rock, and this follow-up, written by Rivers Cuomo while he was studying at Harvard, was a deliberate departure. The album is darker, rawer and more personal than its predecessor, full of songs about alienation, obsession and Cuomo's complicated feelings about his fans, and its title, a reference to the opera Madama Butterfly, captured its mood of doomed longing. It was a commercial disappointment, with fans expecting more of the same, and critics savaged it, but its reputation has grown enormously, and it is now regarded as one of the most influential records of the decade. It is the sound of a band that refused to repeat itself.

name: Maladroit
teaser: 2002 Weezer's fourth album is their heaviest: 'Dope Nose', 'Keep Fishin'', and 'Slob' are punchy and immediate. The album was recorded in a month with input from fans. It reached number three on the Billboard chart.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitars — the album's metal riffs are a departure from their pop sound. 'Keep Fishin'' has a Muppets music video.

synopsis: Weezer had spent their third album making a stripped-back record that confused their fans, and this fourth album, released in 2002, was a return to the heavy guitars and power pop that had made them famous. The record was written and recorded quickly, with Cuomo embracing a more spontaneous approach, and its songs, from the opener 'American Gigolo' to 'Dope Nose' and 'Keep Fishin'', are among the heaviest and most direct of the band's career. The album was a modest hit, and its title, a word for clumsiness, captured its loose, unpolished energy. It is a fan favorite, the sound of a band having fun after years of internal tension.

name: Make Believe
teaser: 2005 Weezer's fifth album is their most polished: 'Beverly Hills', 'Perfect Situation', and 'This Is Such a Pity' are radio-ready pop-rock. The album was their first platinum release since Pinkerton. 'Beverly Hills' became their biggest hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — Rick Rubin produced the album's clean sound. 'Beverly Hills' was a response to their celebrity status.

synopsis: Weezer had spent the early 2000s making increasingly inconsistent records, and this fifth album, released in 2005, was their most polished and commercially successful in years. The record's lead single, 'Beverly Hills', with its ironic take on celebrity, became their first top ten hit in a decade, and 'Perfect Situation' and the Rick Rubin-produced 'We Are All on Drugs' continued the run. The album's glossy production and pop-friendly sound divided fans who preferred the band's rawer work, but it was a commercial success, and its title, a phrase Cuomo's therapist had used, hinted at the self-examination beneath the surface. It is the sound of a band trying to win back the mainstream.

name: The Red Album
teaser: 2008 Weezer's sixth album features all four members singing lead: 'Pork and Beans', 'Troublemaker', and 'The Greatest Man That Ever Lived' are eclectic and ambitious. The album was a return to their experimental streak. 'Pork and Beans' has a famous internet video.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the variety — the album spans power pop, metal, and ballads. 'Pork and Beans' references dozens of viral videos.

synopsis: Weezer had spent their career as the vision of Rivers Cuomo, and this sixth album was a deliberate experiment: for the first time, all four members sang lead, and each brought in his own songs. The result is the most varied record of the band's career, full of power pop, folk, metal and even a collaboration with Lil Wayne, and its highlights, from the opener 'Troublemaker' to the gorgeous ballad 'Heart Songs' and the epic 'The Angel and the One', show a band willing to try anything. The record was a hit, and its title, a reference to the band's first album cover, signaled a return to their roots. It is a sprawling, uneven, endlessly interesting record.

name: Raditude
teaser: 2009 Weezer's seventh album is their most pop-oriented: '(If You're Wondering If I Want You to) I Want You to', 'Can't Stop Partying', and 'Memories' are glossy and catchy. The album was co-written with outside hitmakers. It divided fans.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the pop — the album was a deliberate attempt at radio hits. 'Can't Stop Partying' features Lil Wayne.

tracks.title: (If You're Wondering If I Want You To) I Want You To
I Don't Want to Let You Go

synopsis: Weezer had spent the 2000s making increasingly serious records, and this seventh album, released in 2009, was a deliberate turn toward pure pop. The record was made with producer Dr. Luke, the hitmaker behind some of the biggest pop songs of the decade, and its songs, from the opener '(If You're Wondering If I Want You To) I Want You To' to the bizarre 'In the Mall', are the most overtly commercial of the band's career. The album's centerpiece, 'Can't Stop Partying', a Lil Wayne collaboration that Cuomo later disowned, became infamous, and the record divided fans who saw it as a sellout. It is a strange, fascinating artifact of a band trying to stay relevant in a changing pop landscape.

name: Hurley
teaser: 2010 Weezer's eighth album is a back-to-basics record: 'Memories', 'Ruling Me', and 'Unspoken' are simple, punchy rock. The album's cover features actor Jorge Garcia of Lost. It was a modest success after the pop experiments.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the simplicity — the album was recorded quickly with a rock band feel. 'Memories' is about looking back at the band's past.

synopsis: Weezer had spent their previous album chasing pop trends, and this eighth record, released in 2010, was a return to the band's guitar-driven roots. The album is named for the friend of the band's manager who inspired its cover, and its songs, from the nostalgic 'Memories' to 'Ruling Me' and 'Trainwrecks', are among the most straightforward rock songs the band had written in years. The record was made quickly and cheaply, with the band playing live in the studio, and its lack of polish was the point. It was a modest success and is regarded as a return to form by many fans. It is the sound of a band remembering what made them great.

name: Everything Will Be Alright in the End
teaser: 2014 Weezer's ninth album was a return to their classic sound: 'Back to the Shack', 'Da Vinci', and 'The British Are Coming' are power-pop anthems. The album was produced by Ric Ocasek, who made their debut. It is considered their best modern record.

exploreAction.targetName: Everything Will Be Alright in the End (2014) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — Ocasek's return gave the album the sound of their debut. 'Back to the Shack' is an apology to fans.

tracks.title: I've Had It Up to Here
The Futurescope Trilogy" *I. "The Wasteland" *II. "Anonymous" *III. "Return to Ithaka

synopsis: Weezer had spent years making increasingly inconsistent records, and this ninth album, released in 2014, was a deliberate attempt to return to the sound that had made them famous. The record is structured as a concept album about love and memory, and its first half, full of the power pop and self-deprecating lyrics of their early work, is among the best music they had made in a decade. 'Back to the Shack', 'Da Vinci' and 'Cleopatra' showed the band at its most confident, and the album was hailed as their best in years. It is the sound of a band reclaiming its identity, and it remains the high point of their later career.

name: Pacific Daydream
teaser: 2017 Weezer's tenth album is their most pop: 'Feels Like Summer', 'Mexican Fender', and 'Beach Boys' blend surf pop with modern production. The album was a deliberate radio move. It divided their core fans.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the surf pop — the album was inspired by California summer music. 'Feels Like Summer' was a moderate radio hit.

synopsis: Weezer had spent their previous album returning to their classic sound, and this tenth record, released in 2017, was a sharp turn into pure pop. The album was inspired by the band's desire to write songs that could compete with the pop hits of the moment, and its sound, full of glossy production and upbeat melodies, was a departure from their guitar-driven work. 'Feels Like Summer', 'Mexican Fiesta' and 'Happy Hour' showed the new direction, and the record's title, a reference to the California coast, captured its sunny mood. It divided fans who preferred the band's rock side, but its pop experiments were a commercial success. It is the sound of a band chasing the charts.

name: Van Weezer
teaser: 2021 Weezer's album of arena rock: 'The End of the Game', 'Hero', and 'Beginning of the End' are anthemic guitar rock in the style of Van Halen. The album was delayed by the pandemic. It is their heaviest modern work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar solos — the album was designed as a tribute to 80s arena rock. 'Hero' was used in a Bill & Ted film.

synopsis: Weezer had spent the late 2010s making pop records, and this twelfth album, released in 2021, was a return to the arena rock of their youth. The record was originally planned as a companion to their Hella Mega Tour with Green Day and Fall Out Boy, and its songs, from the opener 'The End of the Game' to 'Hero' and 'All My Favorite Songs', are full of the big guitars and huge choruses of classic rock. The album's title, a play on the band's name and the Van Halen album, captured its debt to the arena rockers of the 80s. It was a fan favorite, and its straightforward rock and roll was a relief after years of experimentation.

name: OK Human
teaser: 2021 Weezer's orchestral album: 'All My Favorite Songs', 'Grapes of Wrath', and 'Playing My Piano' pair power pop with a full orchestra. The album was recorded with strings and a choir. It is their most unusual work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the strings — the album was recorded entirely with a live orchestra. 'All My Favorite Songs' is about trying to stay positive.

synopsis: Weezer had spent 2021 releasing two albums, and if Van Weezer was their arena rock record, this companion release was its opposite: a lush, orchestral album recorded with a full string section. The record was inspired by Cuomo's love of classical music, and its songs, from the opener 'All My Favorite Songs' to 'Grapes of Wrath' and 'Aloo Gobi', are built on strings, horns and the kind of baroque arrangements that had always lurked beneath the band's power pop. It was hailed as one of their most interesting records in years, and its melancholy, introspective mood made it a cult favorite. It is the sound of a pop band stretching its wings.

name: Relayer
teaser: 1974 Yes's seventh album replaced Rick Wakeman with Swiss keyboardist Patrick Moraz: 'The Gates of Delirium' is a 22-minute epic about war, and 'Sound Chaser' and 'To Be Over' complete the trio of long pieces. The album's jazz-fusion textures made it their most adventurous work. It reached number five in the UK.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Gates of Delirium' — the battle section builds to chaos before resolving into a peaceful coda. Moraz's keyboards give the album a distinct voice.

synopsis: Yes had spent their early 70s making increasingly ambitious music, and this seventh album was made under enormous pressure, with the band trying to follow their epic double album Tales from Topographic Oceans. The record was made after keyboardist Rick Wakeman left the band, replaced by the Swiss musician Patrick Moraz, and its centerpiece, 'The Gates of Delirium', a twenty-minute suite inspired by Tolstoy's War and Peace, is one of the most powerful things the band ever recorded. The album also contains the fan favorite 'Sound Chaser' and the beautiful 'To Be Over'. It is a difficult, demanding record, but its best moments are extraordinary.

name: Tales from Topographic Oceans
teaser: 1973 Yes's double album of four side-long suites: 'The Revealing Science of God', 'The Remembering', 'The Ancient', and 'Ritual' are dense, mystical, and controversial. The band's ambition divided critics and fans. It reached number one in the UK.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the themes — each suite explores a text from Indian scripture. The album rewards patient, full-length listens.

tracks.title: The Revealing Science of God (Dance of the Dawn)

synopsis: Yes had spent their early 70s making increasingly ambitious albums, and this sixth record, a double album of four side-long suites, was the summit of their ambition. The album's concept, inspired by the ancient Indian text the Shastric scriptures, divided the band, with Rick Wakeman, who quit during the sessions, dismissing it as pretentious, and its four long pieces are among the most demanding music ever released by a major rock band. 'The Revealing Science of God' and 'Ritual' are the highlights, full of the band's trademark virtuosity and Jon Anderson's soaring vocals. It topped the charts in Britain, but its reputation has never recovered from the critical backlash. It is a monument to prog rock's excess, for better or worse.

name: Going for the One
teaser: 1977 Yes's return to shorter songs and Rick Wakeman: 'Going for the One', 'Wonderous Stories', and 'Awaken' blend pop accessibility with prog ambition. The album was recorded in Switzerland. 'Awaken' is considered one of their greatest pieces.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Awaken' — the 15-minute closer weaves organ, choir, and guitar into a cathedral of sound. The album marked their commercial comeback.

synopsis: Yes had spent their mid-70s making increasingly long and complex records, and this eighth album, released in 1977, was a return to shorter songs and a more direct sound. The record was made after the return of Rick Wakeman, and its title track, a soaring anthem about spiritual aspiration, became one of the band's most beloved songs. 'Wonderous Stories', 'Awaken' and the beautiful 'Parallels' completed a record of unusual warmth and accessibility, and the album was a commercial success, reaching number one in Britain. It is the sound of a band that had stopped trying to be the most complex group in rock and started trying to be the best.

name: Tormato
teaser: 1978 Yes's ninth album divided the band: 'Don't Kill the Whale', 'Madrigal', and 'Release, Release' are lighter and poppier. The album's production was controversial. It was the last with the classic lineup until 1983.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the blend — the album mixes prog structures with pop hooks. 'Don't Kill the Whale' became a minor hit.

tracks.title: On the Silent Wings of Freedom

synopsis: Yes had spent the late 70s making increasingly accessible records, and this ninth album, released in 1978, found the band in turmoil. The record was made during a period of intense conflict, with singer Jon Anderson and keyboardist Rick Wakeman both unhappy, and its songs, from the environmental anthem 'Don't Kill the Whale' to the Latin-tinged 'Madrigal', show a band losing its way. The album's notorious cover, a painting of tomatoes, became a symbol of the band's decline, and Anderson and Wakeman both quit after its release. It is a transitional record, made by a band that was about to fall apart, and its best moments are overshadowed by its overall aimlessness.

teaser: 1983 Yes's commercial rebirth: 'Owner of a Lonely Heart', 'Leave It', and 'It Can Happen' are synth-pop hits that reached number one. The album was recorded by a new lineup called Cinema before the Yes name returned. It sold 6 million copies.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — Trevor Horn's electronic sound defined the album. 'Owner of a Lonely Heart' became their only US number-one single.

synopsis: Yes had spent the early 80s broken up, with its members pursuing solo careers, and this tenth album, released in 1983, was their unlikely rebirth. The record was made by a new lineup built around bassist Chris Squire and guitarist Trevor Rabin, with Alan White on drums and the returning Jon Anderson on vocals, and its sound, full of the glossy production and pop hooks of the early 80s, was a complete departure from the band's prog roots. The centerpiece, 'Owner of a Lonely Heart', became their only number one single, and the album sold millions. It divided old fans who mourned the prog era, but it saved the band from extinction. It is the sound of a legend adapting to survive.

name: Big Generator
teaser: 1987 Yes's follow-up to 90125: 'Love Will Find a Way', 'Rhythm of Love', and the title track continue their pop-prog sound. The album was recorded with producer Trevor Horn again. It reached number 15 in the US.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — the album polishes the electronic sound of 90125. 'Love Will Find a Way' was a minor hit.

synopsis: Yes had spent their previous album 90125 becoming a commercial pop force, and this follow-up, recorded with the same lineup and producer Trevor Horn, tried to repeat the formula. The record's sound is even glossier than its predecessor, full of the big drums and polished production of late-80s rock, and its singles, 'Love Will Find a Way' and 'Rhythm of Love', were modest hits. The album was made during a period of internal tension, with singer Jon Anderson growing frustrated with the band's direction, and it lacks the spark of its predecessor. It sold respectably but was a commercial disappointment, and Anderson quit shortly after its release. It is the sound of a band running out of steam.

name: Union
teaser: 1991 Yes's reunion album combined two factions of the band: 'Lift Me Up', 'Saving My Heart', and 'Miracle of Life' feature eight members. The album was assembled from separate recordings. It sold a million copies and reached number 15 in the US.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the lineup — the album mixes the classic era with the 80s members. 'Lift Me Up' became a rock radio hit.

Take the Water to the Mountain

synopsis: Yes had spent the late 80s fractured into two factions, one led by guitarist Steve Howe and the other by bassist Chris Squire, and this 1991 album was an attempt to reunite them, with producer Trevor Horn overseeing a lineup that at times included eight members. The record is a strange hybrid, full of the contrasting styles of the two camps, and its best songs, including the opener 'Lift Me Up' and the gorgeous ballad 'Miracle of Life', showed that the magic could still work. The album was a commercial success, but the tour that followed was a disaster, with the two factions barely speaking, and the experiment was not repeated. It is a fascinating document of a great band trying to be one again.

name: The Ladder
teaser: 1999 Yes's return to band-based recording: 'Homeworld', 'If Only You Knew', and 'The Messenger' are melodic and organic. The album was recorded live in the studio after years of producer-driven work. It is their most cohesive album of the 90s.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the band interplay — the album was recorded in a mansion with the whole group playing together. 'Homeworld' was written for a video game.

tracks.title: It Will Be a Good Day (The River)

synopsis: Yes had spent the 90s in decline, releasing increasingly forgettable records, and this eighteenth album, released in 1999, was a return to the band-based recording that had made them great. The record was made with a stable lineup and a producer who encouraged the band to play together live in the studio, and its songs, from the opener 'Homeworld' to the epic 'The Messenger', have a warmth and spontaneity that their recent work had lacked. The album was a modest success, and its title, a reference to the band's belief in the power of music to elevate, captured its optimistic mood. It is the sound of a band remembering what it was for.

name: Magnification
teaser: 2001 Yes's album with a full orchestra: 'Magnification', 'In the Presence Of', and 'Give Love Each Day' pair the band with 60 musicians. The album was a response to losing their keyboardist. It is their most orchestral work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the orchestra — the strings and brass replace the keyboards throughout. The album rewards a full listen.

tracks.title: In the Presence Of" / I. "Deeper" / II. "Death of Ego" / III. "True Beginner" / IV. "Turn Around and Remember

synopsis: Yes had spent the late 90s rebuilding their reputation, and this nineteenth album, released in 2001, was their most ambitious in years, recorded with a full symphony orchestra. The band wrote the songs with the orchestra in mind, and the arrangements, full of strings and brass, gave their music a grandeur that their synthesizers could never match, from the opener 'Magnification' to the epic 'In the Presence Of'. The record was made with singer Jon Anderson on fine form, and its blend of prog rock and classical music was a return to the band's roots. It was a critical success, and its title captured its sense of scale. It is the sound of a legend thinking big.

name: Fly from Here
teaser: 2011 Yes's album produced by Trevor Horn: 'Fly from Here', 'The Man You Always Wanted Me to Be', and 'Hour of Need' blend classic and modern Yes sounds. The title suite was written with Horn in the 80s. It is their first album with new singer Benoit David.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title suite — the 24-minute epic bookends the album. The production is clean and detailed.

synopsis: Yes had spent the 2000s in a state of constant lineup change, and this twentieth album, released in 2011, was produced by Trevor Horn, the man behind their 80s rebirth. The record's title track, a suite originally written in the early 80s and never completed, was finally finished for this album, and its blend of the band's classic prog and Horn's glossy production was a reminder of what had made them great. The album also contains 'The Man You Always Wanted Me to Be' and the beautiful ballad 'Hour of Need'. It was a modest success, and its best moments showed that the old magic could still work. It is the sound of a band honoring its past.

name: Heaven & Earth
teaser: 2014 Yes's 21st album with singer Jon Davison: 'Believe Again', 'The Game', and 'Step Beyond' are melodic and gentle. The album was their last with bassist Chris Squire before his death. It is a bittersweet farewell.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the melodies — the album is warmer than their previous work. 'The Game' has a singable chorus.

tracks.title: In a World of Our Own

synopsis: Yes had spent the early 2010s touring with a new lineup, and this twenty-first album, released in 2014, was the first with singer Jon Davison, a young American who had grown up idolizing the band. The record is a warm, melodic collection that tries to recapture the sound of the band's classic era, with Davison's voice, uncannily similar to Jon Anderson's, floating over the familiar instrumental textures. 'Believe Again' and 'The Game' showed the new lineup gelling, but the album lacked the spark of the band's best work, and it was greeted with polite indifference. It is a competent but unremarkable record, made by a band that had become a tribute act to itself.

name: In the Wake of Poseidon
teaser: 1970 King Crimson's second album continued their debut's dark prog: 'Pictures of a City', 'Cadence and Cascade', and the title track are symphonic and ominous. The album was recorded quickly after lineup changes. It reached number four in the UK.

exploreAction.targetName: In the Wake of Poseidon (1970) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the echoes of their debut — the album revisits similar structures with new twists. The title track's vocal section is haunting.

tracks.title: The Devil's Triangle (instrumental) :I. Merday Morn (3:47) :II. "Hand of Sceiron (4:01) :III. "Garden of Worm

synopsis: King Crimson had spent their debut album inventing progressive rock, and this follow-up, recorded in 1970, continued their exploration of dark, complex music. The record's centerpiece is the twenty-two minute 'The Devil's Triangle', a terrifying instrumental based on a theme from Gustav Holst's Mars, and it also contains the beautiful title track, which features Gordon Haskell's fragile vocals, and the jazz-tinged 'Pictures of a City'. The band was in turmoil, with Robert Fripp the only constant member, and the album's fragmented quality reflects that instability. It is a difficult, uneven record, but its best moments are among the most powerful in the band's catalog.

name: Lizard
teaser: 1970 King Crimson's third album is their most experimental: 'Lizard', 'Indoor Games', and 'Happy Family' blend jazz, classical, and avant-garde sounds. The album features guest vocals and a full brass section. It is their most divisive early work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the jazz — the album's brass arrangements were contributed by Keith Tippett. The title suite is a 23-minute epic about a lizard king.

synopsis: King Crimson had spent their first two albums establishing a sound of dark, complex prog, and this third record, released in 1970, was their most experimental yet. The album's centerpiece is the twenty-three minute title suite, a sprawling, shape-shifting piece that moves from delicate chamber music to thunderous rock, and it is surrounded by the jazzy 'Lady of the Dancing Water' and the avant-garde 'Indoor Games'. The band was falling apart, with only Robert Fripp remaining from the original lineup, and the album was recorded with a shifting cast of musicians, including Jon Anderson of Yes on vocals. It is a strange, fascinating record, the sound of a band in its death throes producing some of its most adventurous music.

name: Islands
teaser: 1971 King Crimson's fourth album is their most melodic: 'Islands', 'Formentera Lady', and 'Sailor's Tale' are lyrical and atmospheric. The album featured a full orchestra on the title track. It was the last with the original lineup.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the orchestral arrangement is among the most beautiful in prog. 'Sailor's Tale' features a searing guitar solo.

synopsis: King Crimson had spent their first three albums in a state of constant upheaval, and this fourth record, released in 1971, was the last with the poet Peter Sinfield as lyricist. The album is the band's most melodic, full of the pastoral beauty and gentle melancholy that Sinfield's lyrics inspired, and its title track, with its wordless vocalise and Mellotron washes, is one of the most beautiful pieces in their catalog. 'Formentera Lady' and the epic closing track 'The Sailor's Tale' showed the band's range, and the record's overall mood of island isolation, inspired by the band's time in the Balearic islands, gives it a unique atmosphere. It is the sound of a band finding a strange, fragile peace before the storm.

name: Larks' Tongues in Aspic
teaser: 1973 King Crimson's fifth album reinvented the band: 'Larks' Tongues in Aspic, Part One', 'Exiles', and 'The Talking Drum' are dark, percussive, and angular. The new lineup included violinist David Cross. It is the beginning of their heaviest era.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the percussion — drummer Bill Bruford and percussionist Jamie Muir create a unique rhythmic world. The title piece is a masterpiece of tension.

tracks.title: Larks' Tongues in Aspic, Part One
Larks' Tongues in Aspic, Part Two

synopsis: King Crimson had spent the early 70s in a state of constant change, and this fifth album, released in 1973, marked a complete reinvention. The new lineup, featuring violinist David Cross, bassist John Wetton and drummer Bill Bruford, was louder and more aggressive than anything the band had done, and the album's title track, an eighteen-minute suite built on violent, angular riffs, became the template for their new sound. 'Easy Money', 'The Talking Drum' and the closing 'Larks' Tongues in Aspic Part Two' completed a record of extraordinary power and invention. It is the album where King Crimson stopped being a prog band and became something harder, darker and more modern.

name: Starless and Bible Black
teaser: 1974 King Crimson's sixth album: 'The Great Deceiver', 'Fracture', and the title track are improvised and composed in equal measure. The album was assembled from live recordings. 'Fracture' is one of Robert Fripp's greatest compositions.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Fracture' — the 11-minute piece is a guitar tour de force. The album's improvisations reward attention.

synopsis: King Crimson had spent their fifth album reinventing themselves, and this sixth record, released in 1974, continued the new sound. The album was recorded live in the studio, and its improvisatory energy is palpable, from the theatrical 'The Great Deceiver' to the searing 'Fracture', an eleven-minute instrumental that is one of the most demanding pieces in the band's catalog. The title track, an eerie improvisation named for a Mark Twain phrase, shows the band at its most atmospheric, and the album's overall mood of darkness and dread reflected the troubled state of the world. It is a difficult, rewarding record, the sound of a band at the peak of its power and on the verge of collapse.

name: Discipline
teaser: 1981 King Crimson's return after seven years: 'Frame by Frame', 'Thela Hun Ginjeet', and 'Discipline' are built on interlocking guitar patterns. The new lineup with Adrian Belew and Tony Levin created a totally new sound. It is the beginning of their 80s era.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitars — Fripp and Belew weave intricate counterpoint throughout. 'Thela Hun Ginjeet' uses recorded street sounds in its chorus.

synopsis: King Crimson had broken up in 1974, and this seventh album, released in 1981 after a seven-year silence, was Robert Fripp's unlikely rebirth of the band. The new lineup, featuring guitarist Adrian Belew, bassist Tony Levin and drummer Bill Bruford, played a radically new kind of music, built on interlocking guitar patterns and the rhythmic innovations of gamelan music, and the record's opener, 'Frame by Frame', with its dizzying guitar figures, announced the new direction. 'Thela Hun Ginjeet', 'Indiscipline' and the title track showed a band that had reinvented itself completely. It is one of the most influential records of the 80s, the sound of a legend being reborn.

name: Beat
teaser: 1982 King Crimson's ninth album continues their 80s sound: 'Neal and Jack and Me', 'Heartbeat', and 'Waiting Man' are rhythmic and pop-adjacent. The album used the same guitar-bass-drum quartet. It is their most accessible 80s work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the rhythm section — Tony Levin's Chapman Stick and Bill Bruford's electronic drums define the sound. The songs are tighter than Discipline.

synopsis: King Crimson had returned in 1981 with a radically new sound, and this ninth album, released in 1982, continued the experiment. The record is dominated by the extraordinary playing of guitarist Adrian Belew, whose angular, talkative solos and surreal lyrics gave the band a new personality, and its centerpiece, 'Neal and Jack and Me', is a tribute to the band's rhythm section. 'Waiting Man', 'Sartori in Tangier' and the manic 'Requiem' showed the band's range, from delicate atmosphere to full-throttle assault. The album was recorded quickly after extensive touring, and its live energy is palpable. It is the sound of a band at the peak of its second incarnation.

name: Three of a Perfect Pair
teaser: 1984 King Crimson's tenth album completes their 80s trilogy: 'Three of a Perfect Pair', 'Model Man', and 'Sleepless' blend pop songs with instrumental experiments. The album was their last for a decade. It is the most varied of the trilogy.

exploreAction.targetName: Three of a Perfect Pair (1984) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the split — the album's first half is song-based, the second half is instrumental. 'Sleepless' features danceable electronics.

tracks.title: Nuages (That Which Passes, Passes Like Clouds)

synopsis: King Crimson had spent the early 80s reinventing themselves with a new, gamelan-inspired sound, and this tenth album, released in 1984, completed their trilogy of that era. The record is the most diverse of the three, from the mathy title track and 'Model Man' to the beautiful ballad 'Man with an Open Heart' and the atmospheric closer 'Larks' Tongues in Aspic Part III'. The band's interlocking guitar work and Tony Levin's distinctive bass playing, including his Chapman Stick, defined the sound, and the album's blend of complexity and accessibility made it a fan favorite. It was the last record of this lineup, and the band broke up again shortly after its release.

name: THRAK
teaser: 1995 King Crimson's double-trio album: 'THRAK', 'Dinosaur', and 'VROOOM' are heavy, complex, and rhythmic. The lineup featured two bassists and two drummers. The album is the sound of the band at maximum power.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the twin drummers — Bruford and Pat Mastelotto create a massive rhythmic force. The album's title track is a relentless machine.

synopsis: King Crimson had broken up in 1984, and this eleventh album, released in 1995, marked Robert Fripp's most ambitious rebirth yet: the band returned as a double trio, with two guitarists, two bassists and two drummers. The record is a thunderous, overwhelming experience, full of the layered, polyrhythmic music that only such a lineup could produce, and its centerpiece, the twenty-minute 'THRAK', is a relentless assault of sound. 'Dinosaur' and 'VROOOM' showed the band's new power, and the album's title, a word Fripp invented, captured its industrial mood. It is a demanding, exhausting record, the sound of a band doubling down on its most extreme tendencies.

name: The ConstruKction of Light
teaser: 2000 King Crimson's twelfth album is their most abrasive: 'The ConstruKction of Light', 'ProzaKc Blues', and 'FraKctured' are dense and dissonant. The album divided fans. It is their most experimental work of the modern era.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the complexity — the album's rhythms and harmonies are among the most intricate in rock. It rewards repeated listens.

synopsis: King Crimson had spent the late 90s touring with their double trio lineup, and this twelfth album, released in 2000, was their most abrasive studio record yet. The band had been reduced to a quartet, but the music was no less intense, built on the fractal, stop-start patterns that guitarist Adrian Belew and Robert Fripp had perfected, and the title track's crushing riffs were among the heaviest things the band had ever recorded. The album's second half, which includes the ambient 'ProzaKc Blues' and the terrifying 'Larks' Tongues in Aspic Part IV', is among the strangest music in their catalog. It is a difficult, alienating record, but its uncompromising vision has won it a devoted following.

name: The Power to Believe
teaser: 2003 King Crimson's thirteenth and final studio album: 'The Power to Believe', 'Level Five', and 'Happy with What You Have to Be Happy With' return to their heavy sound. The album features spoken samples and dense riffing. It is a fitting finale.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the themes — the album's lyrics and samples explore faith and doubt. 'Level Five' is a ferocious instrumental.

tracks.title: The Power to Believe I: A Cappella
Happy with What You Have to Be Happy With
The Power to Believe IV: Coda

synopsis: King Crimson had spent the early 2000s as a quartet, and this thirteenth and final studio album, released in 2003, was the culmination of that era. The record's title, a reference to the band's belief in the healing power of music, captured its mood, and its songs, from the brutal 'The Power to Believe II' to the delicate 'Eyes Wide Open' and the epic 'Level Five', showed a band still capable of astonishing range. The album was recorded with the same lineup as its predecessor, and its blend of heavy riffs, electronic textures and Belew's surreal lyrics made it a fitting capstone. It is the last studio statement of one of the most important bands in progressive rock.

name: Aqualung
teaser: 1971 Jethro Tull's breakthrough concept album: 'Aqualung', 'Cross-Eyed Mary', and 'Locomotive Breath' are flute-driven rock songs about faith and hypocrisy. The album sold 7 million copies. It defined the band's sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the flute — Ian Anderson's playing is the album's signature. The title track's heavy riff was a departure for the band.

tracks.title: Excerpts from the Ian Anderson Interview
Life is a Long Song promotional video

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the late 60s as one of Britain's most popular blues-rock bands, and this fourth album, released in 1971, was their transformation into something entirely different. The record's centerpiece is the title track, a scathing portrait of a hypocritical religious man, and it is surrounded by songs that range from the delicate 'Mother Goose' to the folk-metal of 'Cross-Eyed Mary' and the epic 'My God'. Ian Anderson's flute, voice and theatrical stage presence defined the band, and the album's blend of folk, rock and social commentary made it a massive hit. It is the record that made Jethro Tull one of the biggest bands in the world, and it remains their best-loved work.

name: Thick as a Brick
teaser: 1972 Jethro Tull's single 44-minute song split across two sides: 'Thick as a Brick' tells a sprawling story inspired by a fictional schoolboy's epic poem. The album reached number one in the US. It is the definitive prog concept album.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the continuity — the album is one continuous piece with recurring themes. The lyrics are a parody of epic poetry.

tracks.title: Thick as a Brick, Part One
Thick as a Brick, Part Two

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent their breakthrough album Aqualung being hailed as a concept record, a label Ian Anderson dismissed, and this fifth album was his response: a single 44-minute song, split across two sides, that parodied the very idea of the concept album. The piece, which follows a boy named Gerald Bostock through a series of absurd adventures, is full of the band's trademark blend of folk, rock and classical influences, and its lyrics, dense with wordplay and satire, are among Anderson's most clever. It topped the British charts and made the band stars, and its single-song structure became legendary. It is the ultimate prog rock statement, a record that both celebrates and mocks its genre.

name: A Passion Play
teaser: 1973 Jethro Tull's follow-up concept album: 'A Passion Play' continues the single-song format with a story about a man's afterlife. The album was divisive, with critics and fans split. It reached number one in the UK.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the narrative — the album follows its protagonist through judgment and rebirth. The band defended it fiercely.

tracks.title: The Story of the Hare Who Lost His Spectacles

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent their previous album Thick as a Brick parodying the concept album, and this sixth record, released in 1973, was a genuine attempt at one. The album tells the story of a man's journey through the afterlife, from his death to his judgment, and its single continuous piece is full of the band's trademark shifts and surprises, from delicate folk passages to thunderous rock. The record was made under enormous pressure, with the band struggling to follow their masterpiece, and its reception was mixed, with critics and fans divided. It has been reassessed in recent years, and its ambition and invention are now more appreciated. It is a difficult, fascinating record, the sound of a band pushing itself to its limits.

name: War Child
teaser: 1974 Jethro Tull's album of songs written for an unmade film: 'Bungle in the Jungle', 'Skating Away on the Thin Ice of the New Day', and 'Only Solitaire' are melodic and theatrical. The album sold a million copies. It is their most accessible of the 70s.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the melodies — the album's songs are catchier than their concept epics. 'Bungle in the Jungle' became their biggest US hit.

tracks.title: Skating Away on the Thin Ice of the New Day

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the early 70s making concept albums, and this seventh record, released in 1974, was originally written as the soundtrack to an unmade film. The album's songs, from the rousing 'Bungle in the Jungle' to the delicate 'Skating Away on the Thin Ice of the New Day' and the epic 'Only Solitaire', are more varied and accessible than the band's recent work, and its blend of folk, rock and theatricality made it a commercial success. Anderson's flute and voice are in fine form, and the record's lighter, more playful mood was a relief after the heaviness of its predecessor. It is a fan favorite, the sound of a band having fun again.

name: Minstrel in the Gallery
teaser: 1975 Jethro Tull's return to harder rock: 'Minstrel in the Gallery', 'Cold Wind to Valhalla', and 'Baker St. Muse' are long, acoustic, and electric. The album was recorded on tour. It is their most personal work of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the dynamics — the album swings between delicate acoustic passages and heavy riffs. 'Baker St. Muse' is a 17-minute suite.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the early 70s making increasingly theatrical concept albums, and this eighth record, released in 1975, was a return to harder rock. The album's title track, an eleven-minute suite, is among the most powerful things the band ever recorded, and 'Cold Wind to Valhalla' and 'Black Satin Dancer' continued the darker mood. The record was made after the departure of longtime guitarist Martin Barre's predecessor, and the new lineup, featuring Barre's increasingly prominent playing, gave the music a harder edge. It was a critical and commercial success, and its blend of folk, rock and medieval imagery made it a favorite of fans. It is the sound of a band returning to its rock roots.

name: Too Old to Rock 'n' Roll: Too Young to Die!
teaser: 1976 Jethro Tull's concept album about an aging rocker: 'Too Old to Rock 'n' Roll', 'Rocks on the Road', and 'The Whistler' are bittersweet and melodic. The album was based on a comic strip. It is their most humorous work.

exploreAction.targetName: Too Old to Rock 'n' Roll: Too Young to Die! (1976) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the story — the album follows its hero from the 50s to the present. 'The Whistler' became a live favorite.

tracks.title: From a Dead Beat to an Old Greaser
Too Old to Rock 'n' Roll: Too Young to Die

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the mid-70s making increasingly serious records, and this ninth album, released in 1976, was a concept record about an aging rocker, told with the band's trademark humor and pathos. The record's title track, about a man who refuses to give up rock and roll despite his age, became one of the band's most beloved songs, and 'Salamander' and 'Taxi Grab' showed Anderson's gift for character sketches. The album's blend of rock and music hall styles, full of witty lyrics about the generation gap, made it a hit, and its themes of aging and nostalgia have only grown more resonant. It is the sound of a band contemplating its own future.

name: Songs from the Wood
teaser: 1977 Jethro Tull's folk-rock masterpiece: 'Songs from the Wood', 'The Whistler', and 'Ring Out, Solstice Bells' are warm, pastoral, and English. The album marked their turn from prog to folk. It is considered one of their best.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the harmonies — the album's vocal arrangements are the band's richest. The title track celebrates rural England.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the mid-70s making concept albums about rockers and afterlives, and this tenth record, released in 1977, found them embracing the English folk music that had always been part of their sound. The album is a celebration of the countryside, full of songs about woods, seasons and ancient customs, from the rousing title track to the beautiful 'Velvet Green' and the epic 'The Whistler'. Anderson's flute and voice are perfectly suited to the material, and the band's new keyboardist, David Palmer, added rich orchestrations. It is the band's most cohesive and beloved record of the era, the sound of a group finding its true home in the English landscape.

name: Heavy Horses
teaser: 1978 Jethro Tull's second folk-rock album: 'Heavy Horses', 'Moths', and 'Rover' continue their pastoral turn. The title track is a tribute to working horses. The album is the quieter sequel to Songs from the Wood.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the acoustic textures — the album is built on mandolin, flute, and string quartets. 'Moths' is one of their most beautiful songs.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had found a new direction with their folk-rock masterpiece Songs from the Wood, and this eleventh album, released in 1978, continued in the same vein. The record is full of songs about horses, harvests and the rhythms of rural life, from the title track's celebration of working horses to the delicate 'Moths' and the epic 'Rover'. The band, now including two keyboardists, had a fuller, richer sound, and Anderson's songs about nature and nostalgia were among his most heartfelt. The album was a commercial success and is regarded as the equal of its predecessor by many fans. It is the sound of a band at peace with itself.

name: Stormwatch
teaser: 1979 Jethro Tull's final album with the classic lineup: 'North Sea Oil', 'Orion', and 'Dun Ringill' are folk-rock songs about the sea and land. The album was recorded as the band was falling apart. It closes their folk era.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the themes — the songs are about ecology and the elements. The album rewards a full listen.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the late 70s making folk-rock records, and this twelfth album, released in 1979, was their last with the classic lineup that had made them famous. The record's songs, from the opener 'North Sea Oil' to the beautiful 'Flying Dutchman' and the elegiac 'Dun Ringill', are full of the folk and rock blend the band had perfected, but its mood is darker, reflecting the tensions that were tearing the band apart. Bassist John Glascock, dying of a heart condition, played his last sessions on the record, and Anderson's lyrics are full of anxiety about the future. It is a transitional record, the end of an era, made by a band that could feel its own ending approaching.

name: Broadsword and the Beast
teaser: 1982 Jethro Tull's synth-heavy album: 'Broadsword', 'Beastie', and 'Flying Dutchman' blend folk themes with 80s electronics. The album reached number 27 in the US. It is their most distinctive album of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — the album's synthesizers date it to the 80s but the melodies endure. 'Broadsword' is a powerful opener.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the early 80s in a state of flux, with Ian Anderson rebuilding the band after a series of departures, and this fourteenth album, released in 1982, found them embracing the synthesizers that were dominating the era's rock. The record's title track, with its martial drums and medieval imagery, and the rollicking 'Beastie' showed the new sound, and 'Flying Colours' and 'Pussy Willow' displayed Anderson's continuing gift for melody. The album was a commercial success in Europe, and its blend of the band's folk roots with modern technology was a sign of the times. It is a transitional record, caught between the band's past and its electronic future.

name: Under Wraps
teaser: 1984 Jethro Tull's electronic album: 'Lap of Luxury', 'Under Wraps', and 'Nobody's Car' use drum machines and synths almost exclusively. The album damaged Ian Anderson's voice from strained delivery. It is their most controversial work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the experiment — the album abandoned guitars and flute for electronics. It is a curiosity in their catalog.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the early 80s incorporating synthesizers into their sound, and this fifteenth album, released in 1984, took that experiment to its extreme. The record is almost entirely electronic, built on drum machines and synthesizers, with Anderson's flute and voice floating over the programmed rhythms, and its songs, from the title track to 'Lap of Luxury' and the pop-tinged 'Said She Was a Dancer', were a radical departure from everything the band had done before. The album was a commercial disaster, and the tour that followed, with Anderson unable to play guitar due to a hand injury, nearly ended the band. It is a strange, fascinating failure, the sound of a folk band losing its way in the electronic age.

name: Crest of a Knave
teaser: 1987 Jethro Tull's comeback album: 'Farm on the Freeway', 'Steel Monkey', and 'Said She Was a Dancer' are blues-rock songs that won the Grammy for Best Hard Rock/Metal Performance, beating Metallica. The album sold 3 million copies. It is their biggest hit of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the blues — the album is heavier and more straightforward than their 70s work. The Grammy controversy made it famous.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the early 80s making increasingly electronic records, and this sixteenth album, released in 1987, was their return to the hard rock that had made them famous. The record's sound, full of Martin Barre's bluesy guitar and Anderson's flute, was a deliberate reaction against the synthesizers of their recent work, and its songs, from the epic 'Farm on the Freeway' to the hit 'Steel Monkey' and the driving 'Jump Start', are among the strongest of the band's late period. It was a huge commercial success, and its surprise Grammy win over Metallica's ...And Justice for All became one of the most infamous moments in rock history.

name: Rock Island
teaser: 1989 Jethro Tull's album of cynical rock songs: 'Kissing Willie', 'Rock Island', and 'Big Riff and Mando' are bluesy and humorous. The album's cover was censored. It is a minor entry in their catalog.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar — Martin Barre's playing is the album's highlight. The songs are more straightforward than their prog work.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the late 80s making a successful comeback, and this seventeenth album, released in 1989, continued in the same hard rock vein. The record's songs, from the opener 'Kissing Willie' to the bluesy 'Rocks on the Road' and the political 'Another Christmas Song', are among the most cynical and direct of the band's career, full of Anderson's withering observations about the music industry and the state of the world. The album was recorded with a new lineup, and its sound, full of Barre's guitar and Anderson's flute, was a continuation of their recent success. It was a modest hit, and its title, a reference to the record company's island headquarters, captured its mood of disillusionment. It is a solid, unremarkable record from a band in decline.

name: Catfish Rising
teaser: 1991 Jethro Tull's blues-rock album: 'Rocks on the Road', 'Still Loving You Tonight', and 'Doctor to My Disease' return to a live band sound. The album was recorded with a smaller lineup. It is a return to basics.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the blues — the album is rooted in American blues forms. The band plays together throughout.

tracks.title: Gold-Tipped Boots, Black Jacket and Tie

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the late 80s making hard rock records, and this eighteenth album, released in 1991, found them turning toward the blues that had inspired their earliest music. The record is full of bluesy, bar-band rock, from the opener 'Rocks on the Road' to 'Still Loving You Tonight' and the title track, and its stripped-down sound was a reaction against the polish of their recent work. Anderson's harmonica playing, which he had largely abandoned, returned on several tracks, and the album's loose, live feel was a deliberate change of pace. It was a modest success and is regarded as a minor entry in their catalog.

name: Roots to Branches
teaser: 1995 Jethro Tull's world-music album: 'Roots to Branches', 'Rare and Precious Chain', and 'Another Harry's Bar' blend folk, rock, and Eastern influences. The album was their first studio work in four years. It is their most adventurous late work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the exotic scales — the album uses Indian-influenced melodies. The title track is a strong opener.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the early 90s exploring blues and hard rock, and this nineteenth album, released in 1995, found them incorporating world music influences into their sound. The record was made after Anderson's travels through Africa and India, and its songs, from the opener 'Roots to Branches' to 'Rare and Precious Chain' and the epic 'Another Harry's Bar', blend the band's folk rock with the rhythms and melodies of those traditions. Anderson's flute playing, influenced by the music he had heard on his travels, is among his most inventive, and the album's exploratory mood was a return to the band's progressive roots. It was a critical success, and it remains a favorite of fans who prefer the band's adventurous side.

name: J-Tull Dot Com
teaser: 1999 Jethro Tull's album exploring the internet age: 'Dot Com', 'Hot Mango Flush', and 'Hunt by Numbers' are folk-rock songs about technology. The album was recorded with a keyboardist. It is a modest late entry.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the themes — the album's lyrics comment on the digital age. 'Hot Mango Flush' is a playful highlight.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the 90s making increasingly eclectic records, and this twentieth album, released in 1999, found them confronting the internet age. The record's songs, from the title track to 'Hot Mango Flush' and the epic 'The Secret Language of Birds', are full of Anderson's wry observations about the digital revolution, and its blend of the band's folk rock with electronic textures and world music gave it a contemporary feel. The album was made with a stable lineup, and its title, a play on the band's name and the internet domain, captured its theme. It was a modest success and is regarded as one of the better records of the band's later period.

name: The Jethro Tull Christmas Album
teaser: 2003 Jethro Tull's holiday collection: 'Birthday Card at Christmas', 'Holly Herald', and re-recordings of 'A Christmas Song' blend carols with the band's folk-rock. The album was a surprise hit. It is a warm seasonal entry.

exploreAction.targetName: The Jethro Tull Christmas Album (2003) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the carols — the band reworks traditional tunes with flute and mandolin. The album is a fan favorite at the holidays.

tracks.title: Jack Frost and the Hooded Crow

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent decades as one of the most successful bands in rock, and this holiday collection, released in 2003, was an unlikely addition to their catalog. The record mixes traditional Christmas songs, from 'God Rest Ye Merry Gentlemen' to 'We Three Kings', with original compositions by Ian Anderson, including 'Birthday Card at Christmas' and the beautiful 'A Winter Snowscape'. The band's folk rock sound, full of flute, guitar and Anderson's wry vocals, gives the familiar carols a fresh, warm feel, and the album's blend of reverence and humor made it a seasonal favorite. It is a charming, unexpected record, the sound of a band celebrating the season in its own way.

name: The Zealot Gene
teaser: 2022 Jethro Tull's first studio album in 19 years: 'The Zealot Gene', 'Shoshana Sleeping', and 'Mine Is the Mountain' are song-based folk-rock with biblical themes. The album was written over a decade. It was a successful return.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the songcraft — the album trades epics for concise songs. 'The Zealot Gene' is a strong title track.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent nineteen years without releasing a studio album, and this twenty-second record, released in 2022, was Ian Anderson's return after a long silence. The album's title, a reference to the ancient religious texts that Anderson had been studying, captured its theme of spiritual searching, and its songs, from the title track to 'Jacob's Tale' and the epic 'Mine Is the Mountain', are full of the folk rock and biblical imagery that had defined his career. The record was made with a new generation of musicians, and Anderson's voice, older and more weathered, gives the material a new depth. It is a thoughtful, mature record, the sound of a legend reflecting on a lifetime of faith and music.

name: RökFlöte
teaser: 2023 Jethro Tull's Norse-themed album: 'Voluspo', 'Ginnungagap', and 'Hammer on Hammer' explore Norse mythology with folk rock. The album was a critical success. It is their most ambitious modern work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the themes — each song explores a Norse myth. The album's production is rich and detailed.

synopsis: Jethro Tull had spent the early 2020s returning to the studio after a long silence, and this twenty-third album, released in 2023, found Ian Anderson exploring Norse mythology. The record's songs, from the opener 'Voluspo', named for the ancient Norse poem, to 'Ginnungagap', about the void at the beginning of creation, and the epic 'Hammer on Hammer', draw on the gods, giants and sagas of the old north, and Anderson's flute and the band's folk rock give the material an appropriately ancient, elemental feel. It is a concept album in the classic Tull tradition, full of the wit and storytelling that had defined Anderson's career, and its blend of rock and folklore made it a welcome return.

name: Movement
teaser: 1981 New Order's debut continued Joy Division's sound: 'Dreams Never End', 'Truth', and 'ICB' are dark, rhythmic, and transitional. The album was recorded as the band mourned Ian Curtis. It is the bridge to their electronic era.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the transition — the album mixes post-punk guitars with early synthesizers. 'Dreams Never End' hints at their dance future.

synopsis: New Order had formed from the ashes of Joy Division after singer Ian Curtis's suicide, and this debut album, released in 1981, was their attempt to find a way forward. The record continues the cold, austere sound of Joy Division, with Bernard Sumner's sparse guitar and Peter Hook's melodic bass, but it also hints at the electronic direction that would define the band, and its centerpiece, 'Dreams Never End', and the eerie 'Truth' showed a band in transition. The album was a modest success, and its darkness reflected the grief of its makers. It is a difficult, transitional record, but it contains the seeds of everything that followed.

name: Low-Life
teaser: 1985 New Order's fifth album is their most human: 'Love Vigilantes', 'The Perfect Kiss', and 'Sub-culture' blend electronics with warmth. The album was recorded in their new studio. It is a fan favorite.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — the album was recorded at home with new equipment. 'The Perfect Kiss' became a club anthem.

synopsis: New Order had spent their first albums moving from Joy Division's legacy toward the dance music that would define them, and this fifth album, released in 1985, found the two sides of the band in perfect balance. The record's songs, from the country-tinged 'Love Vigilantes' to the anthemic 'The Perfect Kiss' and the gorgeous 'Bizarre Love Triangle', mix guitars, bass and sequencers with a warmth that their earlier work lacked, and Bernard Sumner's plain, human voice had never sounded more confident. It was a critical and commercial success, and its blend of rock and dance made it the blueprint for the next decade of alternative music. It is the album where New Order became themselves.

name: Brotherhood
teaser: 1986 New Order's album split between dance tracks and guitar songs: 'Bizarre Love Triangle', 'All Day Long', and 'Every Little Counts' balance both sides. The album reached number nine in the UK. 'Bizarre Love Triangle' is a dance classic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the split — the first half is electronic, the second half is guitar-based. 'Bizarre Love Triangle' remains their most beloved song.

tracks.title: As It Is When It Was

synopsis: New Order had spent the mid-80s as the most influential band in alternative music, and this sixth album, released in 1986, split their sound in two. The record's first side is dominated by sequencers and electronic textures, from the opener 'Paradise' and the brooding 'Weirdo' to 'As It Is When It Was', while its second side is built on guitars, with 'Broken Promise', the menacing 'Angel Dust' and the gorgeous closer 'Every Little Counts' showing the band's rock side. The brooding title track, with its tense verses and explosive chorus, became a live favorite. It was another hit, and its two-sided structure showed a band equally at home on the dance floor and in the rock club.

name: Technique
teaser: 1989 New Order's acid house album: 'Fine Time', 'Round & Round', and 'Vanishing Point' are Ibiza-influenced dance music. The album was recorded between nights out in Ibiza. It reached number one in the UK.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the acid house — the album embraces the late-80s rave sound. 'Fine Time' has a spoken-word intro over a pumping groove.

synopsis: New Order had spent the 80s as pioneers of the fusion of rock and dance music, and this seventh album, released in 1989, found them embracing the acid house movement that had taken over British clubs. The record was recorded in Ibiza, the spiritual home of the new sound, and its songs, from the opener 'Fine Time' to 'Round & Round' and the euphoric 'Vanishing Point', are full of the squelchy synths and rolling beats of acid house, while still carrying the band's trademark melodies. The album was a commercial and critical success, and its title captured its technical mastery. It is the sound of a band that had helped invent the future of dance music, arriving just in time to enjoy it.

name: Republic
teaser: 1993 New Order's electronic peak: 'Regret', 'World in Motion', and 'Ruined in a Day' are polished dance-pop. The album was their biggest commercial success in the US. It is their last album for a decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — the album was recorded in the wake of their label's bankruptcy. 'Regret' became a global hit.

synopsis: New Order had spent the late 80s at the peak of their commercial and critical success, and this eighth album, released in 1993, was their most electronic record yet. The album was recorded with producer Stephen Hague and a new keyboardist, Gillian Gilbert's return after maternity leave, and its sound, full of sequencers and drum machines, was a complete embrace of the dance music that the band had helped create. 'Regret', the album's lead single, became their biggest hit in America, and 'World in Motion', originally released for the 1990 World Cup, and 'Ruined in a Day' showed the band's range. It was a commercial success, and its title, a reference to the band's love of technology, captured its mood. It is the sound of a band fully in command of its electronic identity.

name: Get Ready
teaser: 2001 New Order's return with rock guitars: 'Crystal', '60 Miles an Hour', and 'Someone Like You' blend their dance history with a live band. The album was produced by Steve Osborne. It is their most guitar-heavy album since the 80s.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitars — the album was a deliberate return to rock. 'Crystal' is a soaring opener.

synopsis: New Order had spent the 90s making increasingly electronic records, and this ninth album, released in 2001 after a long silence, found them returning to their rock roots. The record is dominated by guitar, with Bernard Sumner and the new guitarist Phil Cunningham trading riffs, and its songs, from the opener 'Crystal' to '60 Miles an Hour' and the Billy Corgan duet 'Turn My Way', are among the heaviest and most direct of the band's career. The album was a critical and commercial success, and its title captured the mood of a band ready to start again after years of uncertainty. It is the sound of a band reintroducing itself.

name: Waiting for the Sirens' Call
teaser: 2005 New Order's album of return: 'Krafty', 'Waiting for the Sirens' Call', and 'Jetstream' are polished synth-pop. The album was their last with bassist Peter Hook. It is a bittersweet finale to their classic era.

exploreAction.targetName: Waiting for the Sirens' Call (2005) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the melodies — the album's hooks are as strong as their classics. 'Krafty' is a warm, nostalgic single.

synopsis: New Order had spent the early 2000s rebuilding their career, and this tenth album, released in 2005, continued in the rock vein of its predecessor. The record's songs, from the opener 'Krafty' and the title track to the driving 'Jetstream', show the band's familiar blend of guitars, bass and sequencers, and the dance track 'Guilt Is a Useless Emotion', with vocals by Ana Matronic of Scissor Sisters, reminded fans of their club roots. It was a modest success, and its title, taken from a short story, captured its mood of longing. It is a solid, if unremarkable, record from a band that had settled into comfortable middle age.

name: Lost Sirens
teaser: 2013 New Order's collection of outtakes from their 2005 sessions: 'I'll Stay with You', 'Hellbent', and 'Sugarcane' are polished leftovers. The album was released without Peter Hook's involvement. It is a minor but welcome entry.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the outtakes — the songs were recorded for the previous album but left off. 'Hellbent' is a danceable highlight.

synopsis: New Order had recorded enough material for their 2005 album Waiting for the Sirens' Call to fill two records, and this collection, released in 2013, gathered the leftovers. The album's eight tracks, from the opener 'I'll Stay with You' to the driving 'Hellbent' and the atmospheric title track, were recorded in the same sessions as its parent album, and they show the band in the same confident, melodic form. The release was a surprise, coming years after the band had moved on, and it was greeted as a pleasant gift for fans. It is a minor entry in their catalog, but its best moments are as good as anything on the album it was cut from.

name: Music Complete
teaser: 2015 New Order's return after a decade: 'Restless', 'Plastic', and 'Tutti Frutti' are their most electronic album since Technique. The album features guests like Iggy Pop and La Roux. It is a strong late-career statement.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — the album embraces disco and house sounds. 'Tutti Frutti' with La Roux is a highlight.

synopsis: New Order had spent a decade apart, with Bernard Sumner and Stephen Morris pursuing other projects, and this eleventh album, released in 2015, was their return. The record was made with a new lineup, including Tom Chapman on bass and the return of Gillian Gilbert, and its sound, full of the band's trademark blend of guitars, bass and sequencers, was a welcome homecoming. 'Restless', 'Plastic' and the gorgeous 'Tutti Frutti', with vocals by Elly Jackson of La Roux, showed the band hadn't lost its touch, and the album was hailed as their best in years. Its title, a phrase from a fan letter, captured its sense of completion. It is the sound of a band reuniting on its own terms.

name: Vol. 2... Hard Knock Life
teaser: 1998 Jay-Z's commercial breakthrough: 'Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)', 'Money, Cash, Hoes', and 'Can I Get A...' made him a superstar. The album sampled the musical Annie for its title track. It sold 5 million copies.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the crossover — the album balanced street credibility with pop hooks. 'Hard Knock Life' became an unlikely anthem.

synopsis: Jay-Z had spent the early 90s as a respected but commercially struggling rapper, and this album, his third, was the record that made him a star. The record's centerpiece is 'Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)', which sampled the musical Annie to create one of the most unlikely hits in rap history, and its success carried the album to number one. 'Money, Cash, Hoes' and 'Can I Get A...' with Amil and Ja Rule showed the slick, confident style that would define his career, and the album sold over five million copies. It is the record where Jay-Z stopped being a cult favorite and became the biggest rapper in the world.

name: Vol. 3... Life and Times of S. Carter
teaser: 1999 Jay-Z's fourth album: 'Big Pimpin'', 'Jigga My Nigga', and 'Things That U Do' are brash and funky. The album was a response to his legal troubles. It is a transitional work between his eras.

exploreAction.targetName: Vol. 3... Life and Times of S. Carter (1999) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production — Timbaland and Swizz Beatz contribute distinctive beats. 'Big Pimpin'' became a summer anthem.

tracks.title: Do It Again (Put Ya Hands Up)
Hova Song (Outro)" / "Jigga My Nigga" / "Girl's Best Friend

synopsis: Jay-Z had spent his previous album becoming a star, and this fourth record, released in 1999, was his attempt to consolidate his success. The record's lead single, 'Big Pimpin'', with its Timbaland production and memorable hook, became one of his biggest hits, and 'Jigga My Nigga' and 'Things That U Do' continued the run. The album was made during a period of intense label politics, with Jay-Z taking control of Def Jam, and its best songs show a rapper at the height of his confidence. It sold over three million copies, and its title, a reference to his growing empire, captured his ambitions. It is a solid, if not classic, entry in his catalog.

name: The Dynasty: Roc La Familia
teaser: 2000 Jay-Z's album credited to Roc-A-Fella Records: 'I Just Wanna Love U (Give It 2 Me)', 'The R.O.C.', and 'Change the Game' showcase his label's roster. The album was recorded in two weeks. It is a celebration of his empire.

exploreAction.targetName: The Dynasty: Roc La Familia (2000) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the label showcase — the album features Beanie Sigel, Memphis Bleek, and others. 'I Just Wanna Love U' became a hit.

tracks.title: I Just Wanna Love U (Give It 2 Me)

synopsis: Jay-Z had spent the late 90s building a commercial empire, and this fifth album, released in 2000, was credited to his label Roc-A-Fella Records rather than to Jay-Z himself, a gesture of collective ownership. The record features his labelmates, including Beanie Sigel, Memphis Bleek and Amil, alongside Jay-Z's own verses, and its centerpiece, 'I Just Wanna Love U (Give It 2 Me)', became one of his biggest hits. 'The R.O.C.' and 'This Can't Be Life' showed the label's depth, and the album sold over three million copies. It is a fascinating document of a rapper building an institution around himself, and its best songs are as good as anything in his solo catalog.

name: The Blueprint 2: The Gift & The Curse
teaser: 2002 Jay-Z's double album: 'Excuse Me Miss', '03 Bonnie & Clyde', and 'Hovi Baby' are sprawling and ambitious. The album sold 3 million copies. It is a mixed bag but contains gems.

exploreAction.targetName: The Blueprint 2: The Gift & The Curse (2002) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the range — the double album spans pop hits and dense street tracks. '03 Bonnie & Clyde' with Beyoncé was a hit.

tracks.title: A Ballad for the Fallen Soldier
What They Gonna Do, Part II

synopsis: Jay-Z had spent the early 2000s as the undisputed king of rap, and this double album, released in 2002, was his most ambitious statement yet. The record's first disc, subtitled The Gift, is full of the commercial hits that had made him famous, from 'Excuse Me Miss' to the Kanye West-produced '03 Bonnie & Clyde', a duet with his new girlfriend Beyoncé, while its second disc, The Curse, is darker and more personal. The album sold over two million copies in its first month, and its title, a reference to the double-edged nature of fame, captured its theme. It is a sprawling, uneven record, but its best moments are among the most confident of his career.

name: The Black Album
teaser: 2003 Jay-Z's 'retirement' album: '99 Problems', 'Dirt off Your Shoulder', and 'Encore' are a victory lap. Each track had a different producer, from Kanye West to Rick Rubin. It sold 4 million copies.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the production variety — every song sounds distinct. '99 Problems' with Rick Rubin is a hard-rock rap classic.

synopsis: Jay-Z had announced that this eighth album would be his last, and its title, a reference to the Beatles' famous record, signaled his intention to go out on top. The record is a showcase for his skills, full of the slick wordplay and effortless confidence that had made him the greatest rapper of his generation, from '99 Problems', with its legendary Rick Rubin production, to 'Dirt off Your Shoulder' and the emotional 'Moment of Clarity'. It debuted at number one and has sold over three million copies, and its title track, 'December 4th', tells the story of his life from birth to success. It is regarded as one of his best records, the sound of a king taking his throne and laying down his crown.

name: Kingdom Come
teaser: 2006 Jay-Z's comeback album: 'Show Me What You Got', 'Lost One', and '30 Something' address his return to rap. The album was criticized for being out of touch. It still debuted at number one.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the maturity — the album reflects on his success and age. 'Lost One' is a poignant tribute to a fallen friend.

synopsis: Jay-Z had spent three years 'retired' from rapping, and this ninth album, released in 2006, was his return. The record was made with producers including Kanye West, Just Blaze and Dr. Dre, and its sound, full of the glossy production of the mid-2000s, was a deliberate attempt to reclaim the throne he had abdicated. 'Show Me What You Got', 'Lost One' and the beautiful 'Hollywood' showed a rapper who had lost none of his skills, but the album was criticized for lacking the hunger of his best work. It was a commercial success, debuting at number one, and its best songs proved the king had not lost his touch. It is a solid, if not classic, comeback.

name: American Gangster
teaser: 2007 Jay-Z's concept album inspired by the film: 'Blue Magic', 'Roc Boys (And the Winner Is)...', and 'American Dreamin'' are cinematic street sagas. The album was produced in the spirit of 70s soul. It is his strongest work of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the concept — the album follows a drug dealer's rise and fall. The soul samples give it a vintage feel.

synopsis: Jay-Z had spent the mid-2000s as a businessman and mogul, and this tenth album, released in 2007, was inspired by the film American Gangster, which he saw as a metaphor for his own rise. The record is a concept album about the drug trade and its costs, full of the cinematic storytelling that had made him famous, from 'Blue Magic' and 'Roc Boys (And the Winner Is...)', which samples the film's score, to the elegiac 'Fallin''. It was a critical and commercial success, and its blend of street narratives and symphonic production made it his most ambitious work in years. It is the sound of a legend returning to the streets that made him.

name: Magna Carta Holy Grail
